 **ArgoCD URL** External link to the ArgoCD dashboard, plus a command to retrieve the admin password 
 **Components** Control plane, databases, caches, and DNS — each with its endpoint (copy buttons) and its own derived status

records.title: Clusters
records.heading: kubeconfig Commands

records.title: Clusters
records.heading: Pre-Installed Components
records.text:
Every cluster comes with these components installed via ArgoCD (see [GitOps & ArgoCD](/concepts/gitops-argocd)):

 Component Purpose 
 ----------- --------- 
 **ArgoCD** GitOps continuous delivery 
 **AWS Load Balancer Controller** Ingress via ALB/NLB (AWS) 
 **External DNS** Automatic DNS record sync 
 **External Secrets Operator** Cloud secrets → Kubernetes Secrets 
 **Karpenter** Just-in-time node provisioning (AWS) 
 **Metrics Server** CPU/memory metrics for HPA 
 **Storage Class** GP3 EBS / Persistent Disk / Managed Disk

records.title: Clusters
records.heading: Live Updates
records.text: The Clusters page polls every 5 seconds while the tab is focused (TanStack Query pauses the interval in the background) — the interim reconciliation cadence. When a project's default environment reaches `ACTIVE` (deploy completes), the next poll surfaces the new cluster.

records.title: Clusters
records.heading: Data Source
records.text: Cluster information comes from the DEPLOY job's `finalizeDeployment()` server action, which extracts OpenTofu outputs (cluster name, endpoint, ARN, ArgoCD URL, database/cache endpoints) and writes them to the project's component tables.

records.title: Alibaba Connector
records.text: Alibaba Connector. Keyless + account-free access via a RAM OIDC provider and AssumeRoleWithOIDC.

records.title: Alibaba Connector
records.heading: Alibaba Connector
records.text:
Connecting Alibaba registers a **cloud identity** (`cloud_identities`) that is **keyless and account-free**. Alethia's control plane is its own OIDC issuer;
you register a **RAM OIDC provider** that trusts it and a **RAM role** that trusts that provider. Alethia
assumes the role by presenting a short-lived minted assertion (STS `AssumeRoleWithOIDC`) — Alethia holds
no Alibaba account, generates no AccessKey, and stores nothing but the role ARN. See
[Security Architecture](/concepts/security).

 
**Is this safe?** You create the trust entirely in **your own** Alibaba account — Alethia holds no Alibaba
account and generates no AccessKey. It signs in with a short-lived token (≤10 min) that Alibaba STS verifies
and swaps for a ~1-hour credential. The only thing stored is the **RAM role ARN** (a public identifier).
**Revoke anytime** by deleting the role.

records.title: Alibaba Connector
records.heading: Setup
records.text:
The connect dialog gives you two equivalent options — a one-line `aliyun` command for the
**Alibaba Cloud Shell** (nothing to install), or the **OpenTofu module** for teams that manage
infrastructure as code. Both create everything in **your** Alibaba account:

records.title: Alibaba Connector
records.heading: Create the RAM OIDC provider
records.text:
A RAM OIDC provider named `alethia` trusting Alethia's issuer (`https://alethialabs.io/api/oidc`), with
client id `sts.aliyuncs.com`. The provider name is fixed — Alethia derives its ARN from your role ARN.
The provider pins the issuer's **CA certificate fingerprints** (the stable intermediate/root, not the
rotating Cloudflare edge leaf); if the issuer's cert chain ever rotates its CA, re-run the setup to refresh
them.

records.title: Alibaba Connector
records.heading: Create the RAM role
records.text:
A role whose trust policy allows `AssumeRoleWithOIDC` from that provider, scoped to Alethia's workload
identity (`oidc:sub = alethia-connector`, `oidc:aud = sts.aliyuncs.com`) — a wrong subject/audience is
rejected.

records.title: Alibaba Connector
records.heading: Attach provisioning permissions
records.text:
The setup attaches **4 enumerated custom RAM policies** — `ComputeCluster` (ACK + its transitive node-pool
ECS + API-server/Service SLB), `Network` (VPC/vSwitch/NAT/SNAT + EIP), `Data` (RDS/KVStore/OSS/Tablestore/
KMS), and `EdgeReg` (Container Registry/AliDNS/MNS) — each listing the **specific
create/read/modify/delete/tag actions** the templates issue, never a `service:*` wildcard or an admin
policy. Service-linked roles ACK/NAT need are covered by a narrow `ram:CreateServiceLinkedRole`-only policy.

records.title: Alibaba Connector
records.heading: Paste the role ARN into Alethia
records.text:
Run `tofu output` and paste `role_arn` — it looks like `acs:ram:: :role/ `. That's the
only value Alethia needs (the OIDC-provider ARN is derived from it).

records.title: Alibaba Connector
records.heading: Verification
records.text:
Alethia verifies the cloud identity **instantly, server-side** (no runner):

1. The console mints an OIDC assertion (audience `sts.aliyuncs.com`) and calls Alibaba STS
 `AssumeRoleWithOIDC` with your role + provider ARNs
2. Alibaba validates the assertion against the RAM OIDC provider and returns temporary credentials
3. A successful assume is the proof of access → `Connected` / `Disconnected`

records.title: Alibaba Connector
records.heading: What's Stored
records.text:
- The **RAM role ARN**
- The derived **RAM OIDC provider ARN** (`acs:ram:: :oidc-provider/alethia`)
- The **account id** (parsed from the role ARN)

**No credentials, ever.** Revoke access by deleting the RAM role (or the OIDC provider) in your account.

records.title: AWS Connector
records.text: AWS Connector. Keyless, issuer-direct IAM role — an IAM OIDC provider trusting the Alethia issuer, set up in AWS CloudShell or with OpenTofu.

records.title: AWS Connector
records.heading: AWS Connector
records.text:
Connecting AWS registers a **cloud identity** (`cloud_identities`) that is **keyless and issuer-direct**: your account registers an **IAM OIDC provider** that trusts
Alethia's OIDC issuer, plus an IAM role Alethia assumes via **`AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`** — no access keys, no
external id, and no trust in an Alethia AWS account. This is the same model GCP, Azure, and Alibaba use. See
[Security Architecture](/concepts/security) for the full model.

 
**Is this safe?** You create the trust entirely in **your own** AWS account — Alethia never sees a key.
It signs in with a short-lived token (≤10 min) that AWS verifies and swaps for a ~1-hour credential. The
only thing Alethia stores is the **role ARN** (a public identifier). **Revoke anytime** by deleting the
IAM role (and its OIDC provider).

records.title: AWS Connector
records.heading: Setup Methods
records.text:
Two equivalent, keyless paths — the **AWS CloudShell** script (nothing to install) or the **OpenTofu**
module. Both create the same IAM OIDC provider + `AlethiaProvisionerRole` in your account.

 
 
 

 ### Open AWS CloudShell
 Open [AWS CloudShell](https://console.aws.amazon.com/cloudshell/home) — the `aws` CLI is
 preinstalled and already authenticated. (Or run the script locally with a configured `aws` CLI.)

 ### Run the setup script
 Paste the one-liner from the connect sheet — `curl -sO …/alethia-aws-setup.sh && bash alethia-aws-setup.sh`.
 It creates the **IAM OIDC provider** for the Alethia issuer + `AlethiaProvisionerRole` (whose trust
 allows **only** `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` from that provider, pinned to audience
 `sts.amazonaws.com` and subject `alethia-connector`), attaches the five least-privilege policies, and
 prints `role_arn`. Self-hosters pass their issuer as the first argument.

 ### Copy Role ARN
 Copy the `role_arn` the script prints and paste it into the form, then click "Connect."

 
 
 
 

 ### Apply the OpenTofu module
 Download the module ("Download module" in the connect sheet) and run `tofu apply`. It creates the
 IAM OIDC provider + role that tr

records.title: AWS Connector
records.heading: Verification
records.text:
After submitting, Alethia verifies the cloud identity **instantly, server-side** (no runner):

1. The console mints a short-lived assertion and calls `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` on your role
2. Calls `sts:GetCallerIdentity` to confirm the assumed identity (proof of access)
3. Runs a small capability probe (representative reads) → the cloud identity is `Connected`, or `Degraded`
 when provisioning permissions are missing, or `Disconnected` when auth fails

If verification fails, the error message explains what went wrong (e.g., trust policy misconfiguration,
missing permissions). Existing resources (VPCs, subnets, …) are discovered separately by the
server-side [asset inventory](/console/connectors/health-and-inventory), not during this probe.

records.title: AWS Connector
records.heading: IAM Role Permissions
records.text:
What the role may *do* is independent of *who may assume it* (the OIDC trust above) — a separate axis.

**Exactly what Alethia provisions in your account** (feature-gated — a given Project uses a subset): EC2/VPC
(subnets, NAT, route tables, security groups, VPC endpoints), EKS (cluster, managed node groups, add-ons, the
IRSA OIDC provider + controller roles), RDS (Aurora), ElastiCache (Redis/Valkey), Route 53, ACM, Secrets
Manager, DynamoDB, SQS/SNS, ECR, S3, KMS envelope keys, CloudWatch Logs + Kinesis Firehose, EventBridge
(Karpenter), Application Auto Scaling, and the in-cluster controller IAM roles (external-dns, AWS Load
Balancer Controller, EBS CSI, Karpenter).

 
**Least-privilege by default — no account admin, fully action-enumerated.** The setup attaches **five scoped
policies** instead of `AdministratorAccess`: `…-ComputeNet`, `…-ComputeScale`, `…-Data`, `…-Edge` — the
data-plane, each listing the **specific `ec2:`/`eks:`/`rds:`/… actions** the templates issue (not
`service:*`; split into net/scale to fit AWS's 6144-char managed-policy limit) — plus an action-enumerated
`…-IAM` policy. The IAM policy lets the templates create the EKS/IRSA roles they need but **explicitly

records.title: AWS Connector
records.heading: What's Stored
records.text:
Only the **Role ARN** (`arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/AlethiaProvisionerRole`) is stored. No access keys,
secret keys, session tokens, or external id are ever persisted — every credential is a short-lived assertion
minted at call time.

records.title: Azure Connector
records.text: Azure Connector. Keyless Azure access — a managed identity in your own subscription, no client secrets.

records.title: Azure Connector
records.heading: Azure Connector
records.text:
Connecting Azure registers a **cloud identity** (`cloud_identities`) that is **keyless** and
**customer-side**. You create a **user-assigned managed identity** in your own subscription (a plain ARM
resource — no App Registration, no directory-admin rights) with a Federated Identity Credential that
trusts the Alethia OIDC issuer. Both the console (verification) and the runner (provisioning) authenticate
**as that identity** by presenting a short-lived OIDC assertion; Azure validates it and issues an ARM
access token. **You store no client secret**, and there is **no platform Entra app** — parity with the GCP
Workload Identity Federation model. See [Security Architecture](/concepts/security).

 
**Is this safe?** You create the identity in **your own** subscription and grant it a least-privilege role.
Alethia signs in with a short-lived token (≤10 min) that Entra ID verifies and swaps for a ~1-hour
credential. The only things stored are your **tenant, subscription, and managed-identity client id** (all
public). **Revoke anytime** by deleting the managed identity.

records.title: Azure Connector
records.heading: Setup
records.text:
The connect dialog gives you a one-line `az` command (or an OpenTofu module). It runs entirely in **your**
subscription:

records.title: Azure Connector
records.heading: Create the managed identity + federated credential
records.text:
`az identity create` provisions a user-assigned managed identity, and
`az identity federated-credential create` adds a credential trusting the Alethia issuer (subject
`alethia-connector`, audience `api://AzureADTokenExchange`). No App Registration, no secret.

records.title: Azure Connector
records.heading: Assign the least-privilege role
records.text:
The script creates and assigns the **Alethia Provisioner** custom role — scoped to exactly the services
the project templates create, with an ABAC condition that limits role-assignment writes to the single
DNS Zone Contributor role (no path to self-escalation).

records.title: Azure Connector
records.heading: Enter details in Alethia
records.text:
Paste back the three values the script prints:
- **Tenant ID** — your Entra directory ID
- **Client ID** — the managed identity's application id
- **Subscription ID** — the target Azure subscription

records.title: Azure Connector
records.heading: Verification
records.text:
Same as other providers — Alethia verifies access **instantly, server-side** (no runner):

1. The console mints an OIDC assertion for your managed identity and presents it to your tenant
2. Azure validates it against the identity's federated credential and returns an ARM access token
3. A small ARM read confirms provisioning access → `Connected` / `Degraded` / `Disconnected`

Existing VNets, subnets, and DNS zones are discovered separately by the server-side
[asset inventory](/console/connectors/health-and-inventory).

records.title: Azure Connector
records.heading: What's Stored
records.text:
- **Tenant ID**
- **Client ID** (your managed identity's application id)
- **Subscription ID**

**No client secrets, ever.** Revoke access by deleting the managed identity (or its role assignment)
in your subscription.

records.title: Chart Repositories
records.text: Chart Repositories. Connect a private Helm or OCI chart source so Alethia can scan and deploy charts it holds.

records.title: Chart Repositories
records.heading: Chart Repositories
records.text:
A **chart repository** connector stores the credential Alethia uses to read Helm charts from a private
source — an OCI registry such as GitHub Container Registry, or a classic HTTPS chart repository.

It is the sibling of a [container registry](/console/design-project/container-registry) connector, and
the difference matters: a container registry credential becomes a Kubernetes `imagePullSecret` so your
*workloads* can pull *images*. A chart repository credential becomes an ArgoCD **repository
credential**, so *Alethia* can read *charts*. Connecting one does not let your pods pull images, and
connecting the other does not let Alethia read a chart.

You only need a chart repository if your charts are private. Public charts work without any connector.

records.title: Chart Repositories
records.heading: Providers
records.text:
Connect these from **Connectors → Chart repositories**. Every provider authenticates with a username
and a token.

 Provider Registry host Credential 
 ---------- --------------- ------------ 
 **HTTPS Helm Repository** You supply the full repository URL Username · Password / token 
 **GitHub Container Registry** `ghcr.io` Username · Password / token 
 **Docker Hub** `registry-1.docker.io` Username · Access token 
 **GitLab Container Registry** `registry.gitlab.com`, or your own Username · Password / token 
 **Scaleway Container Registry** Your Scaleway host, e.g. `rg.fr-par.scw.cloud` Secret key 
 **Generic OCI Registry** You supply the host — Harbor, JFrog, or any OCI-compliant registry Username · Password / token 

 
**Amazon ECR and ECR Public are not available yet.** ECR authenticates with a token that expires after
twelve hours, so there is no stable password to store. Supporting it needs a credential that refreshes
itself inside the cluster, which is tracked separately. Charts in every other provider above work today.
 

Only the token is secret. The repository URL and registry host are stored as ordinary configuration and
appear in the project's configuration snapshot; the

records.title: Chart Repositories
records.heading: Selecting one on a project
records.text:
A connector holds a credential. To use it, add a **chart repository** to the environment on the canvas
and pick the connected provider. Adding it per environment means staging and production can read charts
from different registries.

records.title: Chart Repositories
records.heading: How Alethia matches a chart to a credential
records.text:
Alethia does not ask which credential a chart should use. It matches the chart's **host** against the
chart repositories you connected, taking the most specific match:

- An OCI chart matches by URL prefix, so a credential for `oci://ghcr.io` covers
 `oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts/payments`.
- An HTTPS chart repository matches exactly.

This is the same rule ArgoCD applies, which is what keeps one credential in play from end to end: the
same match authenticates the [safety scan](/console/design-project/bring-your-own-charts#the-safety-scan)
when you attach a chart and ArgoCD's pull when it deploys. A chart whose host matches nothing you
connected is read anonymously — correct for a public chart, and a clear authentication failure for a
private one.

The credential is delivered to the Runner out of band, when it claims the job. It is never written into
the project's configuration, the job record, or the job logs.

records.title: Chart Repositories
records.heading: Where the charts are used
records.text:
The same connector serves both kinds of chart:

- [Bring-your-own charts](/console/design-project/bring-your-own-charts) — your own packaged application.
- Marketplace add-ons, when you point one at a private mirror instead of its public chart.

records.title: Chart Repositories
records.heading: Registries on a private network
records.text:
By default the Runner refuses to pull a chart from a private or link-local address. The Runner holds
platform credentials, so an operator-supplied chart URL that resolves inside the network — or to the
cloud metadata service — would be a way to reach things it should not.

If your registry genuinely sits on an internal network (a self-hosted Harbor or JFrog on RFC1918
space), set `ALETHIA_HELM_REGISTRY_ALLOW_PRIVATE=1` on the Runner. See
[Self-hosted runner](/runner/self-hosted#environment-variables). Loopback and link-local addresses stay
blocked either way.

records.title: Chart Repositories
records.heading: Adding a provider
records.text:
The provider set is defined in the connector catalog. To add one, follow the recipe in
[Pluggable connectors](/console/connectors/pluggable#adding-a-new-provider) — a chart repository
provider supplies a repository credential rather than an OpenTofu module, so it needs no module path.

See also: [Bring Your Own Helm Charts](/console/design-project/bring-your-own-charts) ·
[Pluggable Connectors](/console/connectors/pluggable) ·
[Managing Connections](/console/connectors/managing-connections)

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.text: Cross-Account Secret Managers. Read secrets from a cloud secret manager in a different account, project, or subscription — keyless.

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.heading: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.text:
A Project's workloads sometimes need secrets that live in a **different** cloud account than the cluster — a central AWS Secrets Manager account, a shared GCP Secret Manager project, an Azure Key Vault in another subscription, or an Alibaba KMS Secrets Manager in another RAM account. The **cross-account secret manager** connectors let the cluster read those secrets **keylessly**: no access key is created, and Alethia never holds admin in the account that owns the secrets.

 Connector Reads from Auth method 
 ----------- ----------- ------------- 
 **AWS Secrets Manager (cross-account)** Secrets Manager in another AWS account `iam_role` 
 **GCP Secret Manager (cross-project)** Secret Manager in another GCP project `service_account` 
 **Azure Key Vault (cross-subscription)** Key Vault in another Azure subscription (same tenant) `service_principal` 
 **Alibaba KMS Secrets Manager (cross-account)** KMS Secrets Manager in another RAM account `ram_role`

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.heading: How it works
records.text:
Each cluster runs the [External Secrets Operator](/console/design-project/secrets). It already authenticates to the cluster's own cloud with the cluster's workload identity (IRSA on AWS, Workload Identity on GCP, workload identity on Azure, RRSA on Alibaba). A cross-account connector points that same identity at a secret manager in another account through a **trust grant the secret owner creates**:

1. **You bootstrap a least-privilege read grant** in the account that owns the secrets, using a small OpenTofu module Alethia ships. The grant trusts your cluster's identity and allows **read only**.
2. **You paste the grant's references** (a role ARN, a project id, a vault URL) into the connector. No key is stored — only references.
3. **The operator reads across the boundary.** Alethia renders an additional `ClusterSecretStore` that resolves secrets from the other account, alongside the cluster's native store.

This is the same [zero-credential model](/concepts/security) the rest of Alethia uses: the secret owner grants the least privilege, and the control plane only references it.

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.heading: Set up a cross-account connector
records.text: Each connector needs a one-time bootstrap in the account that **owns the secrets**. The OpenTofu modules live in the Alethia repository under `infra/connector/ /secrets-xacct/`, each with a README.

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.heading: AWS Secrets Manager
records.text:
Run `infra/connector/aws/secrets-xacct` in the secrets account. It creates a read-only role that trusts your cluster's external-secrets identity and grants `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` on the secrets you name. Enter the printed **Target Role ARN**, the **target account id**, and the **region** in the connector.

Name the secret ARNs you intend to share. The module has no wildcard fallback, so it refuses to apply rather than granting read on every secret in the account.

You can also set an `external_id` on the module to require an `sts:ExternalId` on the assume. If you do, enter the same value in the connector's **External ID** field: the operator sends it with the assume, and AWS rejects the read when the two disagree. This control is AWS-only — the other three clouds bind the grant to a specific principal instead, so there is nothing equivalent to set.

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.heading: GCP Secret Manager
records.text: Run `infra/connector/gcp/secrets-xacct` in the secrets project. It grants your cluster's external-secrets service account `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` on each secret you name. Enter the **target project id** in the connector.

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.heading: Azure Key Vault
records.text: Run `infra/connector/azure/secrets-xacct` in the subscription that owns the vault. It assigns your cluster's workload identity the **Key Vault Secrets User** role on the target vault. Enter the **target subscription id** and the **vault URL** in the connector.

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.heading: Alibaba KMS Secrets Manager
records.text: Run `infra/connector/alibaba/secrets-xacct` in the secrets account. It registers your cluster's OIDC issuer as a RAM OIDC provider and creates a read-only KMS role that trusts your cluster's external-secrets service account. Enter the printed **Target Role ARN** and **Target OIDC Provider ARN** in the connector.

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.heading: Keep the grant working when you rebuild a cluster
records.text:
Each grant above names your cluster's external-secrets identity. On AWS that identity has a stable
name, so a rebuild keeps working. On GCP and Azure it does not:

- **GCP** treats a recreated service account as a new identity, even with the same name. The old
 grant is left pointing at the deleted one.
- **Azure** generates a new object id for the managed identity, and the role assignment binds that
 id.

So on those two clouds, destroying and recreating a cluster breaks the cross-account read until you
re-run the bootstrap.

To avoid that, create the identity yourself once and tell the cluster template to use it:

 Cloud Variable 
 --- --- 
 GCP `external_secrets_service_account_email` 
 Azure `external_secrets_identity_name` and `external_secrets_identity_resource_group` 

The template then federates and grants against your identity instead of creating its own, and never
creates, changes or deletes it. Grant that identity access in the secrets account once, and it keeps
working across rebuilds.

Leave the variables unset to keep the default behavior, where the template owns the identity.

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.heading: What is not supported
records.text:
Two combinations are out of scope, by cloud-platform limits rather than choice:

- **Hetzner** has no cloud secret manager. Use the [HashiCorp Vault connector](/console/connectors/pluggable) for secrets on Hetzner.
- **Azure cross-tenant** is not available keyless. An Azure managed or workload identity cannot be used across tenants. The Azure connector reads across **subscriptions within one tenant**; a vault in a different tenant needs an app registration and federated credential in that tenant, which is outside this connector.

records.title: Cross-Account Secret Managers
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [Pluggable Connectors](/console/connectors/pluggable) — API-key connectors for DNS, secrets, registry, and observability.
- [Secrets](/console/design-project/secrets) — choosing a secrets provider per Project.
- [Security model](/concepts/security) — how Alethia keeps the zero-credential guarantee.

records.title: GCP Connector
records.text: GCP Connector. Workload Identity Federation setup with OIDC token exchange.

records.title: GCP Connector
records.heading: GCP Connector
records.text:
Connecting GCP registers a **cloud identity** (`cloud_identities`) that uses **Workload Identity Federation (WIF)** with **direct OIDC** — your project's WIF pool
trusts Alethia's issuer directly (no AWS hop), and Alethia federates in with a short-lived minted JWT. No
service account JSON keys are created or stored. See [Security Architecture](/concepts/security).

 
**Is this safe?** You create the trust entirely in **your own** GCP project — no service account key is
ever generated. Alethia signs in with a short-lived token (≤10 min) that GCP verifies and swaps for a
~1-hour access token. The only thing stored is the **WIF trust configuration** (no secret). **Revoke
anytime** by deleting the pool or unbinding the service account.
 

The connect sheet gives you two one-shot paths that create everything for you. When they finish, you enter
just **two values** — your **Project ID** and **Project Number** — and Alethia assembles the WIF credential
configuration for you (there is no JSON to copy). Both paths pin the same values the console mints: issuer
`https://alethialabs.io/api/oidc`, audience `alethia-gcp-wif`, subject `alethia-connector`, and the fixed
pool `alethia-pool` / provi

records.title: GCP Connector
records.heading: Verification
records.text:
Alethia verifies the cloud identity **instantly, server-side** (no runner):

1. The console presents an OIDC token to GCP's Security Token Service (Workload Identity Federation)
2. GCP validates the token against the registered issuer/subject and returns a short-lived access token
3. A small Compute read confirms provisioning access → `Connected` / `Degraded` / `Disconnected`

Existing resources (VPC networks, subnets, DNS zones) are discovered separately by the server-side
[asset inventory](/console/connectors/health-and-inventory).

records.title: GCP Connector
records.heading: Service Account Permissions
records.text:
What the service account may *do* is independent of *who may impersonate it* (the WIF trust above).

**Exactly what Alethia provisions in your project** (feature-gated — a given Project uses a subset):
Compute/VPC (networks, subnets, Cloud Router + NAT, firewall rules, Cloud Armor), GKE (cluster + node
pools), Cloud SQL, Memorystore (Redis), Cloud DNS, Artifact Registry, Secret Manager, Cloud Storage,
Firestore, Pub/Sub, and the workload-identity service accounts + bindings for in-cluster controllers.

 
**Least-privilege by default — no `roles/editor`.** The provisioner service account gets **11 predefined
roles + 5 custom roles**:

- **11 predefined roles** for services whose Google-maintained admin set is already tightly scoped and
 churns with new features (`container.admin`, `compute.networkAdmin`, `compute.securityAdmin`,
 `servicenetworking.networksAdmin`, `cloudsql.admin`, `redis.admin`, `dns.admin`, `artifactregistry.admin`,
 `secretmanager.admin`, `cloudkms.admin`, `iam.serviceAccountUser`) — hand-enumerating those buys nothing.
 `cloudkms.admin` creates the customer-managed key that encrypts Kubernetes Secrets in etcd. It grants no
 permission to *use* the key: `cryptoKe

records.title: GCP Connector
records.heading: Optional APIs you enable yourself
records.text:
Alethia cannot turn APIs on in your project. Enabling one needs
`serviceusage.services.enable`, which would let the provisioner switch on **any** API in your
project, including billable ones you did not ask for. There is no narrower version of that
permission, so Alethia does not hold it. The provisioner can only *read* whether an API is on
(`serviceusage.services.get`), which is what lets a deployment tell you a prerequisite is missing
instead of silently doing nothing.

One feature needs an API you enable once per project:

 Feature API Enable with 
 --- --- --- 
 Container registry → **Vulnerability scanning** `containerscanning.googleapis.com` `gcloud services enable containerscanning.googleapis.com --project ` 

Artifact Registry has no per-repository "on" switch for scanning — a repository can only *follow the
project default* or opt out. So the switch does nothing unless the API is enabled for the project.

If you turn the switch on without it, the deployment **stops before it changes anything** and tells
you which API to enable. Nothing is half-applied, and no repository is created claiming to be
scanned when it is not. Enable the API, then deploy again.

Leaving the switch

records.title: GCP Connector
records.heading: Password-free Cloud SQL
records.text:
Alethia can run your app against Cloud SQL with **no database password**: the pod impersonates a
Google service account through GKE Workload Identity and the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy mints a
short-lived IAM token from it.

This is **opt-in on Google Cloud**, and it needs one value from you. After running the setup, take
the `alethia-appdb` account it created and set it in Alethia as:

cloud_sql_app_service_account_email = alethia-appdb@ .iam.gserviceaccount.com

The Terraform module outputs it as `cloud_sql_app_service_account_email`; the shell script prints it
at the end. Leave it unset and your apps keep using password authentication — nothing breaks, and
turning on IAM auth without it simply warns that keyless is not wired.

records.title: GCP Connector
records.heading: Why you create this account instead of Alethia
records.text:
`roles/cloudsql.client` and `roles/cloudsql.instanceUser` can only be granted **on the whole
project**. A Cloud SQL instance does not carry its own IAM policy, so there is no way to scope those
roles to a single database instance the way Alethia scopes DNS to one zone and Secret Manager to one
secret.

Granting a project-wide role needs `resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy` — the permission that
lets a principal grant itself *anything*. Alethia deliberately does not hold it. So this one grant
is made by you, once, at setup, rather than by the provisioner on every deployment.

 
**One database identity per Google Cloud project.** Every Alethia environment in the project shares
the `alethia-appdb` account, so an app in one environment can log in to another environment's Cloud
SQL instance. What it may *do* inside a database is still scoped by the SQL grants Alethia issues
per database. If you need environments isolated at the identity level, run them in **separate Google
Cloud projects**.

records.title: GCP Connector
records.heading: How this differs from AWS and Azure
records.text:
On AWS and Azure the equivalent identity is created per environment during deployment, because both
let the role be scoped to the individual database — AWS through IRSA and RDS IAM auth, Azure through
Entra. Google Cloud's IAM model does not offer that scope for Cloud SQL, so Google Cloud is the one
provider where password-free database auth needs a setup step and shares one identity per project.

records.title: GCP Connector
records.heading: What's Stored
records.text:
- **GCP Project ID** and **Project Number**
- **WIF configuration** — assembled by the console from those two IDs: the pool + provider audience, the
 service account impersonation URL, and the token-file credential source. The provisioner service account
 is referenced by that impersonation URL; there's no separate key field.

No service account JSON keys. Access is revoked by deleting the WIF pool or unbinding the service account.

records.title: Git Providers
records.text: Git Providers. GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket OAuth integration with automatic token refresh.

records.title: Git Providers
records.heading: Git Providers
records.text: Git provider integrations enable repository access for GitOps workflows. Three providers are supported via OAuth.

records.title: Git Providers
records.heading: Supported Providers
records.text:
Provider Auth Method Token Refresh 
 ---------- ----------- --------------- 
 GitHub OAuth 2.0 Automatic via refresh token 
 GitLab OAuth 2.0 Automatic via refresh token 
 Bitbucket OAuth 2.0 Automatic via refresh token

records.title: Git Providers
records.heading: Click Connect
records.text: Click "Connect" on the provider card in the Connectors page.

records.title: Git Providers
records.heading: OAuth Authorization
records.text: You're redirected to the provider's authorization page. Grant the application access to your repositories.

records.title: Git Providers
records.heading: Callback
records.text: The provider redirects back to Alethia with an authorization code. Better Auth exchanges it for access and refresh tokens.

records.title: Git Providers
records.heading: Token Storage
records.text: Better Auth stores the provider tokens in its `account` table — one row per linked account.

records.title: Git Providers
records.heading: Token Refresh
records.text:
Git tokens have limited lifetimes. The `getValidProviderToken()` server action wraps Better Auth's `getAccessToken`, which handles refresh transparently:

1. Better Auth reads the linked account from the `account` table
2. If the access token has expired, it refreshes using the stored refresh token against the provider's token endpoint
3. It returns a valid access token and persists the refreshed one

This happens transparently whenever a Git operation is needed.

records.title: Git Providers
records.heading: What Tokens Are Used For
records.text:
- **Repository listing** — the Design a Project form shows repos from your connected provider
- **ArgoCD access** — after deploying, ArgoCD uses the token to watch repositories for changes
- **Template cloning** — infrastructure templates can be sourced from your repositories

records.title: Git Providers
records.heading: Disconnecting
records.text:
Disconnecting a Git provider:

1. Calls `deleteProviderToken()`, which unlinks the account via Better Auth (`unlinkAccount`) — deleting its `account` row
2. Existing ArgoCD installations that use this token will lose repository access

 
Disconnecting a Git provider affects all projects that use repositories from that provider. ArgoCD will show "sync failed" until a new token is provided.

records.title: Connection Health & Inventory
records.text: Connection Health & Inventory. How Alethia verifies cloud connections and keeps their asset inventory fresh — server-side, no runner.

records.title: Connection Health & Inventory
records.heading: Connection Health & Inventory
records.text:
Once a cloud account is connected, Alethia does two things **entirely server-side in the console** — no
[Runner](/runner) is involved. The runner is provisioning-only; it never tests connections or lists
resources.

 
 Every cloud identity is **platform-managed**: the control plane (the hosted service, or your own console when
 self-hosted) mints the short-lived credentials on demand — it federates off the Alethia OIDC issuer, so it
 holds no standing cloud credential (Alibaba is even account-free). There is no "bring the token to a
 self-hosted runner" path.

records.title: Connection Health & Inventory
records.heading: Connection health
records.text:
The moment you connect (and continuously afterward), Alethia runs an **instant health probe**:

1. **Auth** — assume the customer role / exchange the federated token / present the API token, using the
 platform credentials. Success proves access.
2. **Provisioning-capability probe** — a small set of representative reads to confirm the cloud identity can
 actually see what Alethia provisions into.

The result is one of three statuses, surfaced on the connector card:

 Status Meaning 
 -------- --------- 
 **Connected** Authenticated and the capability probe passed. Ready to provision. 
 **Degraded** Authenticated, but some provisioning permissions look missing — provisioning may fail until the role/policy is widened. The missing permissions are listed. 
 **Disconnected** Authentication failed (revoked trust, a trust policy that no longer pins the Alethia issuer, expired/invalid token). 

Health is re-checked on a schedule and can be re-run on demand with **Re-verify**. Because it's a direct
API call, it resolves in well under a second — there is no queue and no job to wait on.

records.title: Connection Health & Inventory
records.heading: Asset inventory
records.text:
Alethia keeps a normalized inventory of the resources you provision alongside (VPCs/networks, subnets,
NICs, Kubernetes clusters, databases, caches, queues, topics, NoSQL tables, container registries,
secrets, storage buckets, DNS zones, and regions). It powers the **"use existing VPC"** picker on the
canvas and gives the verification agent real-world context.

The inventory is maintained server-side:

- **On connect** — a first sync populates the baseline.
- **Reconciliation sweep** — an in-process scheduler (no external cron) re-lists per cloud identity via the
 cloud SDKs on a TTL cadence (health ~10 min, inventory ~1 h), upserts the typed `cloud_*` tables,
 soft-removes anything no longer present, and **backfills** cloud identities that were never synced. This is
 the reliable backstop and is **on by default**.
- **Event-driven updates (opt-in, near-real-time)** — a per-cloud forwarder can stream change events so
 the inventory reflects a new/deleted resource within seconds (**AWS** EventBridge → Lambda; **GCP**
 Cloud Asset Inventory → Pub/Sub → Cloud Function; **Azure** Event Grid → Function App; **Alibaba**
 ActionTrail → EventBridge → Function Compute). Each normalizes
 the

records.title: Connection Health & Inventory
records.heading: Data custody — how the inventory is stored
records.text:
The inventory is a **minimized, encrypted, expiring projection** — the cloud stays the source of truth:

- **Minimized** — only the identifiers features need (resource id, name, region, kind + low-sensitivity
 typed fields). We do **not** store resource tags (they routinely carry owner emails / cost centers /
 secrets); only the `Name` tag becomes the row name.
- **Encrypted at rest** — reconnaissance-sensitive attributes (CIDRs, IPs, endpoints, DNS domains) are
 sealed in a single AES-GCM `sensitive` blob per row, decrypted only in-app when a feature needs them.
- **Expiring + purged** — soft-removed rows are garbage-collected after a retention window
 (`ALETHIA_INVENTORY_RETENTION_DAYS`, default 7); **disconnecting a cloud identity purges its inventory
 entirely**.

Storing this metadata doesn't weaken the keyless model — a resource id or CIDR is not a
credential, and a breach grants no cloud access (that still requires the role trust, which Alethia holds
no key for).

records.title: Connection Health & Inventory
records.heading: What the Runner does NOT do
records.text:
For clarity, the [Runner](/runner) is **provisioning-only**. It does **not**:

- test cloud connections (server-side, above),
- discover or list cloud resources (server-side asset inventory, above),
- cache resource lists.

It claims `PLAN` / `DEPLOY` / `DESTROY` (and the runner-lifecycle + drift) jobs, runs OpenTofu, streams
logs, and runs the [verify gate](/runner). See [Runner Jobs](/runner/job-execution).

records.title: Hetzner Connector
records.text: Hetzner Connector. Scoped, project-scoped API token — encrypted at rest, decrypted only on the runner. Provisions a self-managed Talos Linux Kubernetes cluster on cheap Hetzner VMs.

records.title: Hetzner Connector
records.heading: Hetzner Connector
records.text:
Connecting Hetzner Cloud registers a **cloud identity** (`cloud_identities`) that is **token-based**. Unlike AWS, GCP, Azure, and Alibaba — which are
**keyless** (Alethia federates into a role you grant via short-lived, minted OIDC assertions) —
Hetzner Cloud offers **no OIDC or workload-identity federation**. Its only auth primitive is a
**project-scoped API token**. So Alethia connects with a token you create, **encrypted at rest
(AES-GCM)** and **decrypted only on the runner** at provision time — never written into a project
snapshot. This is the best-available model for a cloud without federation. See
[Security Architecture](/concepts/security) for the full model.

 
**Is this safe?** The token is stored **encrypted** (AES-256-GCM) and is only ever decrypted on the
runner during a provisioning job — it never appears in a job's config snapshot. A Hetzner token is
scoped to a **single Hetzner project** (the tightest boundary Hetzner offers). **Revoke anytime** by
deleting the token in the Hetzner Cloud Console — that instantly cuts Alethia's access.

records.title: Hetzner Connector
records.heading: What Hetzner provisions
records.text:
Hetzner Cloud has no managed Kubernetes or managed data services. Instead, Alethia provisions a
**self-managed [Talos Linux](https://www.talos.dev/) Kubernetes cluster** on Hetzner's inexpensive
VMs (ARM `CAX` or x86 `CX`/`CPX`/`CCX`), with Cilium networking and the Hetzner CSI driver for block
storage. Data services (Postgres, cache, queue) that would be managed cloud resources on a
hyperscaler run **in-cluster via Helm** — CloudNativePG (Postgres), Valkey (cache), and RabbitMQ
(queue) — deployed through ArgoCD. See
[Health & Inventory](/console/connectors/health-and-inventory) for how cloud identities are probed.

records.title: Hetzner Connector
records.heading: Setup
records.text:
### Create a project-scoped API token
 In the [Hetzner Cloud Console](https://console.hetzner.cloud/), open your project, then
 **Security → API Tokens → Generate API token**. Give it **Read & Write** permission —
 provisioning creates servers, networks, and volumes. The token is scoped to just that one
 project.

 ### Paste into Alethia
 Paste the token into the Alethia connect sheet and click **Connect**. Alethia encrypts it at rest
 (AES-GCM) and verifies it immediately against the Hetzner Cloud API.

 
 
 
 

 ### Run a self-hosted runner
 If you operate your own runner, set **`HCLOUD_TOKEN`** in the runner's own environment. Alethia
 then stores **no token at all** — the runner supplies it directly at provision time. This is the
 zero-storage path for federation-less clouds.

 ### Connect
 Mark the cloud identity self-managed; provisioning jobs claimed by your runner use its environment's
 `HCLOUD_TOKEN` and Alethia never persists a credential.

records.title: Hetzner Connector
records.heading: Verification
records.text:
After you submit, Alethia verifies the cloud identity **instantly, server-side** (no runner): it decrypts
the stored token and calls a cheap authenticated Hetzner Cloud API endpoint
(`GET https://api.hetzner.cloud/v1/datacenters`).

- `200` → the cloud identity is **Connected**
- `401` / `403` → the token was rejected (bad or revoked) → **Disconnected**

On success, Alethia also syncs the project's **regions** (used for placement) into the asset
[inventory](/console/connectors/health-and-inventory). If verification fails, the error explains what
went wrong.

records.title: Hetzner Connector
records.heading: What's Stored
records.text:
- **Managed:** only your **encrypted API token** (AES-256-GCM), decrypted solely on the runner at
 provision time — never in a project snapshot.
- **Self-hosted runner:** **nothing** — the runner carries `HCLOUD_TOKEN` in its own environment.

Rotate or revoke the token in the Hetzner Cloud Console at any time to cut access.

records.title: Connectors Overview
records.text: Connectors Overview. Connect cloud providers and Git accounts to enable infrastructure provisioning.

records.title: Connectors Overview
records.heading: Connectors
records.text: The **connector** catalog is the registry of provider *types* you can connect. Each account you actually connect becomes a **cloud identity** (`cloud_identities`) — the credential anchor a project provisions against. The catalog spans the **federated clouds** (AWS, GCP, Azure, Alibaba) and the **token clouds** (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, Civo), plus Git providers (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket) and **pluggable per-category providers** (DNS, secrets, registry, chart repositories, observability). At least one cloud identity and one Git provider must be connected before provisioning; pluggable providers are optional — they let a project use a tool you already run instead of the cloud-native default.

records.title: Connectors Overview
records.heading: How It Works
records.text:
Connectors are displayed as cards organized by category:

 Category Providers Auth 
 ---------- ----------- ------ 
 **Cloud Providers** AWS, GCP, Azure, Alibaba keyless federation off the Alethia OIDC issuer (no stored keys) 
 **Token Clouds** Hetzner, DigitalOcean, Civo the customer's own API token (encrypted at rest) 
 **Git Providers** GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket OAuth 
 **DNS** Cloudflare API key 
 **Secrets** HashiCorp Vault API key 
 **Registry** Docker Hub API key 
 **Chart repositories** GitHub Container Registry, Docker Hub, GitLab, Scaleway, generic OCI, HTTPS API key 
 **Observability** Datadog, Grafana Cloud API key 

Each card shows:
- Provider icon and name
- Connection status — a grayscale status badge (dot + label, no color): **Connected**, **Needs Reconnection**, or **Not Connected**
- Connected account identifier (AWS Account ID, GCP Project, GitHub username)
- Action button (Connect / Disconnect / Reconnect)

records.title: Connectors Overview
records.heading: Connection Status
records.text:
Status Meaning 
 -------- --------- 
 **Connected** Credentials valid and verified 
 **Needs Reconnection** Git token expired, automatic refresh failed 
 **Not Connected** No credentials on file 
 **Coming Soon** Provider supported but not yet implemented

records.title: Connectors Overview
records.heading: Cloud Provider Connections
records.text:
The four **federated clouds** use the platform's [zero-credential model](/concepts/security) — the customer's
role/pool/provider trusts the Alethia OIDC issuer directly, and Alethia federates in with a short-lived minted
assertion. **No static keys are stored.**

 
 Keyless IAM role via an IAM OIDC provider 
 Workload Identity Federation — enter Project ID + Number, config assembled for you 
 Federated credential on your own managed identity — no platform Entra app 
 RAM AssumeRoleWithOIDC (account-free) 
 

The **token clouds** (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, Civo) instead use the customer's own API token — there is no
account to federate into. The token is encrypted at rest (`ALETHIA_CRED_ENCRYPTION_KEY`) and only decrypted
on the runner at provision time.

After connecting, Alethia verifies the credentials **instantly, server-side** (an auth + provisioning-permission probe — no runner, no job) and marks the cloud identity `Connected`, `Degraded`, or `Disconnected`. Existing resources (VPCs, subnets, DNS zones) are discovered + kept fresh by the server-side, event-driven asset inventory. See [Connection health & inventory](/console/connectors/health-and-inventory).

records.title: Connectors Overview
records.heading: Git Provider Connections
records.text: Git connections use standard OAuth. See [Git Providers](/console/connectors/git-providers) for details.

records.title: Connectors Overview
records.heading: Pluggable Connectors
records.text:
DNS, secrets, registry, chart repository, and observability providers authenticate with an **API key / token**. Secret fields are encrypted at rest (`ALETHIA_CRED_ENCRYPTION_KEY`) and only decrypted on the runner at provision time — never stored in a Project snapshot. After connecting, a verification ping confirms the credential works.

 
 Cloudflare · Vault · Docker Hub · Datadog · Grafana Cloud 
 Private Helm and OCI chart sources

records.title: Connectors Overview
records.heading: Disconnecting
records.text:
- **Cloud providers**: Removes the `cloud_identities` record. Existing projects referencing that identity can no longer run jobs.
- **Git providers**: Removes the Better Auth `account` record and revokes the OAuth grant.
- **Pluggable connectors**: Removes the `connector_credentials` record. Projects referencing that provider fall back to failing validation until reconnected.

records.title: Managing Connections
records.text: Managing Connections. Add a second account to a cloud provider, re-verify a connection, rename an account, and disconnect one — all from the connector detail sheet.

records.title: Managing Connections
records.heading: Managing Connections
records.text:
Every account you connect becomes a **cloud identity** (`cloud_identities`). A single provider can hold
**more than one** connected account — each verified account is a distinct identity row. Cloud connections
are **org-scoped**: every member of the org sees them (subject to their role), and mutating a connection
requires the `manage_identities` permission.

This page covers the day-2 actions on the connector detail sheet: adding another account, re-verifying,
renaming, and disconnecting. To connect an account for the first time, see the per-provider guides linked
from [Connectors Overview](/console/connectors).

 
 These actions are managed **entirely server-side in the console** — no [Runner](/runner) and no job. A
 re-verify is a direct API call — a live probe against the provider, not a queued job. See
 [Connection Health & Inventory](/console/connectors/health-and-inventory).

records.title: Managing Connections
records.heading: Open the connector detail sheet
records.text:
Every action below starts from the same place.

1. Open the **Connectors** page.
2. Select the provider card.

The detail sheet lists each connected account for that provider, with its status and per-account actions.
If you don't have the `manage_identities` permission, the mutating actions are hidden.

records.title: Managing Connections
records.heading: Add another account
records.text:
Connect a second account to a provider that already has one — for example a second AWS account or a second
GCP project.

1. Open the provider's detail sheet.
2. Select **Add another account**.
3. Complete the provider's connect flow.

Each **Connect** starts a fresh pending identity, so verifying it adds a new account row rather than
replacing the existing one. The provider's own guide describes the credential steps (for example
[AWS](/console/connectors/aws) or [GCP](/console/connectors/gcp)).

records.title: Managing Connections
records.heading: Re-verify a connection
records.text:
Re-check an account's health without re-entering its credentials — use this when an account shows
**Limited permissions** or **Verification failed**, for example after you widen a role or policy to
clear a permissions gap. The per-account **Re-verify** action is shown only for those two states.

1. Open the provider's detail sheet.
2. Find the account.
3. Select **Re-verify**.

Alethia flips the account to `testing`, re-runs the auth and provisioning-permission probe against the
stored credentials, and updates the status to one of:

 Status Meaning 
 -------- --------- 
 **Connected** Authenticated and the capability probe passed. 
 **Limited permissions** Authenticated, but some provisioning permissions look missing. The missing permissions are listed. 
 **Verification failed** Authentication failed.

records.title: Managing Connections
records.heading: Rename an account
records.text:
Give an account a recognizable label instead of its default (for example `AWS Account (123456789012)`).

1. Open the provider's detail sheet.
2. Find the account.
3. Select **Rename**.
4. Enter a new name and confirm.

The name is trimmed and stored per account. Renaming does not change the account's credentials or status.

records.title: Managing Connections
records.heading: Disconnect an account
records.text:
Remove Alethia's access to a single account.

1. Open the provider's detail sheet.
2. Find the account.
3. Select the account's disconnect action.

Disconnecting resets the account to its pending state and:

- **clears all stored credentials** for that identity,
- **unlinks any projects** that referenced it (`projects.cloud_identity_id` is set to `null`), so those
 projects can no longer provision against it,
- **purges the account's asset inventory** — Alethia keeps no projection of a cloud it can no longer
 access.

 
 Disconnect targets a **single account**. Other accounts connected to the same provider are untouched.

records.title: Managing Connections
records.heading: Related
records.text:
The connector catalog and how cloud identities are authenticated. 
 How Alethia verifies connections and keeps their asset inventory fresh.

records.title: Pluggable Connectors
records.text: Pluggable Connectors. Bring your own DNS, secrets, registry, chart repository, and observability tools via API-key connectors.

records.title: Pluggable Connectors
records.heading: Pluggable Connectors
records.text:
Beyond cloud and Git, Alethia supports **pluggable per-category connectors** that let a Project mix in the tools you already use instead of the cloud-native default — Cloudflare for DNS, HashiCorp Vault for secrets, Docker Hub for a registry, a private Helm or OCI source for charts, and Datadog / Grafana Cloud for observability.

These connectors authenticate with an **API key / token** (`auth_method = api_key`) rather than cloud federation or OAuth.

records.title: Pluggable Connectors
records.heading: Categories and providers
records.text:
Category Cloud-native default Pluggable provider Credential fields 
 ---------- ---------------------- -------------------- ------------------- 
 **DNS** Route 53 / Cloud DNS / Azure DNS **Cloudflare** API token 
 **Secrets** Secrets Manager / Secret Manager / Key Vault **HashiCorp Vault** Address, token 
 **Registry** ECR / Artifact Registry / ACR **Docker Hub** Username, access token 
 **Chart repositories** — (public charts need no credential) **[GitHub Container Registry, Docker Hub, GitLab, Scaleway, generic OCI, HTTPS](/console/connectors/chart-repositories)** Username, password / token 
 **Observability** — (none) **Datadog** API key, app key 
 **Observability** — **Grafana Cloud** Instance ID, API token 

The catalog is data-driven — each provider is one row in the `connectors` table, seeded from a single manifest (`packages/core/categories/catalog.json`). See [Connectors Architecture](/concepts/connectors) for how this works end to end.

records.title: Pluggable Connectors
records.heading: Connecting a provider
records.text:
1. Open **Connectors**, pick the provider card, and choose **Connect**.
2. Fill in the API credential — the form fields are generated from the provider's credential specification.
3. Alethia runs a lightweight **verification ping** against the provider's API (e.g. Cloudflare's token-verify endpoint, Vault's token lookup, Docker Hub login, Datadog's key-validate endpoint). A verified credential turns the card green; an unverified one is still saved so you can retry.

records.title: Pluggable Connectors
records.heading: How credentials are stored
records.text:
Secret fields (tokens, passwords) are **encrypted at rest** with AES-256-GCM before being written to the `connector_credentials` table; non-secret fields (a Vault address, a Docker Hub username) are stored in clear. The encryption key comes from `ALETHIA_CRED_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (see [Configuration](/self-hosting/configuration)).

 
Secrets are **never** placed in a Project's `config_snapshot`. They are decrypted and attached to a job only at **claim time**, then injected into the runner's OpenTofu variables in memory — preserving the [zero-credential model](/concepts/security).

records.title: Pluggable Connectors
records.heading: Using a connector in a Project
records.text:
Once connected, pick the provider per component in the [Project designer](/console/design-project):

- [DNS & WAF](/console/design-project/dns) — choose **Cloudflare** instead of cloud-native DNS.
- [Secrets](/console/design-project/secrets) — choose **Vault**.
- [Container Registry](/console/design-project/container-registry) — choose **Docker Hub**.
- [Chart repositories](/console/connectors/chart-repositories) — add one per environment so Alethia can read your private charts.
- [Observability](/console/design-project/observability) — choose **Datadog / Grafana Cloud**.

At provision time the runner composes the chosen provider's module into the plan and **skips** the cloud-native resource for that category.

records.title: Pluggable Connectors
records.heading: Chart repositories
records.text:
A chart repository works differently from the categories above: it provisions nothing. It tells Alethia which credential to use when ArgoCD pulls a Helm chart from a private repository.

1. Connect the provider under **Chart Repos** on the Connectors page.
2. On the Project canvas, add a **Chart repository** component (**Add → DevOps → Chart repository**) and pick the connected provider. Providers that serve a single fixed host — GitHub Container Registry, Docker Hub — need nothing more. For a self-hosted or generic registry, give the bare registry host (`registry.acme.io`, no scheme and no path); for an HTTPS Helm repository, give the full `https://` URL.
3. Deploy. Before it syncs any chart, the runner writes an ArgoCD **repository credential** for that repository. ArgoCD matches a chart to a credential by URL prefix, so the host you enter must match the host your charts are addressed by.

You need one only for a **private** repository. Public charts, including everything in the add-on marketplace, pull without a credential.

To use a private chart, attach it with **Add → Bring your own Helm chart**, choose **OCI registry**, and give the whole reference including the chart name (

records.title: Pluggable Connectors
records.heading: Adding a new provider
records.text:
Pluggable connectors are an open-ended catalog. Adding a sixth provider takes four steps and **no** changes to routes, the runner core, or the form engine:

1. Add a row to `packages/core/categories/catalog.json` (category, slug, auth_method, icon, credential + provider_config fields).
2. Add a `CategoryProvider` Go impl under `packages/core/categories/` (its `Tfvars`/`Validate` behavior).
3. Add the OpenTofu module under `infra/templates/categories/ / /`. A chart-repo provider has no module — it implements `RepoCred` instead, and must also get a host rule in `apps/console/lib/connectors/helm-registry-hosts.ts` so the console resolves the same credential URL the Go provider seeds.
4. Run `pnpm -F console gen:connectors` to regenerate the registry + catalog seed.

See [Connectors Architecture](/concepts/connectors) for the contract details.

records.title: Dashboard Overview
records.text: Dashboard Overview. The main dashboard page — stats, cloud identity status, and recent jobs.

records.title: Dashboard Overview
records.heading: Dashboard Overview
records.text: The dashboard is the landing page after login. It provides a quick summary of your infrastructure state.

records.title: Dashboard Overview
records.heading: Layout
records.text:
The dashboard shell wraps all authenticated pages with:

- **Header** — breadcrumbs, notifications bell (unread job count), user dropdown (profile, sign out)
- **Sidebar** — main navigation (Overview, Design a Project, Clusters, Jobs, Connectors, Runners) plus a dynamic project list
- **Real-time subscriptions** — established on layout mount for job status and project status updates (see [Real-time Architecture](/concepts/realtime))

records.title: Dashboard Overview
records.heading: Overview Page
records.text:
The overview page shows four stat chips at the top:

 Stat Source 
 ------ -------- 
 Total Projects Count of all projects 
 Active Projects Projects with status `ACTIVE` 
 Online Runners Runners with heartbeat within 60 seconds 
 Total Jobs Count of all provision jobs 

Below the stats:

records.title: Dashboard Overview
records.heading: Connectors Panel
records.text: Shows connected and disconnected [cloud identities](/console/connectors) as badges. Connected providers show a green indicator and account identifier (AWS Account ID, GCP Project, GitHub username). Disconnected providers link to the connectors page.

records.title: Dashboard Overview
records.heading: Recent Jobs
records.text:
A data table showing the 5 most recent jobs with columns:
- **Type** — job type with icon (PLAN, DEPLOY, DESTROY, etc.)
- **Status** — color-coded badge (green=SUCCESS, red=FAILED, yellow=PROCESSING, gray=QUEUED)
- **Project** — target project name
- **Created** — relative timestamp

Clicking a job row navigates to the [job detail page](/console/jobs/job-detail).

records.title: Dashboard Overview
records.heading: Notifications
records.text:
The notifications bell in the header shows a badge with the count of unread job state changes. Clicking it opens a popover with recent notifications. Clicking a notification navigates to the relevant job. "Mark all read" clears the count.

Notifications are driven by the real-time subscription to `jobs` — every status change (QUEUED → PROCESSING → SUCCESS/FAILED) creates a notification.

records.title: Dashboard Overview
records.heading: Sidebar Navigation
records.text:
The sidebar has two sections:

**Main Navigation:**
- Overview (`/dashboard`)
- Design a Project (`/dashboard/design`)
- Clusters (`/dashboard/clusters`)
- Jobs (`/dashboard/jobs`)
- Connectors (`/dashboard/connectors`)
- Runners (`/dashboard/runners`)

**Projects List:**
- Dynamically loaded from the projects store
- Projects show status dots (green=ACTIVE, yellow=PROVISIONING, red=FAILED) and provider icons
- Active project is highlighted based on current URL
- "Design a Project" link shown if no projects exist

records.title: Project Detail
records.text: Project Detail. The project detail page — services, infrastructure, plan, jobs, and lifecycle actions.

records.title: Project Detail
records.heading: Project Detail
records.text: Each project has a detail page at `/{org}/{project}` showing the complete infrastructure configuration and its deployment state.

records.title: Project Detail
records.heading: Header
records.text:
The header displays:
- **Project name** and provider icon (AWS/GCP/Azure)
- **Region** and **environment stage** (production/staging/development)
- **Status badge** — DRAFT, QUEUED, PROVISIONING, ACTIVE, FAILED, DESTROYING, DESTROYED
- **Estimated monthly cost**
- **Action buttons**: Plan, Apply, and a dropdown menu

records.title: Project Detail
records.heading: Action Dropdown
records.text:
Action Description 
 -------- ------------- 
 **Plan** Queue a PLAN job → Runner runs `tofu plan` 
 **Apply** Queue a DEPLOY job → Runner runs the [verify gate](/console/jobs/plan-and-apply#verify-gate) then `tofu apply` + installs ArgoCD 
 **Quick Duplicate** Create a copy with the same config 
 **Duplicate & Edit** Open the Design a Project form pre-filled with this project's config 
 **Delete** Delete the project record (does NOT destroy cloud resources) 

Plan and Apply actions open the **Runner Select Popover** where you choose which Runner executes the job. See [Job Queue Pattern](/concepts/job-queue).

records.title: Project Detail
records.heading: Configuration Tab (Default)
records.text:
Shows quick stat chips:
- Service count (databases + caches + queues + topics + NoSQL + secrets)
- Estimated monthly cost
- Current status
- Provider and region

Then displays two sub-sections:

**Infrastructure** — read-only display of:
- Network: VPC/VNet (create new or existing), CIDR block, NAT gateway mode
- Cluster: Kubernetes version, node sizing (min/desired/max), instance types, autoscaler
- DNS: domain, certificate, WAF settings (if enabled)
- Repositories: application repo (if configured)
- General: OpenTofu version (`iac_version`), region, environment

**Services** — grid of service buttons for each configured component:
- Databases (engine, capacity, endpoints if provisioned)
- Caches (engine, node type, endpoint if provisioned)
- Queues (FIFO/standard, visibility timeout)
- Topics (subscription count)
- NoSQL tables (key schema, billing mode)
- Secrets (length, generation settings)

Each service button opens a **Service Popover** with full details, including:
- Configuration parameters
- Status with timestamp
- Endpoint (if provisioned, with copy button)
- Monthly cost estimate

**Recent Jobs** — table showing the last 5 jobs for this project (type, status, created, d

records.title: Project Detail
records.heading: Plan Tab
records.text:
Visible after running a Plan job. Shows:

- **Plan Summary Bar** — resource counts (add/change/destroy) and estimated cost
- **Resource Groups** — collapsible sections grouped by resource type, each showing individual resources with their action (create/update/delete) and cost
- **Verify Report** — the [verify gate](/console/jobs/plan-and-apply#verify-gate) result (`verify_result`): per-control pass / fail / `not_evaluable` over the plan JSON
- **Apply Button** — queues a DEPLOY job using this plan's artifact

See [Plan & Apply](/console/jobs/plan-and-apply) for the full workflow.

records.title: Project Detail
records.heading: Cluster Access
records.text:
After a successful DEPLOY, the project detail shows:
- **Cluster endpoint** (copy button)
- **kubeconfig command** (provider-specific, copy button)
- **ArgoCD URL** (external link to ArgoCD dashboard)
- **ArgoCD admin credentials**

records.title: Project Detail
records.heading: Project Duplication
records.text:
The **Duplicate & Edit** action opens the Design a Project form pre-filled with the project's current configuration. If you select a different cloud identity (e.g., switching from AWS to GCP), the configuration is converted automatically. See [Multi-Cloud Conversion](/concepts/multi-cloud-conversion) for how this works.

Conversion warnings are displayed in the form if any settings couldn't be mapped directly (e.g., instance types, WAF rules, DNS zones).

records.title: Bring Your Own Helm Charts
records.text: Bring Your Own Helm Charts. Attach your own Helm chart, scan it for safety, and describe the workloads it deploys as first-class canvas nodes you can bind to provisioned infrastructure.

records.title: Bring Your Own Helm Charts
records.heading: Bring Your Own Helm Charts
records.text:
Not every workload starts as a Dockerfile in a repo. When you already package an application (or a
third-party one) as a **Helm chart**, you can bring it straight onto the canvas: Alethia deploys the
chart as-is, scans it for safety, and **describes what it actually deploys** so the chart stops being
an opaque box and becomes something you can see, configure, and wire into the rest of your
architecture.

The guiding principle: **Alethia describes and binds your chart — it never rewrites it.** Your chart
stays the single unit that gets deployed (as one hardened ArgoCD Application). Everything below is
about *understanding* and *connecting* that chart, not re-authoring it.

records.title: Bring Your Own Helm Charts
records.heading: Attaching a chart
records.text: A chart comes from one of two places: a Git repository, or an OCI registry.

records.title: Bring Your Own Helm Charts
records.heading: From a Git repository
records.text:
Attach the chart from a [connected Git provider](/console/connectors/git-providers):

 Field Description 
 ------- ------------- 
 **Repository** The Git repo that holds the chart 
 **Chart path** The chart directory within the repo (e.g. `charts/payments`) 
 **Ref** The branch, tag, or commit to deploy 
 **Namespace** The Kubernetes namespace to install into 
 **Values** Your chart values (schema-validated knobs, or raw `values.yaml`)

records.title: Bring Your Own Helm Charts
records.heading: From an OCI registry
records.text:
Attach the chart by its `oci://` reference. There is no chart path — the repository path *is* the
chart:

 Field Description 
 ------- ------------- 
 **Chart reference** `oci:// / / ` (e.g. `oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts/payments`) 
 **Chart version** The chart version to deploy. `*` deploys the latest release 
 **Namespace** The Kubernetes namespace to install into 
 **Values** Your chart values (schema-validated knobs, or raw `values.yaml`) 

To use a **private** registry, connect it as a
[chart repository](/console/connectors/chart-repositories) on the environment. Alethia matches your
chart's host against the chart repositories you connected and authenticates with that credential —
both when it scans the chart and when ArgoCD pulls it at deploy time. A public chart needs no
connector.

If your registry sits on an internal network rather than the public internet, the Runner needs an
opt-in as well — see
[`ALETHIA_HELM_REGISTRY_ALLOW_PRIVATE`](/runner/self-hosted#environment-variables).

At deploy time the Runner renders the chart into a hardened, per-project ArgoCD `AppProject` locked to
your repo and namespace. See [GitOps & ArgoCD](/concepts/gitops-argocd) for how the Application

records.title: Bring Your Own Helm Charts
records.heading: The safety scan
records.text:
Before a chart is trusted to run, Alethia renders it (`helm template`) inside a **sandboxed,
network-isolated** environment and runs the [Elench](/elench/architecture) verification engine over
the resulting Kubernetes manifests — checking for privileged containers, host access, wildcard RBAC,
missing resource limits, and mutable image tags. The result is attached to the chart as a verify
report you can read on the canvas. The render holds **no secrets and has no network egress** — it only
reads the local chart.

This works the same way for both chart sources. The Runner fetches the chart first — cloning the Git
repo, or pulling it from the OCI registry — and only then renders it in the isolated sandbox. Fetching
happens outside that sandbox, so your registry credential is never exposed to the chart being
rendered.

 
Charts hosted in **Amazon ECR** cannot be scanned yet. ECR issues a short-lived token rather than a
stored password, so it is served by a different mechanism that is still in progress. Charts in every
other supported registry — GitHub Container Registry, GitLab, Docker Hub, Scaleway, and generic OCI
registries — scan normally.

records.title: Bring Your Own Helm Charts
records.heading: Described workloads
records.text:
A Helm chart is rarely one thing — it can render several Deployments, a StatefulSet, a CronJob, and
more. From the **same render** the safety scan produces, Alethia **describes each workload the chart
deploys** as its own node:

 What's described From 
 ------------------ ------ 
 **Kind** Deployment · StatefulSet · DaemonSet · CronJob · Job 
 **Image** The workload's primary container image 
 **Ports** The container ports it exposes 
 **Environment** The environment variable **names** it reads (values are never captured) 
 **Resources** The CPU/memory requests and limits it declares 
 **Replicas** The rendered replica count (Deployments and StatefulSets) 

These are **read-mostly descriptions** — they mirror what your chart renders, refreshed every time the
chart is re-scanned. They are deliberately kept separate from Alethia-built services, so a described
workload is never accidentally deployed twice: your chart's ArgoCD Application remains the one and
only thing that deploys it.

 
Environment is captured as variable **names only** — a described workload never stores a rendered
value, so a secret baked into a chart's manifests is never read back into Alethia.

records.title: Bring Your Own Helm Charts
records.heading: On the canvas
records.text:
Once a chart is scanned, its workloads appear as **child nodes beneath the chart node** — a line from
the chart to each thing it deploys. A workload node is drawn as a read-mostly card with a dashed, "not
owned by the design" treatment that sets it apart from an Alethia-built service, so you can tell at a
glance which nodes you author and which your chart brings.

Select a workload to open its **inspector**. The top of the panel is the description above —
image, ports, environment variable names, resources, and replicas, all read-only because they mirror
the chart. Below it is the only part you edit: the **overlay** — bindings, a couple of overrides, and
the value-paths those write to.

records.title: Bring Your Own Helm Charts
records.heading: Binding a chart to your infrastructure
records.text:
Because each workload is described, you can **bind** it to the databases, caches, queues, and secrets
you provisioned elsewhere on the canvas — the same [bindings](/console/design-project/databases) model
Alethia-built services use. A binding injects the provisioned connection details into the running
chart by writing into the chart's **values** (for example, pointing the chart at an existing secret):

- **Endpoints and ports** are written as plain values.
- **Credentials** are written as a **reference** to a keyless, cluster-provisioned Kubernetes Secret —
 never as a plaintext value in your chart's values or Git. This keeps the
 [keyless](/concepts/security) guarantee intact end to end.

Binding works by writing into a **declared path** in your chart's values (for example
`postgresql.auth.existingSecret`). Alethia suggests the path from the chart's own conventions, and you
can override it. A chart that exposes no way to accept an existing secret is flagged honestly rather
than having a credential forced into it.

records.title: Bring Your Own Helm Charts
records.heading: Overrides: replicas and environment
records.text:
Beyond bindings, a described workload carries a small **editable overlay** you set from the inspector
without touching the chart:

- **Replicas** — override the rendered replica count.
- **Environment** — add or override environment variables (name → value).

Like bindings, these are written into the chart's values at deploy — they never re-author the chart,
and they survive a re-scan. Everything else on the card stays a read-only mirror of what the chart
renders.

records.title: Bring Your Own Helm Charts
records.heading: Value-path overrides
records.text:
Every binding and override needs to know **where** in your chart's values to write. Alethia infers
these paths from common chart conventions (`replicaCount`, `image.tag`,
`*.existingSecret` / `auth.existingSecret`) when it scans. When your chart's shape is non-standard, the
inspector's **value-paths** editor lets you correct any knob → dot-path mapping by hand — your override
always wins over the inferred default, and it's preserved across re-scans.

 
Bring-your-own Helm charts are an **opt-in** capability, enabled per deployment and — in the current
trusted-charts phase — scoped to charts you own on your own cluster. Described workloads and binding
roll out behind the same gate. Ask your operator whether it's enabled on your instance.

records.title: Bring Your Own Helm Charts
records.heading: How it fits together
records.text:
1. **Attach** the chart from a connected repo (repo · chart path · ref · values) or an OCI registry
 (chart reference · version · values).
2. **Scan** — the Runner fetches the chart, renders it in the sandbox, and Elench verifies the
 manifests.
3. **Describe** — from that render, each workload the chart deploys becomes a canvas node.
4. **Bind & override** — from a workload's inspector, connect it to your provisioned infrastructure and
 set its replicas/environment overlay; bindings and overrides are written into the chart's values
 (credentials as keyless secret references) at the inferred or overridden value-paths.
5. **Deploy** — your chart, unchanged, syncs as a single ArgoCD Application with the bound values applied.

See also: [The Canvas](/console/design-project/the-canvas) · [Repositories](/console/design-project/repositories) · [Bring Your Own IaC](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac).

records.title: Bring Your Own IaC
records.text: Bring Your Own IaC. Point a project environment at your own OpenTofu root module so Alethia provisions from it instead of the built-in template, behind a static safety scan.

records.title: Bring Your Own IaC
records.heading: Bring Your Own IaC
records.text:
Alethia normally provisions an environment from its built-in per-cloud template. **Bring-your-own IaC**
lets you point that environment at a git repo holding your **own OpenTofu root module** — Alethia
plans, scans, and applies *your* module instead. This is a **replace-mode** capability: the module
takes over the environment, and the built-in template no longer applies.

This guide covers attaching a module, reading its safety scan, and detaching it. For the design behind
the safety gate and the module contract, see [Bring Your Own IaC (concepts)](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac).

 
Bring-your-own IaC is **opt-in**, enabled per instance with `ALETHIA_BYO_IAC_ENABLED=true`. With the
flag off, attaching, scanning, and provisioning a module all refuse. Ask your operator whether it's
enabled on your instance.

records.title: Bring Your Own IaC
records.heading: Before you start
records.text:
- Link the git provider that hosts your module. The attach dialog reads from your
 [connected git providers](/console/connectors/git-providers) — if you have none, the repository
 selector offers a connect step.
- Use an environment with **no deployed (or in-flight) template infrastructure**. A replace-mode
 module would orphan existing template state, so attaching is rejected until you destroy that
 environment first.

records.title: Bring Your Own IaC
records.heading: Attach a module
records.text:
The attach flow is a four-step dialog: **Repository → Path & ref → Variables → Review**.

1. Open the canvas command menu (⌘K) and choose **Bring your own IaC** from the **Sources** group.
2. **Repository** — select the git repo that holds your module.
3. **Path & ref** — set the **root-module path** (the directory inside the repo that holds the root
 `*.tf`; leave blank for the repo root) and, optionally, the **git ref** (a branch, tag, or commit;
 leave blank for `HEAD`).
