4. **Variables** — add any non-secret tfvars the module needs. Each variable is a name, a type, and a
 value.
5. **Review** — confirm the repo, path, ref, and variable count, then select **Attach source**.

Attaching pins a single IaC source on the environment and **queues a safety scan automatically** — you
don't need to trigger the scan yourself.

records.title: Bring Your Own IaC
records.heading: Variables
records.text:
Variables on the Variables step are **scalar, non-secret tfvars** only:

 Field Rule 
 ------- ------ 
 **Name** Letters, digits, and underscores; must start with a letter or underscore. Names must be unique. 
 **Type** `string`, `number`, or `bool`. 
 **Value** Must parse as the chosen type (`number` must be numeric; `bool` must be `true` or `false`). 

 
Never put secrets here. These values are stored as plain tfvars. Keep credentials in your cloud's
secret store or your module's own data sources.
 

Leave the list empty to run the module with its own defaults.

records.title: Bring Your Own IaC
records.heading: Read the safety scan
records.text:
Once attached, the module appears on the canvas as an **External IaC** card carrying its provenance —
repo, ref, path, the commit the scan pinned, and a scan-status chip. Select the chip to open the
**IaC safety scan** sheet.

The scan clones the repo, pins the commit it checked out, inventories the module's providers and module
sources, and runs `tofu validate` plus the static `iacsafety` checks. The sheet shows:

- A **verdict** — "No blocking issues found", or "Issues found — resolve before deploying".
- A **`tofu validate`** status pill and a per-severity summary (`critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low`,
 `info`).
- **Finding cards**, worst-first — each with a rule id, a `file:line` coordinate, and a detail message.
- The **providers** and **modules** the scan discovered.

Re-run the scan any time with **Rescan** in the scan sheet (open it from the node's scan-status chip)
— for example after pushing a fix to the module.

 
Only a clean scan pins the commit a deploy will apply. A **not-ok scan clears the deploy pin**, so
provisioning stays locked until a clean re-scan. This also protects against a swap between scan and
apply: the pinned commit is exactly what runs.

records.title: Bring Your Own IaC
records.heading: Provision from the module
records.text:
While an enabled source exists, that environment's plan, deploy, and destroy run **your module**
instead of the built-in template. The module's resources appear as their own read-only cards on the
board; the component palette is disabled for a BYO environment, because the module — not the design —
is the source of truth.

The External IaC card tracks live state: it marks the environment **DEPLOYED** or **NOT DEPLOYED** and
shows the commit the last deploy applied alongside the pinned commit.

At plan time, the same verify verdict template provisioning gets (keyless / least-privilege / OIDC-sub)
is attached to each deploy's **Plan** tab.

records.title: Bring Your Own IaC
records.heading: Detach a module
records.text:
To return an environment to the built-in template, open the External IaC card and select the detach
(**✕**) control.

 
You can only detach a source that has **never deployed**. Once a deploy has applied the module (or the
environment is in an active or in-flight status), detaching would drop the only handle to that live
infrastructure — destroy the environment first, then detach.

records.title: Bring Your Own IaC
records.heading: Bring your own Helm chart
records.text:
Alongside a full OpenTofu module, you can attach a single **Helm chart** from a git repo. Open the
command menu (⌘K), choose **Bring your own Helm chart** from **Sources**, and step through
**Repository → Chart path → Ref → Review**:

- **Chart path** — the directory inside the repo that contains `Chart.yaml`.
- **Ref** — the branch, tag, or commit ArgoCD tracks (blank for `HEAD`).
- **Review** — set the chart **name**, target **namespace** (defaults to `default`), and optional Helm
 **values**.

The chart is deployed and governed on the cluster through ArgoCD, and it syncs on the next deploy. For
scanning the chart, describing the workloads it deploys, and binding them to your infrastructure, see
[Bring Your Own Helm Charts](/console/design-project/bring-your-own-charts).

records.title: Bring Your Own IaC
records.heading: See also
records.text:
- [Bring Your Own IaC (concepts)](/concepts/bring-your-own-iac) — the safety gate and module contract.
- [Bring Your Own Helm Charts](/console/design-project/bring-your-own-charts) — the chart workflow.
- [The Canvas](/console/design-project/the-canvas) — where sources and their cards live.
- [Git providers](/console/connectors/git-providers) — connecting the repo host.

records.text: Caches. Redis and Valkey cache instances — node types, clustering, and multi-AZ.

records.title: Caches
records.heading: Multi-AZ
records.text: When enabled, the cache replicates data across availability zones for automatic failover. If the primary node fails, a replica in another AZ is promoted automatically. This adds ~50% to the cost (replica nodes).

records.title: Caches

records.text:
The cache card in project detail shows:
- **Primary endpoint** — connection string for writes
- **Reader endpoint** — connection string for reads (if multi-AZ)
- **Port** — typically 6379
- **Status** — ACTIVE, CREATING, or FAILED

records.title: Cluster
records.text: Cluster. Kubernetes cluster configuration — version, instance types, node scaling, Karpenter, and cluster admins.

records.title: Cluster
records.heading: Cluster
records.text: The cluster section configures the Kubernetes control plane and worker nodes.

records.title: Cluster
records.heading: Fields
records.text:
Field Type Description 
 ------- ------ ------------- 
 **Kubernetes Version** Select Provider-specific versions (e.g., 1.32 for EKS, 1.31 for GKE/AKS) 
 **Instance Type** Select A single instance/machine type; the option label shows vCPU and memory per node 
 **Min Nodes** Number Minimum node count (default: 2) 
 **Desired Nodes** Number Target node count (default: 2) 
 **Max Nodes** Number Maximum node count for autoscaling (default: 5) 
 **Autoscaler** Provider default Provider-specific autoscaler (Karpenter on AWS, Autopilot on GKE, Cluster Autoscaler on AKS), enabled at cluster creation 
 **Cluster Admins** Array IAM users/emails with admin access

records.title: Cluster
records.heading: Kubernetes Service
records.text:
- **Elastic Kubernetes Service** with managed node groups
 - Versions: 1.29–1.32
 - Autoscaler: **Karpenter** — just-in-time node provisioning based on pod requirements
 - IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) configured automatically
 - OIDC provider created for workload identity
 
 
 - **Google Kubernetes Engine** with node pools
 - Versions: 1.28–1.31
 - Autoscaler: **GKE Autopilot** — fully managed node provisioning
 - Workload Identity enabled by default
 
 
 - **Azure Kubernetes Service** with node pools
 - Versions: 1.28–1.31
 - Autoscaler: **Cluster Autoscaler** — scales node count based on pending pods
 - Azure AD integration for RBAC

records.title: Cluster
records.heading: Instance Types
records.text:
A single instance type is selected from a dropdown, with each option's label showing the node's vCPU and memory. On any cloud you can instead size the node group portably (vCPU and memory per node) and the runner maps that capability to the nearest instance type at provision time.

 Category AWS GCP Azure 
 ---------- ----- ----- ------- 
 General t3.medium, t3.large e2-medium, e2-standard-2 Standard_D2s_v5, Standard_D4s_v5 
 Compute c5.large, c5.xlarge c2-standard-4 Standard_F2s_v2 
 Memory r5.large n2-highmem-2 Standard_E2s_v5 
 GPU g4dn.xlarge a2-highgpu-1g Standard_NC4as_T4_v3 

The environment's real monthly cost comes from Infracost when you run a plan, shown in the cost chip on the canvas. See [Cost Estimation](/concepts/cost-estimation).

records.title: Cluster
records.heading: Node Scaling
records.text:
Three numbers control the node group size:

- **Min**: Floor for the autoscaler (nodes will never scale below this)
- **Desired**: Initial node count at creation
- **Max**: Ceiling for the autoscaler (nodes will never scale above this)

Each value is bounded individually (1–100); the form does not enforce a min ≤ desired ≤ max ordering.

records.title: Cluster
records.heading: Cluster Admins
records.text:
An array of identities with admin access to the cluster:

 
 
 IAM user or role ARNs (or IAM user names), entered as a free-text list. Admins are bound to the cluster-admin `system:masters` group at cluster creation.
 
 
 Google email addresses granted `roles/container.admin`.
 
 
 Azure AD Object IDs granted cluster admin RBAC.

records.title: Container Registry
records.text: Container Registry. ECR, Artifact Registry, and ACR configuration — tag mutability and image scanning.

records.title: Container Registry
records.heading: Container Registry
records.text: The container registry section creates managed Docker image registries for your application containers. Multiple registries can be added per project.

records.title: Container Registry
records.heading: Fields Per Registry
records.text:
Field Type Description 
 ------- ------ ------------- 
 **Name** Text input Repository name (e.g., `api`, `frontend`, `worker`) 
 **Provider** Select Cloud-native registry or a [pluggable connector](/console/connectors/pluggable) 
 **Tag Mutability** Select `MUTABLE` (tags can be overwritten) or `IMMUTABLE` (once pushed, a tag is permanent) 
 **Scan on Push** Toggle Automatically scan images for vulnerabilities on push

records.title: Container Registry
records.heading: Registry Provider
records.text:
By default a cloud-native registry (ECR / Artifact Registry / ACR) is created. Select **Docker Hub** to use a Docker Hub repository instead:

- Requires a connected [Docker Hub connector](/console/connectors/pluggable) (username + access token).
- Optional **namespace / organization** (defaults to the username).
- Instead of creating cloud registry repos, the composed module wires a Kubernetes `imagePullSecret` so workloads can pull from Docker Hub; the cloud-native registry is skipped.

records.title: Container Registry
records.heading: Services by Provider
records.text:
**ECR** (Elastic Container Registry)
 - Private repositories with IAM-based access
 - Lifecycle policies (auto-expire old images)
 - Integration with EKS for pull authentication
 
 
 **Artifact Registry**
 - Docker and OCI image support
 - IAM-based access control
 - Vulnerability scanning via Container Analysis
 
 
 **ACR** (Azure Container Registry)
 - SKU tiers: Basic, Standard, Premium
 - Geo-replication (Premium)
 - Integration with AKS for pull authentication

records.title: Container Registry
records.heading: Tag Mutability
records.text:
Mode Behavior Use Case 
 ------ ---------- ---------- 
 **MUTABLE** Same tag (e.g., `latest`) can be pushed multiple times Development, CI/CD with `latest` tag 
 **IMMUTABLE** Once a tag is pushed, it cannot be overwritten Production (ensures deployed image is never changed) 

 
Immutable tags prevent accidental overwrites in production. A `v1.2.3` tag always points to the same image digest, making rollbacks deterministic.

records.title: Container Registry
records.heading: After Provisioning
records.text:
The registry card in project detail shows:
- **Repository URL** — full push/pull endpoint (e.g., `123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/api`)
- **Status** — ACTIVE or CREATING

records.title: Cost
records.text: Cost. The cost chip — an environment's monthly cost, taken from its last plan's Infracost breakdown.

records.title: Cost
records.heading: Cost
records.text:
The cost chip sits in the top-right of the Architecture canvas. It shows the environment's estimated monthly infrastructure cost, taken from the **last plan** — not a live client-side estimate.

For a deeper technical explanation, see [Cost Estimation](/concepts/cost-estimation).

records.title: Cost
records.heading: Where the number comes from
records.text:
The runner runs [Infracost](/concepts/cost-estimation) on every **PLAN** and posts the cost breakdown back with the job. The chip reads the resulting monthly total (`monthlyCost`) off the environment's status — so the cost is only ever a real figure the platform computed, never a guess made in the browser.

The chip only appears once a project and environment exist (an existing environment on the Architecture route). In the design-only create flow there is nothing planned yet, so there is no chip.

records.title: Cost
records.heading: States
records.text:
The chip is honest about what it knows:

 State When What it shows 
 ------- ------ --------------- 
 **Not priced** The environment has never been planned (`monthlyCost` is null) A dashed chip reading `Not priced`, tooltip "Run a plan to price this environment." 
 **Priced** A plan has run `Monthly $X.XX` (two decimals), tooltip "From the plan on ` `" when the capture time is known 

A never-planned environment shows `Not priced` rather than `$0.00` — a fabricated zero is worse than an admitted unknown, because you would believe it.

records.title: Cost
records.heading: The full breakdown
records.text:
The single headline number is the chip. The **per-resource breakdown** lives in the plan's artifact panel, under the Plan tab. The console parses the Infracost breakdown JSON (`parseCostBreakdown`) into a ranked list of cost-bearing resources:

- Each resource carries its `monthlyCost`, `hourlyCost`, `resourceType`, and any priced sub-resources.
- Free or cost-unknown resources (monthly cost `0` or absent) are skipped — the list only ranks priced ones.
- Resources are sorted by monthly cost, most expensive first.
- The plan also carries `totalMonthlyCost` and `totalHourlyCost`.

records.title: Cost
records.heading: Limitations
records.text:
- The figure is only as fresh as the **last plan** — change the design and the number is stale until you plan again.
- Infracost prices what appears in the OpenTofu plan JSON. Usage-based resources (NoSQL, messaging, object storage) and data-transfer costs are not estimated up front.
- A malformed or partial breakdown degrades to "unknown cost" rather than surfacing a wrong number.

records.title: Databases
records.text: Databases. Managed relational databases — Aurora, Cloud SQL, Azure Database with engine selection and capacity.

records.title: Databases
records.heading: Databases
records.text: The databases section configures managed relational database instances. Multiple databases can be added per project, each with its own engine, version, and capacity settings.

records.title: Databases
records.heading: Fields Per Database
records.text:
Field Type Description 
 ------- ------ ------------- 
 **Name** Text input Unique per project, lowercase, used in resource naming 
 **Engine** Select Provider-specific engine (see below) 
 **Engine Version** Auto-set Determined by engine selection 
 **Min Capacity** Number Minimum capacity (ACUs for Aurora, vCPUs for Cloud SQL) 
 **Max Capacity** Number Maximum capacity for auto-scaling 
 **Port** Number Database port (default: 5432 for PostgreSQL, 3306 for MySQL) 
 **IAM Auth** Toggle Authenticate with short-lived cloud IAM tokens instead of a password. PostgreSQL and MySQL, on AWS, GCP and Azure. See [Keyless database auth](/console/design-project/keyless-database-auth)

records.title: Databases
records.heading: Engines by Provider
records.text:
**Aurora Serverless v2** — auto-scaling managed database

 Engine Version Capacity Unit 
 -------- --------- --------------- 
 Aurora PostgreSQL 16.6 ACUs (0.5–128) 
 Aurora MySQL 8.0 ACUs (0.5–128) 

 Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs) scale automatically between min and max. Each ACU provides ~2 GiB of memory. At $0.14/ACU-hour, a 0.5–4 ACU database costs approximately $51–$408/month.
 
 
 **Cloud SQL** — managed database instances

 Engine Version Capacity Unit 
 -------- --------- --------------- 
 Cloud SQL PostgreSQL 15 vCPUs (1–96) 
 Cloud SQL MySQL 8.0 vCPUs (1–96)

 Engine Version Capacity Unit 
 -------- --------- ---------------

records.title: Databases
records.heading: Adding Multiple Databases
records.text:
Click **"Add Database"** to add another instance. Each database gets its own card in the form. The first database defaults to:
- Name: `primary`
- Engine: Aurora PostgreSQL (or equivalent)
- Capacity: 0.5–4 ACUs

Common patterns:
- **Primary + Read Replica**: One write database + one read-optimized database
- **Multi-service**: Separate databases per microservice (e.g., `users-db`, `orders-db`)

records.title: Databases
records.heading: After Provisioning
records.text:
Once deployed, the database card in the [project detail](/console/dashboard/project-detail) Services tab shows:
- **Writer endpoint** — primary connection string
- **Reader endpoint** — read replica connection (Aurora only)
- **Master credentials** — stored in Secrets Manager (ARN shown, copy button)
- **Status** — ACTIVE, CREATING, or FAILED

 
**IAM authentication** lets a workload connect using its own cloud identity and a short-lived token
instead of a stored password — nothing to rotate, no secret in the cluster. A service bound to an
IAM-auth database picks this up automatically.

It covers **PostgreSQL and MySQL on AWS, GCP and Azure**. Alibaba Cloud and Hetzner have no
token-based database login, so a database on either stays on the password path even with the toggle
on. See [Keyless database auth](/console/design-project/keyless-database-auth) for how it works per
cloud and its current rollout status.

records.title: DNS & WAF
records.text: DNS & WAF. Domain configuration, managed certificates, and Web Application Firewall options.

records.title: DNS & WAF
records.heading: DNS & WAF
records.text: The DNS section is optional (controlled by a master toggle). When enabled, it configures domain management, SSL/TLS certificates, and web application firewall protection.

records.title: DNS & WAF
records.heading: Fields
records.text:
Field Type Description 
 ------- ------ ------------- 
 **Enabled** Toggle Master switch for DNS configuration 
 **DNS Provider** Select Cloud-native (Route 53 / Cloud DNS / Azure DNS) or a [pluggable connector](/console/connectors/pluggable) 
 **Zone ID** Select or text Existing DNS hosted zone 
 **Domain Name** Text input Auto-filled from zone, or manually entered 
 **Managed Certificate** Toggle Auto-provision SSL/TLS certificate (cloud-native only) 
 **WAF Options** Toggles Provider-specific WAF configuration (cloud-native only)

records.title: DNS & WAF
records.heading: DNS Provider
records.text:
The **DNS Provider** selector decouples *what* the Project needs (a managed zone) from *who* provides it:

- **Cloud-native** (default) — uses the cluster cloud's DNS service; the managed-certificate and WAF toggles apply.
- **Cloudflare** — manages records on Cloudflare instead. Requires a connected [Cloudflare connector](/console/connectors/pluggable); set the **Zone ID** and the **Proxied** option (orange-cloud). The cloud-native DNS/cert resources are skipped at provision time.

When a pluggable provider is selected, its credential is pulled from `connector_credentials` on the runner at provision time — never stored in the Project.

records.title: DNS & WAF
records.heading: DNS Zones
records.text:
The zone selector shows existing DNS zones from Alethia's server-side [asset inventory](/console/connectors/health-and-inventory):

 
 
 **Route 53** hosted zones (public only). Zone ID format: `Z1234567890ABC`.
 
 
 **Cloud DNS** managed zones. Zone name format: `my-zone`.
 
 
 **Azure DNS** zones. Zone name format: `example.com`.
 
 

 
DNS zones are provider-specific. When duplicating a project across providers, the zone ID and domain are cleared and must be re-configured. See [Multi-Cloud Conversion](/concepts/multi-cloud-conversion).

records.title: DNS & WAF
records.heading: Managed Certificates
records.text:
When enabled, the platform provisions a TLS certificate automatically:

 Provider Issued by Validation 
 ---------- ----------- ------------ 
 AWS ACM (AWS Certificate Manager) DNS validation via Route 53 
 GCP cert-manager, in your cluster ACME DNS01 via Cloud DNS 
 Azure cert-manager, in your cluster ACME DNS01 via Azure DNS 
 Alibaba Not available — bring your own — 
 Hetzner Not available — bring your own — 

Certificates are renewed automatically before expiration.

On **GCP and Azure** the certificate is a free Let's Encrypt one, issued and renewed inside your
cluster by cert-manager and served by the cloud's own ingress — the GKE Ingress reads it from a
Kubernetes Secret, and the Application Gateway has it lifted onto its listener by AGIC. Neither
cloud provisions a cloud-native certificate any more.

On **AWS** the certificate stays in ACM. That is not an oversight: an Application Load Balancer can
only reference a certificate by ARN in ACM or IAM, and ACM will not bind a certificate whose private
key it never held — so a cert-manager certificate cannot terminate an ALB at all. ACM is free and
renews itself, so nothing is lost by it.

On **Alibaba and Hetzner** nothing issu

records.title: DNS & WAF
records.heading: In-cluster certificates
records.text:
On AWS, GCP and Azure the same toggle also installs `cert-manager` in the cluster and creates a
`ClusterIssuer` named `letsencrypt-prod`. Reference it from an Ingress to get a Let's Encrypt
certificate for any hostname in your zone:

metadata:
 annotations:
 cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod

The issuer solves ACME **DNS01** challenges, so it works before you have a public ingress, and it
can issue wildcard certificates. It writes its challenge records with the same cloud identity
`external-dns` uses, so there is no API key to supply.

 
Not available on Alibaba Cloud or Hetzner. `cert-manager` ships no DNS01 solver for either DNS
service, so Alethia creates no issuer rather than one whose challenges never complete. Bring your
own certificate on those clouds. The deploy records the skip and its reason with the environment's
other infrastructure-service decisions.

records.title: DNS & WAF
records.heading: Web Application Firewall
records.text:
WAF protects web applications from common attacks (SQL injection, XSS, bot traffic).

Alethia provisions a WAF on AWS, Google Cloud and Azure only. On Alibaba Cloud the switch is disabled and
says why: WAF 3.0 is an account-level purchase there, so a project that owned one would release the whole
account's firewall when it was destroyed. Buy a WAF 3.0 instance in your own account instead and put it in
front of your ingress from the WAF console. Hetzner sells no web application firewall at all.

 
 
 Two WAF options (can enable both):

 Option Protects Cost 
 -------- ---------- ------ 
 **CloudFront WAF** CDN-level protection ~$5/mo base 
 **Application WAF (ALB)** Load balancer level ~$5/mo base 

 AWS WAFv2 with managed rule groups (AWS Managed Rules, Bot Control).
 
 
 **Cloud Armor** — DDoS and application-layer protection at the load balancer.
 
 
 **Azure WAF** — protection via Application Gateway or Front Door.
 
 

WAF costs are reflected in the [cost sidebar](/console/design-project/cost-sidebar) immediately when toggled.

records.title: Design a Project Overview
records.text: Design a Project Overview. The infrastructure design canvas — add services as nodes, configure each in its inspector, then Plan and Deploy.

records.title: Design a Project Overview
records.heading: Design a Project
records.text: The design **canvas** is where you define infrastructure. You add services as nodes, configure each one in its inspector, and Plan then Deploy the environment. The canvas is the sole design surface — the legacy multi-section form has been removed.

records.title: Design a Project Overview
records.heading: The canvas
records.text:
Every project opens on its **Architecture** view. The root **Project node** holds the project's basics — name, environment stage, and cloud region — and pins the stack's core cloud account, which is chosen once when the project is created. Every other service you add is a node wired to the graph.

Under the hood the canvas persists through an abstract Zod schema and a graph ⇄ form round-trip, so a shared `react-hook-form` context still backs a few inspector fields (repository and region pickers). You interact with nodes and inspectors, not a form.

records.title: Design a Project Overview
records.heading: Adding services
records.text:
Add services from the **Add** palette or the `⌘K` command palette. The **Add** palette groups services by domain (Workloads, Data, Storage, Messaging, Security, Networking, Compute, DevOps) and matches on each entry's label and subtitle. The `⌘K` command palette groups services into **Core** and **Periphery** and searches across every provisionable service by name — its per-cloud service names (e.g. `rds`, `postgres`, `redis`, `s3`) and synonyms. Selecting one drops its node on the canvas and opens its inspector; kinds with variants (for example a database engine) ask you to pick the variant first.

The palette is filtered by the project's cloud: a service the target cloud can't provision (Hetzner has no managed pub/sub or NoSQL, for instance) isn't offered, and a singleton already on the canvas is disabled. Services not yet backed by a Terraform module show a `Soon` badge.

records.title: Design a Project Overview
records.heading: Configuring a node
records.text:
Each node opens its **inspector** — a set of collapsible config sections. The node's effective provider drives its fields, region choices, and provider-specific advanced knobs. The cloud account is not set per node; it is inherited from the Project root.

Existing resources you can reuse (VPCs, subnets, and the like) come from Alethia's server-side
[asset inventory](/console/connectors/health-and-inventory), which stays current automatically
(event-driven + a reconciliation sweep). There's no manual refresh.

 
The cloud account is chosen once, at project creation — there is no in-canvas provider switch. When you duplicate a project onto a different cloud, the platform converts the config and surfaces conversion warnings. See [Multi-Cloud Conversion](/concepts/multi-cloud-conversion).

records.title: Design a Project Overview
records.heading: Services
records.text:
Name, environment, region 
 VPC/VNet, CIDR, NAT gateway 
 Kubernetes, instance types, node scaling, Karpenter 
 Aurora, Cloud SQL, Azure Database 
 Redis, Valkey, Memorystore 
 DynamoDB, Firestore, Cosmos DB 
 SQS, Pub/Sub, Service Bus 
 Route53, certificates, WAF 
 Password generation, secret stores 
 ECR, Artifact Registry, ACR 
 Git repos for GitOps 
 Monthly cost from the last plan

records.title: Design a Project Overview
records.heading: Save, Plan, Deploy
records.text:
Saving a project writes a `projects` row and its **default environment** (a `project_environments` row with status `DRAFT`), then a component row per node in the relevant tables (`project_network`, `project_cluster`, `project_databases`, and so on). The project then appears in the project listing.

From the Architecture view you drive the environment with the **Run** menu and the staged-changes bar:

- **Plan** (`PLAN`) — dry-run the OpenTofu plan and price it with Infracost.
- **Deploy** — apply the staged changes. **Destroy** lives in Project settings.
- **Audit**, **Detect drift**, and **Probe cluster** run their respective jobs against the live environment.

records.title: Design a Project Overview
records.heading: Validation
records.text:
Each service's config is validated by its own Zod schema (`lib/validations/project-form.schema.ts`). For example:

- Project name: free-text display name, max 50 characters; the URL slug is derived via `slugify` (must contain at least one letter or number).
- Bucket names: 3–63 lowercase letters, digits, or hyphens; must start and end with a letter or digit.
- Component names (database, cache, queue, topic, table, secret) are required.

A service the target cloud can't provision, or a service binding to a resource that isn't in the environment, is rejected fail-closed at deploy time rather than silently dropped.

records.title: Keyless Database Auth
records.text: Keyless Database Auth. Bind a service to a PostgreSQL or MySQL database that authenticates with short-lived cloud IAM tokens instead of a password — no secret in the cluster, nothing to rotate.

records.title: Keyless Database Auth
records.heading: Keyless Database Auth
records.text:
When you turn on **IAM Auth** on a database, a service bound to it connects using its own **cloud
identity** and a **short-lived token** — not a stored password. No database password sits in the
cluster to leak or rotate. The workload proves who it is to the cloud, and the cloud hands the
database a token that expires in about an hour.

This is the "hold zero keys" principle applied to the last mile — the app→database hop that
previously still needed a password. It works the same way for **PostgreSQL and MySQL**.

records.title: Keyless Database Auth
records.heading: How a binding decides
records.text:
You don't declare "keyless" on the binding. It is **derived** from the database it points at:

- The database's **IAM Auth** toggle is on → the binding's credential facets go keyless.
- The toggle is off → the binding uses the usual provisioned-password path (a Kubernetes Secret
 synced by the External Secrets Operator).

So the database's own configuration is the single source of truth. Flip the toggle and re-deploy;
nothing on the service changes.

records.title: Keyless Database Auth
records.heading: What you bind
records.text:
For a keyless database, wire the binding's facets as usual, but **omit the password**:

- `endpoint` → resolves to `127.0.0.1` (the app talks to a local auth proxy, see below).
- `port` → the engine's port: **5432** for PostgreSQL, **3306** for MySQL.
- `username` → the workload's cloud login identity (filled in for you from the provision).
- `password` → **not needed** and ignored — there is no password.

The port follows the database's engine, not the binding. A MySQL database always gets 3306, on every
cloud, and the proxy in front of it listens on the same port the app is told to dial.

records.title: Keyless Database Auth
records.heading: How it works per cloud
records.text:
All three clouds converge on the same shape: the app connects to a **local proxy sidecar** on
`127.0.0.1`, and the sidecar authenticates upstream with the pod's own identity. Your application
code is unchanged — it connects to localhost with no password and never learns that tokens exist.

There are two mechanisms. GCP has a native auth proxy. AWS and Azure have none, so the pod runs
**`alethia db-authproxy`** — a subcommand of the runner image, already a pinned sidecar.

`db-authproxy` is a handshake and a pipe, not a pooler. For each new upstream connection it gets a
short-lived database token from the pod's Workload Identity. It dials the real database over TLS,
presenting that token as a cleartext password, then byte-splices the two connections. It does no
pooling, no routing and no query parsing.

Two properties follow from minting the token **in-process**:

- **Nothing is ever at rest.** There is no token file, no rotation store and no admin socket. The
 token exists only in the sidecar's memory, and is reused across connections while it stays valid.
- **Rotation stops being a problem.** Both engines authenticate once, at connect time, so an expiring
 token can never invalida

records.title: Keyless Database Auth
records.heading: The app gets a scoped role, never admin
records.text:
The app's cloud identity logs in, but it maps to a **least-privilege database role**, never a
superuser. A one-shot **bootstrap Job**, which Alethia adds to your GitOps repo, creates that role.
The Job runs as an ArgoCD **PreSync hook**, so it finishes before the app deploys. It connects as the
database administrator, runs the grants, and deletes itself on success.

What the role gets depends on the engine:

- **PostgreSQL** — `CONNECT` on its own database, plus `USAGE` and `CREATE` on the `public` schema.
- **MySQL** — `SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE, DROP, ALTER, INDEX, REFERENCES`, scoped to the
 app's own database. Never `*.*`, never `GRANT OPTION`, never `SUPER`.

All three clouds get the same privileges for a given engine. They differ only in how the login is
**bound** to the cloud identity:

 Cloud PostgreSQL MySQL 
 --- --- --- 
 **AWS** a role granted the `rds_iam` group, so it authenticates by IAM token a user created `IDENTIFIED WITH AWSAuthenticationPlugin`. No identity id appears in the SQL — the IAM policy's user name is the binding 
 **GCP** OpenTofu already created the IAM service-account user, so the Job only grants the same — grants only, against the trunc

records.title: Keyless Database Auth
records.heading: Where it doesn't apply
records.text:
On these clouds the canvas shows **IAM authentication** as unavailable and says why, so you cannot
turn it on. If a database carries the setting anyway — imported from another cloud, written by the
CLI, or created before this gate — the deploy **fails** with the same explanation. It does not fall
back to a password: a database you marked as password-free never quietly gets one.

- **Alibaba Cloud (ApsaraDB RDS)** — ApsaraDB has no IAM/RAM token-based database login. RAM controls
 the *management* API, not database logins, so there is no token for a keyless connection to
 authenticate with.
- **Hetzner** — Hetzner databases are in-cluster ArgoCD add-ons, not a managed cloud service with an
 IAM plane, so there is no keyless identity to use.

To use keyless auth on one of these, move the database to AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure. Otherwise
leave IAM authentication off and use the generated-password path, which is fully supported.

records.title: Keyless Database Auth
records.heading: Rollout status
records.text:
Keyless database auth is **behind a feature flag** while it completes real-cloud verification. The
runner enables it with `ALETHIA_KEYLESS_DB_AUTH_ENABLED=true`. With the flag off, an IAM-auth
database binding uses the normal password path unchanged.

Keyless renders schedule the runner image twice: as the `db-authproxy` sidecar, and as the bootstrap
Job. A published runner image carries its own reference, so there is nothing to set. Set
`ALETHIA_RUNNER_IMAGE` only to name a different image than the one running — a private mirror or an
air-gapped registry. A runner built from source has no published reference, so keyless renders fail
closed there; run a published image to exercise this path.

If a keyless binding can't be fully wired at deploy time (a missing identity, for example), it
**fails closed**: the binding is omitted and the reason is surfaced on the deployment's **Deploy** tab
rather than shipping a workload pointed at nothing. The same holds for the bootstrap Job — if its
admin credential can't be resolved, the Job is skipped and reported instead of wedging the sync.

records.title: Keyless Database Auth
records.heading: See also
records.text:
- [Databases](/console/design-project/databases) — the IAM Auth toggle.
- [Security Architecture](/concepts/security) — the keyless / hold-zero-keys model.

records.title: Messaging
records.text: Messaging. Queues and topics — SQS, SNS, Pub/Sub, Service Bus configuration.

records.title: Messaging
records.heading: Messaging
records.text: The messaging section configures message queues and publish/subscribe topics. Queues and topics are configured independently.

records.title: Messaging
records.heading: Queues
records.text:
Field Type Description 
 ------- ------ ------------- 
 **Name** Text input Queue name 
 **Ordered (FIFO) delivery** Toggle Per-key ordering. See [What "ordered" means](#what-ordered-means) 
 **Visibility Timeout** Number 0–43,200 seconds (displayed as human-readable: s/m/h)

records.title: Messaging
records.heading: What ordered means
records.text:
Ordered delivery means one thing on every cloud Alethia supports:

> Messages tagged with the same ordering key are delivered to consumers in the order the service
> received them. Messages with different keys have no relative order and are still processed
> concurrently.

Three consequences apply everywhere. Read them before you turn the toggle on.

**It is per key, never a total order.** No cloud orders a whole queue. AWS orders within a message
group, Azure within a session, and Google Cloud within an ordering key. A queue with no keys is
unordered even with the toggle on.

**It is an application change, not only an infrastructure change.** Your publisher must set a key on
every message. On Azure your consumer must also accept a session instead of receiving plain
messages — once sessions are on, a client that sends or receives regular messages stops working.

**It costs throughput, and on AWS money.** AWS charges more per request for a FIFO queue and caps it
at 300 messages per second, or 3,000 batched. Google Cloud caps each ordering key at 1 MB/s and
raises delivery latency. Azure gives each session to exactly one receiver at a time.

 
Changing this setting on a queue that al

records.title: Messaging
records.heading: Topics
records.text:
Field Type Description 
 ------- ------ ------------- 
 **Name** Text input Topic name 
 **Subscriptions** JSONB (backend) Configured per consumer after provisioning 

 
 
 **SNS** (Simple Notification Service) — fan-out messaging. Subscribers can be SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP endpoints, email, or SMS.
 
 
 **Pub/Sub Topics** — message publishing endpoint. Subscribers create pull or push subscriptions.
 
 
 **Service Bus Topics** — publish/subscribe messaging with subscription filters.

records.title: Messaging
records.heading: Cost
records.text: Messaging services are usage-based (per message/request), so they show $0 in the cost sidebar. Actual costs depend on message volume and size.

records.title: Network
records.text: Network. VPC/VNet configuration — create new or use existing, CIDR blocks, NAT gateways.

records.title: Network
records.heading: Network
records.text: The network section configures the virtual network that contains all provisioned resources.

records.title: Network
records.heading: Create New vs. Use Existing
records.text: Two modes controlled by a toggle:

records.title: Network
records.heading: Create New Network
records.text:
Provisions a new network from scratch. Fields:

 Field Description 
 ------- ------------- 
 **CIDR Block** IP address range (e.g., `10.0.0.0/16`) 
 **NAT Gateway** Single (cost-optimized) or HA (one per availability zone) 

 
 
 Creates a **VPC** with:
 - Public and private subnets across availability zones
 - Internet Gateway for public subnets
 - NAT Gateway(s) for private subnet internet access
 - Route tables for each subnet type
 - Default security group
 
 
 Creates a **VPC Network** with:
 - Custom-mode subnets in the selected region
 - Cloud NAT with Cloud Router
 - Firewall rules for internal communication
 
 
 Creates a **Virtual Network (VNet)** with:
 - Subnets for cluster nodes and services
 - NAT Gateway for outbound traffic
 - Network Security Groups (NSGs)

records.title: Network
records.heading: Use Existing Network
records.text:
Instead of creating a network, attach the project to one that **already exists** in the account — its id
comes from Alethia's server-side [asset inventory](/console/connectors/health-and-inventory) (network id,
name, CIDR, region).

**How it works — brownfield attach (AWS · GCP · Azure).** When you pick "existing", Alethia records the
network id and, at deploy time, the [Runner](/runner) does **not** create a network. Instead the OpenTofu
template *reads* your existing network and wires the cluster into it:

- **AWS** — the runner looks up the VPC's subnets and passes them in (public/private split).
- **GCP** — the template `data`-sources the VPC network and resolves its subnetwork in the project's
 region (including that subnet's pod/service secondary ranges) for GKE.
- **Azure** — the template `data`-sources the VNet and uses one of its subnets for AKS.

 
Existing networks must be in the same region as the project. The list comes from Alethia's server-side
[asset inventory](/console/connectors/health-and-inventory), which stays fresh automatically (a
reconciliation sweep, plus optional event forwarders) — there's no manual refresh.

records.title: Network
records.heading: Reuse existing resources
records.text:
"Use existing network" is one case of a deliberately **narrow** idea: reuse the **shared substrate you
deploy _into_**, instead of creating a duplicate. The test for whether reuse is a provisioning concern is
simple — **does the rest of the infrastructure graph attach to it?**

- ✅ **Network (VPC/VNet + subnets)** — the cluster and nodes attach into its subnets. Available today on
 AWS, GCP, and Azure (a provision-new vs use-existing toggle; at deploy time the template `data`-sources
 the existing network rather than creating one). The list comes from the server-side
 [asset inventory](/console/connectors/health-and-inventory).
- 🚧 **Kubernetes cluster** — your workloads deploy _onto_ it (nobody wants a fresh cluster per app). Same
 toggle, on the roadmap.

That's the whole scope. **Databases, caches, queues, storage, etc. are _not_ "reuse" targets** — nothing
downstream attaches to them in the graph. If a database already exists, there's nothing to provision:
the app simply needs its **connection endpoint + secret**, which is a *connection/config* concern (a value
you supply), not a provisioned component. Trying to model that as "provision vs existing" just reintroduces
a credent

records.title: Network
records.heading: CIDR Block Validation
records.text:
The form validates CIDR notation in real-time and shows a breakdown. For `10.0.0.0/16`:

 Field Value 
 ------- ------- 
 Total addresses 65,536 
 Usable IPs 65,531 
 Range 10.0.0.0 – 10.0.255.255 
 Size Large 

Common ranges:
- `/16` — 65,536 addresses (recommended for production)
- `/20` — 4,096 addresses (suitable for small environments)
- `/24` — 256 addresses (minimal, development only)

records.title: Network
records.heading: NAT Gateway Cost Impact
records.text:
NAT gateways have significant cost implications:

 Mode AWS Cost Description 
 ------ --------- ------------- 
 Single ~$35/mo One NAT in a single AZ (cost-optimized, single point of failure) 
 HA ~$105/mo (3 AZ) One NAT per AZ (high availability, 3x cost) 

The [cost sidebar](/console/design-project/cost-sidebar) reflects the NAT gateway choice immediately.

records.title: Network
records.heading: Allowed CIDR Blocks
records.text: Optional field for restricting inbound access. Enter CIDR ranges that should be allowed to connect to resources within the network. Default: open to the VPC CIDR only.

records.title: The node inspector
records.text: The node inspector. Open a resource's docked side panel to rename it, read its status, cost and activity, edit its configuration, and remove it — all without leaving the canvas.

records.title: The node inspector
records.heading: The node inspector
records.text:
The node inspector is the docked side panel that opens beside the [canvas](/console/design-project/the-canvas)
when you select a resource. It replaces the old full-page configuration form: everything you used to
edit in a form, you now edit here, on the same board you designed. The panel is split into
**Overview**, **Cost**, **Activity** and **Settings** tabs (the cluster adds a **Deploy** tab), with an
editable header and a status strip above them.

 
The inspector is the **Architecture view** only. It appears when a node is selected and slides away
when nothing is.

records.title: The node inspector
records.heading: Open the inspector
records.text:
1. Open a project's **Architecture** view.
2. Click a resource card.

The panel docks on the right. Clicking a different card swaps the panel to that resource; clicking an
empty area of the board, or the **✕** in the panel header, closes it.

Some cards open a purpose-built panel instead of the generic inspector:

- A **Secrets vault** (or any collapsed collection) opens its member list — see [Secrets](/console/design-project/secrets).
- An **external** card from a bring-your-own IaC module opens a read-only resource list — see
 [Bring your own charts](/console/design-project/bring-your-own-charts).
- A described **chart workload** opens its own describe-and-bind panel.

records.title: The node inspector
records.heading: Rename a resource
records.text:
The resource name lives in the panel header, next to the type badge.

1. Click the name field in the header.
2. Type the new name.

Only resources that carry an editable name show an input here — the **project** (its project name) and
the array-style resources you can add many of (databases, caches, secrets, …). For array resources the
name is forced to lowercase as you type, to match cloud naming rules. Resources with no name of their
own show a fixed label instead.

 
The cloud account is **not** set in the inspector. It is chosen once, at project creation, so there is
no per-node cloud selector.

records.title: The node inspector
records.heading: Read the status strip
records.text:
Under the header, a strip shows the resource's **resolved status** — a grayscale dot and a mono label —
followed by the most actionable line for that state (a config issue, a failure message, or a probe
reason). If the real cloud has diverged from what Alethia recorded, a `N drifted` chip rides alongside
the state; hover it to see the Terraform addresses that diverged.

Status merges the design's readiness with the environment's server truth, and picks one state to show.
See [The canvas → Status without colour](/console/design-project/the-canvas) for the full vocabulary and
precedence order.

records.title: The node inspector
records.heading: Check what a resource produced and costs (Overview)
records.text:
The **Overview** tab is a read-only summary of the selected resource:

 Section Shows 
 --- --- 
 **Type / Status** The resource kind and its resolved status label (with the status message, if any) 
 **Environment** For the project only — the real environment's name, stage, and provisioning status 
 **Endpoints** What the deploy produced (for example a database hostname or ArgoCD URL), each with a copy button 
 **Cost** The resource's estimated monthly cost from the last plan 
 **Recent activity** The environment's latest jobs, condensed to the most recent few 
 **Drift** Each drifted Terraform address, listed on its own 
 **Configuration** The resource's scalar configuration values 

Sections that have nothing to show are omitted — Endpoints appears only once the resource is deployed,
and Cost appears only once the resource has been priced.

records.title: The node inspector
records.heading: Break down cost by resource (Cost)
records.text:
The **Cost** tab shows the resource's monthly spend, itemised by Terraform address.

1. Open the **Cost** tab.
2. Read the **Monthly** rollup at the top.
3. Read the **Breakdown** — one line per Terraform address, sorted from most to least expensive.

The rollup and the per-line detail both come from the last plan's Infracost breakdown, and the tab
notes when that plan ran.

 
A resource that has never been priced says **"Not priced yet"** rather than showing `$0` — run a plan
and its estimated monthly cost appears here. See [Cost Sidebar](/console/design-project/cost-sidebar) for
the pre-plan estimate.

records.title: The node inspector
records.heading: Review recent jobs (Activity)
records.text:
The **Activity** tab lists the environment's recent job history. Activity is scoped to the
**environment**, not the single resource — a deploy provisions the whole board, so a node has no jobs of
its own. Each row shows the job type, its status dot, and how long ago it ran. An environment with no
jobs yet reads **"No activity yet for this environment."**

records.title: The node inspector
records.heading: Edit configuration (Settings)
records.text:
The **Settings** tab is where you change the resource. Its fields are built from the resource's own
config schema, so each kind shows only the knobs that apply to it.

1. Open the **Settings** tab.
2. Expand a section to reveal its fields.
3. Edit a field — changes apply to the design immediately.

Portable fields sit in the top sections, which open by default. **Advanced**, cloud-specific sections
are collapsed by default and badged with the provider they belong to (for example `AWS only`), so you
open the door to non-portable ground deliberately. A section whose fields don't apply to your project's
cloud is not shown at all.

For the **project** panel on a provisioned environment, Settings also shows the environment's name and
stage read-only — the stage is a fact of the environment you're viewing, not a field you pick on the
board.

 
A **core** resource placed on a different cloud than the project is **gated**: Settings shows a notice
that it can be drawn but the project will not provision until the resource is colocated.

records.title: The node inspector
records.heading: Duplicate or delete a resource
records.text:
Structural actions live in the collapsed **Danger zone** at the bottom of the **Settings** tab.

- **Duplicate resource** — create a copy with the same configuration. Available for the array-style
 resources you can have many of.
- **Delete resource** — remove the resource from the canvas. You can undo this with **⌘Z**.

The Danger zone is hidden for the project root (which can't be deleted) and for out-of-band resources
such as marketplace add-ons and bring-your-own charts, which are managed where they were installed.

records.title: The node inspector
records.heading: Destroy an environment
records.text:
When you inspect the **project** in an editable environment, the Settings tab also carries a separate
**Destroy environment** action.

1. Open the project's **Settings** tab.
2. Click **Destroy**.
3. Confirm in the dialog.

This queues a `DESTROY` job that tears down the environment's provisioned cloud infrastructure. It
cannot be undone.

records.title: NoSQL
records.text: NoSQL. DynamoDB, Firestore, and Cosmos DB table configuration with key schema and billing modes.

records.title: NoSQL
records.heading: NoSQL
records.text: The NoSQL section configures managed NoSQL database tables. Multiple tables can be added per project.

records.title: NoSQL
records.heading: Fields Per Table
records.text:
Field Type Description 
 ------- ------ ------------- 
 **Name** Text input Table/collection name 
 **Hash Key** Text input Partition key name (default: `id`) 
 **Hash Key Type** Select `S` (String), `N` (Number), `B` (Binary) 
 **Range Key** Text input Optional sort key name 
 **Range Key Type** Select `S`, `N`, or `B` 
 **Billing Mode** Select `PAY_PER_REQUEST` or `PROVISIONED` 
 **Point-in-Time Recovery** Toggle Enable continuous backups 
 **Table Type** Select `standard` or `global` (multi-region replication)

records.title: NoSQL
records.heading: Services by Provider
records.text:
**DynamoDB** — fully managed key-value and document database

 - Hash key (partition key) + optional range key (sort key)
 - On-demand or provisioned capacity billing
 - Global tables for multi-region replication
 - KMS encryption at rest
 - Point-in-time recovery (continuous backups up to 35 days)
 
 
 **Firestore** — document-oriented NoSQL database

 - Document-based model (collections → documents → fields)
 - Serverless with automatic scaling
 - Multi-region replication built-in

 
 Firestore uses a document model rather than a key-value model. When converting from DynamoDB, hash/range keys map to document IDs. See [Multi-Cloud Conversion](/concepts/multi-cloud-conversion).
 
 
 
 **Cosmos DB** — globally distributed multi-model database

 - Partition key (maps to hash key)
 - Multiple APIs: SQL (document), Table (key-value), MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin
 - Multi-region writes for global distribution
 - Serverless or provisioned throughput (RU/s)

records.title: NoSQL
records.heading: Billing Modes
records.text:
Mode Description Best For 
 ------ ------------- ---------- 
 **PAY_PER_REQUEST** Pay per read/write operation, no capacity planning Unpredictable workloads, development 
 **PROVISIONED** Reserved read/write capacity units Predictable workloads, cost optimization 

 
NoSQL tables show $0 in the cost sidebar because pricing is usage-based (per operation), not estimable from configuration alone. Actual costs depend on read/write patterns.

records.title: Observability
records.text: Observability. Ship cluster metrics, logs, and traces to Datadog or Grafana Cloud.

records.title: Observability
records.heading: Observability
records.text: The observability section ships cluster metrics, logs, and traces to an external monitoring platform. Unlike DNS or secrets, observability has **no cloud-native default** — it is a connector-only component, so enabling it means choosing a provider and connecting its credential.

records.title: Observability
records.heading: Fields
records.text:
Field Type Description 
 ------- ------ ------------- 
 **Enabled** Toggle Master switch for observability 
 **Provider** Select Datadog or Grafana Cloud 
 **Provider options** Varies Provider-specific configuration (see below)

records.title: Observability
records.heading: Providers
records.text:
Installs the **Datadog agent** via Helm. Requires a connected [Datadog connector](/console/connectors/pluggable) (API key + application key). Choose the **site** (e.g. `datadoghq.com`, `datadoghq.eu`).
 
 
 Installs the **Grafana Agent** remote-writing metrics to Grafana Cloud. Requires a connected [Grafana Cloud connector](/console/connectors/pluggable) (instance ID + API token) and the **remote-write URL**.
 
 

 
Want a self-hosted metrics stack instead of an external platform? Add the **kube-prometheus-stack** [add-on](/cli/commands/addons) — it installs Prometheus, Grafana, and Alertmanager in-cluster. Prometheus is an add-on (an in-cluster workload), not an observability connector (a credential to an external system).

records.title: Observability
records.heading: Credentials
records.text:
Provider credentials are connected on the [Connectors](/console/connectors/pluggable) page and encrypted at rest. They are decrypted and injected into the runner's OpenTofu variables at provision time — never stored in the Project snapshot.

 
Observability is a **target-state** component — the connector backends and modules exist; the Project-designer selector is rolling out. Track the [Connectors Architecture](/concepts/connectors) page for the current contract.

records.title: Project Basics
records.text: Project Basics. Project name, environment stage, and the OpenTofu (iac_version) default — the Project node's basics.

records.title: Project Basics
records.heading: Project Basics
records.text: The Project node — the root of the design canvas — establishes the project identity and its default target environment. A project owns **N environments** (`project_environments`); creating a project seeds the default one.

records.title: Project Basics
records.heading: Fields
records.text:
The Project node's inspector has two sections — **General** (name, environment) and **Placement** (region).

 Field Type Validation Description 
 ------- ------ ----------- ------------- 
 **Project Name** Text input Required, max 50 chars — free-text display name The URL slug is derived from it via `slugify`; also drives resource naming and OpenTofu state paths 
 **Environment** Radio cards Required `development`, `staging`, or `production` — seeds the default environment's `stage` 
 **Region** Region picker Required The cloud region, grouped by geography and keyed to the project's cloud account 

The cloud account is chosen once when the project is created, not per node. OpenTofu itself is pinned to `1.11.4` (the `iac_version` field); the canvas does not expose a version picker.

records.title: Project Basics
records.heading: Project Name
records.text:
The project name is a free-text display name. Alethia derives a URL slug from it (lowercasing and replacing spaces and punctuation with hyphens) via `slugify`. The derived slug is used for:
- Resource naming in OpenTofu (e.g., `{slug}-{env}-eks-cluster`)
- State file path (see [OpenTofu State](/concepts/terraform-state))

The display name appears in the UI (project cards, job listings).

 
You can type any display name — Alethia slugifies it so the identifier is always safe for cloud resource naming constraints across every provider. The name must contain at least one letter or number.

records.title: Project Basics
records.heading: Environment Stage
records.text:
`stage` is a property of the **environment**, not the project. A project can own several environments
(dev / staging / prod), each independently provisionable with its own `stage`. The three options:

 Stage Purpose Naming Convention 
 ------- --------- ------------------ 
 `development` Dev/testing `{project}-dev-*` 
 `staging` Pre-production `{project}-staging-*` 
 `production` Production workloads `{project}-prod-*` 

The environment stage affects OpenTofu state isolation — each stage gets its own state file, even within the same project and region.

records.title: Repositories
records.text: Repositories. Git repository selection for application deployment via ArgoCD.

records.title: Repositories
records.heading: Repositories
records.text: The repositories section configures the Git repository that ArgoCD watches for application manifests. This is optional — if not configured, ArgoCD is installed but doesn't manage any applications automatically.

records.title: Repositories
records.heading: Fields
records.text:
Field Type Description 
 ------- ------ ------------- 
 **Application Repo** Repository selector Git repo containing Kubernetes manifests or Helm charts

records.title: Repositories
records.heading: Repository Selector
records.text: The selector shows repositories from your connected Git provider (GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket). It fetches the repository list using the stored OAuth token (see [Authentication](/concepts/authentication)).

records.title: Repositories
records.heading: How It Works with ArgoCD
records.text:
When a repository is configured:

1. During DEPLOY, the Runner clones the repo and sets it up as an ArgoCD Application source
2. ArgoCD watches the repo for changes (polling or webhook)
3. Any push to the configured branch triggers ArgoCD to sync the manifests to the cluster
4. The ArgoCD UI shows deployment status, sync state, and health

See [GitOps & ArgoCD](/concepts/gitops-argocd) for the full ArgoCD architecture.

 
The repository is accessed using the OAuth token from your Git provider integration. ArgoCD stores a copy of the token as a Kubernetes Secret in the cluster. Token refresh is handled automatically.

records.title: Secrets
records.text: Secrets. Managed secrets with auto-generation, presets, and cloud-native secret stores.

records.title: Secrets
records.heading: Secrets
records.text: The secrets section creates entries in your cloud provider's secret management service. Secrets can be auto-generated with configurable parameters or set to custom values after provisioning.

records.title: Secrets
records.heading: Fields Per Secret
records.text:
Field Type Description 
 ------- ------ ------------- 
 **Name** Text input Secret name (alphanumeric + hyphens only) 
 **Provider** Select Cloud-native store or a [pluggable connector](/console/connectors/pluggable) 
 **Generate** Toggle Auto-generate a random value 
 **Length** Number 8–128 characters 
 **Special Characters** Toggle Include `!@#$%^&*()` in generated value

records.title: Secrets
records.heading: Secrets Provider
records.text:
By default secrets are created in the cluster cloud's native secret store. Select **HashiCorp Vault** to manage them in a Vault instance instead:

- Requires a connected [Vault connector](/console/connectors/pluggable) (Vault address + token).
- Per-Project knobs: the KV **mount path** and **KV version** (1 or 2).
- The cloud-native secret resources are skipped at provision time; Vault entries are managed by the composed module.

records.title: Secrets
records.heading: Presets
records.text:
Quick-add buttons create secrets with recommended settings:

 Preset Length Special Chars Use Case 
 -------- -------- -------------- ---------- 
 PostgreSQL Password 32 Yes Database master password 
 API Token 48 No Application API key 
 JWT Secret 64 No Token signing key 
 Redis Password 32 No Cache authentication 
 Custom Secret 32 No User-defined

records.title: Secrets
records.heading: Secret Store by Provider
records.text:
**AWS Secrets Manager** — $0.40/secret/month + $0.05 per 10,000 API calls.
 Supports automatic rotation, cross-account access, and integration with RDS for database credential management.
 
 
 **Secret Manager** — $0.06 per 10,000 access operations.
 Supports automatic replication, IAM-based access control, and versioning.
 
 
 **Key Vault** — $0.03 per 10,000 operations.
 Supports secrets, keys, and certificates. Integrates with Azure AD for access control.

records.title: Secrets
records.heading: Integration with Kubernetes
records.text: After provisioning, secrets are synced to Kubernetes via the **External Secrets Operator** (installed by ArgoCD — see [GitOps & ArgoCD](/concepts/gitops-argocd)). This creates Kubernetes `Secret` resources from cloud secret store entries, keeping them in sync automatically.

records.title: Services
records.text: Services. A service is a first-class canvas node for your own code — built from a repo or a prebuilt image, run as a Kubernetes workload with validated ports, environment, resources, health, and bindings.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Services
records.text:
A **service** is the customer's own application code on the cluster. Unlike the infrastructure kinds (databases, caches, secrets), a service is built from your source and run as a Kubernetes workload. The runner turns each service into Kubernetes manifests at deploy time.

A service is a first-class node kind on the [canvas](/console/design-project/the-canvas): it carries its own validated configuration and it binds to the backing infrastructure it depends on.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Adding a service
records.text: Services lead the Add palette in the **Workloads** group. Selecting **Service** drops a node on the canvas and opens its config sheet.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Identity
records.text:
Field Type Notes 
 ------- ------ ------- 
 **Name** Text Required. Unique per project and environment. 
 **Type** Choice The Kubernetes workload kind. Defaults to **Deployment**. 

The workload type is one of:

 Type Description 
 ------ ------------- 
 **Deployment** Long-running, load-balanced. 
 **Job** Runs once to completion. 
 **CronJob** Runs on a schedule. 
 **StatefulSet** Stable identity and storage.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Source
records.text:
A service's image comes from one of two sources:

 Source Fields 
 -------- -------- 
 **Repository** `Repository URL` (required) and an optional `Path` (subdirectory to build from). Alethia builds and pushes the image. 
 **Prebuilt image** `Image` (required) — a pushed image reference deployed as-is, e.g. `ghcr.io/org/api:1.4.0`.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Build
records.text:
The build fields apply only when the source is a **Repository**. Both are optional:

 Field Description 
 ------- ------------- 
 **Dockerfile** Path to the Dockerfile. 
 **Context** Build context directory. 

For a prebuilt image, the Build section does not apply.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Networking
records.text:
Add the container ports the workload exposes. Each port has:

 Field Type Notes 
 ------- ------ ------- 
 **Container port** Number Required. 1–65535. 
 **Protocol** Choice `TCP` or `UDP`. Optional. 
 **Name** Text Optional.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Environment
records.text:
Add plain environment variables as `name` / `value` pairs.

 
Environment variables added here are plain values. To inject a resource's endpoint or credentials,
use a **binding** (below) — Alethia delivers credentials as a Kubernetes `secretKeyRef`, never as a
plain value in the manifest.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Bindings
records.text:
A binding connects the service to a backing resource on the canvas and declares which environment variables that connection injects. Alethia resolves each binding at deploy time — keyless.

A binding targets one resource kind:

 Target kind 
 ------------- 
 Database 
 Cache 
 Queue 
 Secret 

Each binding declares any number of injected variables. Each maps an environment variable name to a **facet** of the connection:

 Facet Delivered as 
 ------- -------------- 
 `endpoint` Templated value in the manifest 
 `port` Templated value in the manifest 
 `username` Kubernetes `secretKeyRef` 
 `password` Kubernetes `secretKeyRef` 
 `connection string` Kubernetes `secretKeyRef` 

The non-secret facets (`endpoint`, `port`) are written into the manifest as templated values; the credential facets (`username`, `password`, `connection string`) are delivered as a `secretKeyRef` and never written into the manifest.

A binding can also target a [bring-your-own IaC](/console/design-project/bring-your-own-charts) resource by its Terraform address, in which case the facets resolve against the customer module's declared output names.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Runtime
records.text:
Field Type Notes 
 ------- ------ ------- 
 **Replicas** Number Defaults to `2`. The inspector accepts 1–5. 
 **CPU request** Text Kubernetes quantity string, e.g. `100m`. 
 **Memory request** Text Kubernetes quantity string, e.g. `128Mi`. 
 **CPU limit** Text Kubernetes quantity string, e.g. `500m`. 
 **Memory limit** Text Kubernetes quantity string, e.g. `512Mi`. 

Resource requests and limits are optional. When they are left unset, the runner's template defaults apply.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Health
records.text:
A service can gate its rollout on a probe. When the health check is enabled:

 Field Type Notes 
 ------- ------ ------- 
 **Probe type** Choice `HTTP` (check an HTTP endpoint) or `TCP` (open a TCP connection). 
 **Path** Text HTTP probes only, e.g. `/healthz`. 
 **Port** Number 1–65535. 

When the health check is disabled, no probe is configured.

records.title: Services
records.heading: Related
records.text:
- [The canvas](/console/design-project/the-canvas) — how nodes and edges model your project.
- [Databases](/console/design-project/databases) — a common binding target; see also [keyless database auth](/console/design-project/keyless-database-auth).
- [Secrets](/console/design-project/secrets) — bind a service to a managed secret.

records.title: Object Storage
records.text: Object Storage. Object storage buckets are a first-class canvas node with their own fields, S3-safe naming rules, and per-provider backing services.

records.title: Object Storage
records.heading: Object Storage
records.text:
A **bucket** is a first-class node on the [architecture canvas](/console/design-project/the-canvas) — the same standing as a database, cache, or container registry. Add one from the palette's **Storage** group to provision object storage for files and assets. Multiple buckets can be added per project.

Each bucket is scoped to the project's cloud account and environment. Its name is unique per project, per environment.

records.title: Object Storage
records.heading: Fields Per Bucket
records.text:
Field Type Default Description 
 ------- ------ --------- ------------- 
 **Name** Text input `assets` Bucket name (S3-safe — see [Naming rules](#naming-rules)) 
 **Versioning** Toggle Off Keep every version of an object; restore or roll back at any time (on Azure this applies to the whole project — see [Azure](#azure)) 
 **Encryption at rest** Toggle On Server-side encryption with the cloud's managed keys 
 **Public access** Toggle Off (private) Allow unauthenticated reads (static assets); off keeps the bucket private 
 **CORS origins** Text Empty Comma-separated origins allowed to read from the browser 

The name, versioning, and encryption fields are grouped under **General**; public access and CORS origins are grouped under **Access**.

records.title: Object Storage
records.heading: Naming rules
records.text:
Bucket names use the strictest cloud rules, so one name works on every provider:

- 3–63 characters.
- Lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens only.
- Must start and end with a letter or digit (no leading or trailing hyphen).

The name field lowercases input and strips disallowed characters as you type; the full rule is validated on save.

 
A single S3-safe name is portable across AWS, GCP, Azure, Alibaba Cloud, and Hetzner, so a bucket you design on one provider provisions unchanged on another.

records.title: Object Storage
records.heading: Backing service by provider
records.text:
Buckets are supported on every provider. The name and toggles map to each cloud's object-storage service:

 Provider Service 
 ---------- --------- 
 **AWS** S3 
 **GCP** Cloud Storage 
 **Azure** Blob Storage 
 **Alibaba Cloud** OSS 
 **Hetzner** MinIO (Object Storage)

records.title: Object Storage
records.heading: Hetzner
records.text:
Compute-only Hetzner projects provision buckets natively via Object Storage (the `aminueza/minio` OpenTofu provider). Two fields differ on Hetzner:

- **Encryption at rest** is not shown — Hetzner Object Storage always encrypts at rest, so there is no per-bucket toggle.
- **CORS origins** is not shown — the provider does not apply CORS to Hetzner's S3 backend.

records.title: Object Storage
records.heading: Azure
records.text:
Two fields behave differently on Azure, because Blob Storage puts the setting on the storage account rather than the container. An Azure project has one storage account, which holds every bucket in the project.

- **Versioning** is an account setting. Turning it on for one bucket versions **every** bucket in that project. Leaving it on for a bucket that no longer needs it costs storage; the alternative — ignoring a bucket that asks for it — loses data on the first overwrite, so Alethia turns versioning on for the account whenever any bucket asks for it.
- **Public access** is applied per bucket, as it is everywhere else. The account permission that allows public containers is opened only when at least one bucket asks for public access, and stays closed otherwise.

records.title: Object Storage
records.heading: Google Cloud
records.text:
**Public access** on Google Cloud does two things: it stops Cloud Storage from refusing public grants on that bucket, and it grants read access to everyone. Uniform bucket-level access stays on for every bucket regardless — it controls per-object ACLs, not public reads, and Cloud Storage will not let it be turned off again once a bucket has had it for 90 days.

 
Many Google Cloud organizations set the `constraints/iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains` organization policy, which blocks public grants everywhere in the organization. Under that policy a public bucket is refused when the project is deployed, and the deployment says so rather than failing part-way through.

records.title: Object Storage
records.heading: Cloud placement
records.text: A bucket inherits the project's cloud account and region. When left unset, its per-resource cloud identity and region fall back to the project's own — so a bucket lands in the same account and region as the rest of the project unless it is placed on another connected account.

records.title: Object Storage
records.heading: On the canvas
records.text:
The bucket card summarizes its configuration without opening the inspector:

- **Access** — `public` or `private`.
- **Versioning** — `on` or `off`.
- **CORS** — the number of allowed origins, or `none`.

records.title: Object Storage
records.heading: After provisioning
records.text: Each bucket carries a lifecycle status — `PENDING`, `CREATING`, `ACTIVE`, `UPDATING`, `FAILED`, `DESTROYING`, or `DESTROYED` — and an estimated monthly cost that rolls up into the [cost sidebar](/console/design-project/cost-sidebar).

records.title: The canvas
records.text: The canvas. How the architecture canvas is designed — what a card tells you, how status reads without colour, why some resources collapse into one card, and how detail changes with zoom.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: The canvas
records.text:
The Architecture view is where a project's infrastructure is designed, deployed, and kept honest.
This page explains how to *read* it — the conventions are deliberate, and once you know them the
board tells you a great deal at a glance.

The canvas is **fully grayscale**. Nothing on it is colour-coded. That is a constraint, not an
oversight: colour is the first thing to fail under a projector, a screenshot, colour-blindness, or a
dark room. So every distinction you can see is carried by **shape, structure, and type** instead —
and the one exception is the cloud provider's own brand mark, which stays in its original colours
because it belongs to someone else.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: What a card tells you
records.text: Every resource is a card, and every card is built from the same four parts.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: The glyph and the eyebrow
records.text:
Top-left: the service's icon and its kind, in uppercase mono. This is the fastest read — *what kind
of thing is this*.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: The facts
records.text:
The middle of the card is a small grid of the **two or three facts that actually matter for that
service**. This is what makes a database look like a database and not like a DNS zone:

 Resource Reads as 
 --- --- 
 Database `PostgreSQL 16 · 0.5–4 · 7 d` 
 Cache `Valkey · cache.t3.medium · 2 · multi-AZ` 
 Bucket `private · on · 2 origins` 
 Cluster `1.31 · 2–5 · m5a.large` 
 Topic `3 subscriptions · push · pull` 

A fact with no value yet draws a **muted dash**, so an unconfigured resource reads as unconfigured
without having to open it.

The facts are **cloud-honest**. On a compute-only cloud like Hetzner there is no managed database
service, so a database is deployed as a CloudNativePG cluster *inside your Kubernetes cluster* — and
the card says exactly that (`Runs as · CloudNativePG`) rather than implying a managed service that
doesn't exist. The same is true of caches (Valkey) and queues (RabbitMQ).

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: The provider chip
records.text:
Which cloud account this resource lands in. A resource with no chip of its own **inherits the
project's** cloud — that's the common case, and the chip says `inherits core`.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: The classification rule
records.text:
The thin band across the **top edge** of the card says what kind of citizen the resource is:

 Rule Meaning 
 --- --- 
 Solid, full ink **Root** — the project itself, the anchor everything inherits from 
 Solid, strong **Core** — must sit on the project's cloud (network, cluster, data services) 
 Hairline **Periphery** — may live on a different cloud (DNS, buckets, registry, secrets, GitOps) 
 Dashed **External** — not managed by this design (a bring-your-own Helm chart or IaC module)

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: Status without colour
records.text:
Status is shown by a **dot**, read by its fill and shape, with a short mono label beside it. There is
no red and no green anywhere.

 Dot State Means 
 --- --- --- 
 Solid **Live** / **Ready** Nominal. The calm state — it shows only the dot, no label. 
 Hollow ring **Needs setup** / **Not deployed** Designed but incomplete, or never applied. 
 Haloed **Queued** / **Updating** / **Update pending** / **Destroying** Something is pending. 
 Blinking **Applying** A runner is changing this resource right now. 
 Hollow-centre **Failed** / **Unreachable** A real, actionable break. 
 Faint **Gated** / **Destroyed** Inert — it won't provision, or it's gone. 

The canvas stays **calm when everything is fine**: a healthy resource shows a dot and nothing else.
Anything that wants your attention carries a label. If the board is quiet, it's quiet because there
is nothing to say.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: One state, chosen deliberately
records.text:
A resource often has several truths at once — its design is invalid, *and* it's live, *and* it has
drifted. The canvas picks one to show, in a fixed order:

1. **Failed** — a real break outranks everything.
2. **In flight** (queued · applying · updating · destroying) — what's *happening* outranks what's *wrong*.
3. **Needs setup** — the design itself is invalid, so the next deploy will not work. This is shown
 *even for a resource that is currently live*, because the deploy you are about to run is the thing
 that matters.
4. **Gated** — valid, but it won't provision (see below).
5. **Destroyed**, then **Not deployed**.
6. **Unreachable** — it exists, but the cluster's API server didn't answer the last probe.
7. **Update pending** — live, but the design has moved ahead of what's deployed.
8. **Live** / **Ready**.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: Drift is an overlay, not a state
records.text:
If the real cloud has diverged from what Alethia recorded, the resource is still **Live** — it just
carries a `2 drifted` chip alongside. Drift never replaces the state, it rides on top of it. The
resource's panel lists exactly which Terraform resources diverged.

Drift that can't confidently be traced back to a specific resource is reported **at the environment**
rather than pinned to a card it might not belong to. An honest "2 resources drifted, unattributed" is
better than a wrong badge on your database.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: Gated
records.text:
A **core** resource placed on a different cloud than the project is drawn as **gated**. It can be
designed and drawn, but the project will not provision until it's colocated. This mirrors the
provisioner's own rule — the canvas will never let you believe something will deploy when it won't.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: Regions — where a resource actually runs
records.text:
The board draws two nested regions, and puts each resource where it really lives:

- The **VPC** — your network. It holds the cluster, and every managed data service.
- The **cluster** — nested inside the VPC. It holds what runs as a workload in Kubernetes.

Everything else — DNS, buckets, the container registry, secrets, the GitOps repository — sits
**outside both**. That isn't an accident of layout: those are exactly the resources that have no VPC,
which is why they're the ones allowed to live on a *different cloud* from the rest of the project.

Drawn flat, a managed database and an in-cluster Grafana look like the same kind of thing. They are
not: the database runs *in* the VPC but *outside* Kubernetes, and Grafana runs *inside* the cluster.
The regions make that difference visible at a glance.

 
On a compute-only cloud like Hetzner there is no managed data plane, so databases, caches and queues
deploy as Helm charts **inside your cluster** — and the board draws them there. The same design lays
out differently on a different cloud, because it genuinely *deploys* differently.
