Regions are derived from the resources inside them, so dragging a card simply re-shapes the region
a

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: Collections — when one card stands for many
records.text:
A real project has thirty or forty secrets. Thirty cards would bury the architecture: the canvas
would stop being a picture of your system and become a wall of near-identical boxes.

So high-cardinality resources **collapse into a single card** — a vault. Secrets work this way today.
The card shows the count, a few names, and **the state of its unhappiest member**: a vault holding one
failed secret can never read *Live*. Collapsing hides the clutter, never the trouble.

Open the vault to get the full list, filter it, add or remove entries, and click through to any single
secret to configure it exactly as you would any other resource. Nothing is taken away — only the
board is kept readable.

 
This is a rendering decision, not a data model. Every secret is still an individual resource with its
own configuration, its own status, and its own line in the deploy diff.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: Bring your own IaC — still an architecture
records.text:
An environment can be provisioned from **your own OpenTofu module** instead of the built-in template.
When it is, the module — not the component design — is the source of truth, so you can't add
components to it.

That doesn't make it a black box. Alethia inventories the module's resources and draws them, so a
bring-your-own environment reads as an architecture like any other:

- Resources are grouped into cards **by kind and by Terraform module** — the `aws_vpc` and its
 subnets become one **Network** card; the `aws_eks_*` resources a **Cluster** card. A real module is
 fifty to two hundred resources, and drawn one per card they would bury the architecture, so the
 same collapsing rule that governs the Secrets vault applies here.
- The cards sit in the **same VPC and cluster regions** as a template environment, because that is
 genuinely where they run.
- They are drawn **dashed** — external. Alethia plans, prices, drifts and audits these resources; it
 does not own their definition. Changing one means editing your Terraform, so the cards are
 read-only. Open one to see every resource inside it: its address, what the last plan would do to
 it, what it costs, and whether it has dri

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: Detail follows zoom
records.text:
Cards shed **detail** before they shed **legibility**, so a large architecture stays readable:

 Zoom Shows 
 --- --- 
 Far out The glyph, the name, and a status dot 
 Middle Header, name, and the single most important fact 
 Close in The full card — facts, provider, status, everything 

Zoom out to see the shape of the system; zoom in to work on it.

records.title: The canvas
records.heading: Reading the board quickly
records.text:
- **Everything quiet, dots only** — the environment is healthy and matches its design.
- **A hollow-centre dot** — something failed or a cluster stopped answering. Start there.
- **A blinking dot** — a deploy is in flight right now.
- **Dashed borders** — resources you brought yourself; Alethia plans and verifies them but does not
 own their definition.
- **Faint dots** — inert. Either gated (won't provision) or already destroyed.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.text: Fleet Pools. Configure a managed warm pool of runners for a cloud so the fleet controller keeps capacity sized to demand.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Fleet Pools
records.text:
A **warm pool** is a declarative target for one cloud's managed runners: a floor of always-ready
runners, a ceiling on spend, and a version to converge to. The **fleet controller** — a 60-second
loop — reads every pool each tick and provisions, drains, or replaces runners to match. Editing a
pool in the console takes effect on the next tick, with no redeploy.

Pools live in the **Pools** panel on the [Runners](/console/runners) page. For the runner agent
itself, see [Runners](/console/runners).

 
Warm pools apply to **managed** runners only — the fleet Alethia operates and bills by provisioned
hours. You don't register or deploy them yourself; you configure a pool and the controller keeps it
sized. Self-operated runners are added from **Add Runner** instead.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Before you start
records.text:
- **This is a self-managed deployment.** The Pools panel is shown only on self-managed installs,
 where the operator is you. On the hosted SaaS the panel is hidden and the fleet actions refuse.
- **You can manage the fleet.** Creating, editing, pausing, and deleting pools is gated to
 owner/admin. Without that capability the panel is read-only and the **Add pool** button is hidden.
- **A cloud provider is wired for real VMs.** Set `FLEET_PROVIDER=hcloud` to provision runners on the
 Hetzner VM fleet. Until then a pool is **advisory** — the controller logs the actions it *would*
 take but creates nothing, and the panel shows a "pools are advisory" notice.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Open the Pools panel
records.text:
1. Go to the [Runners](/console/runners) page.
2. Find the **Pools** panel in the left column. It lists one card per configured pool, or an empty
 state when none exist.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Add a pool
records.text:
Click **Add pool** to open the wizard. It walks five steps — **Cloud → Placement → Capacity →
Version → Review** — and validates each before you advance.

 
There is **one pool per cloud**. A cloud that already has a pool is disabled in the picker, and a
pool's cloud can't change after creation — edit or delete the existing pool instead.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Choose the cloud
records.text:
Pick the **cloud provider** whose runners this pool manages. Optionally set a **display name** shown
on the pool card; it defaults to the provider name.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Set placement
records.text:
Enter **locations** as comma-separated region codes for that cloud (for example, Hetzner `fsn1,
nbg1`). The controller spreads runners across them, so a degraded region doesn't take the pool down.
At least one location is required.

Set a **minimum per location** to keep that many runners in every listed location. Leave it `0` for
no per-region floor.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Set capacity
records.text:
Field Meaning 
 --- --- 
 **Warm minimum** Runners kept booted and ready at all times, even with zero queued jobs. 
 **Maximum** The hard ceiling — the most runners the pool will ever provision, no matter how deep the queue. 
 **Idle buffer** Extra idle runners kept above current demand (N+1 headroom) so a new job rarely waits for a boot. `0` scales exactly to demand. 
 **Slots / runner** How many jobs one runner executes at once. Higher packs more work per VM but shares its CPU and memory. 

A live preview reads the numbers back in plain English. When a runner takes more than one slot, it
also shows the maximum concurrent jobs (maximum × slots per runner).

Two rules are enforced: the maximum must be at least the warm minimum, and the idle buffer can't
exceed the maximum. If the per-location minimum times the number of locations exceeds the maximum,
the wizard warns you to raise the maximum or lower the floor.

Expand **Advanced scaling** for two more knobs:

 Field Meaning 
 --- --- 
 **Rollout surge** Extra runners the controller may run above the ceiling during a version rollout, so it replaces old runners without dropping capacity. 
 **Scale-down grace** Consecutive 60-second

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Choose a version source
records.text:
Pick how the pool tracks runner versions:

- **Channel** — track a moving release stream (usually `stable`). The controller resolves the
 channel to the newest release each tick and auto-updates the pool.
- **Pinned** — hold one exact version until you change it.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Review and create
records.text:
Check the summary and click **Create pool**. The controller wakes immediately and begins converging
the pool toward its target.

 

New capacity is always created at the target version. When you change the version, the controller
rolls runners over one step per tick — draining an outdated runner only while it can surge a
replacement first, so online capacity never drops below the warm floor.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Read a pool card
records.text:
Each card derives its numbers from the pool's configured target joined with the runners it observes:

- **Warm capacity** — online runners over the target, drawn as a segmented meter. Filled segments are
 online runners, hatched segments are online-and-busy, dashed segments are the gap to target. A note
 line shows how many are below floor, busy, and draining.
- **Rollout** — the percentage of live runners already on the target version, with the target and a
 progress bar while a rollout is in flight.
- **Versions** and **Locations** — how live runners are distributed; a tally is flagged when it's off
 the target version or a location has an offline runner.
- **Health** — **Healthy**, or **Degraded** when the pool is below its warm floor or any runner is
 offline. A paused pool is dimmed and labelled **Paused**.
- **Economics** (manager-only) — a month-to-date footer with provisioned hours, estimated cost, and
 utilization.

records.title: Fleet Pools
records.heading: Edit, pause, or delete a pool
records.text:
Open the **⋮** menu on a pool card (visible to managers):

- **Edit** reopens the wizard on that pool. Its cloud is fixed; every other knob is editable, and
 changes converge live on the next tick.
- **Pause** stops the pool. The controller reconciles a paused pool as a teardown target — it drains
 every runner to zero and closes each runner's usage session, so pausing leaves no billable orphans.
 **Resume** rebuilds the warm floor over the next few ticks.
- **Delete** removes the pool. The controller drains and reaps its runners on the next tick before
 the row is removed. This cannot be undone.

 
Pausing and deleting both drain a pool to zero. A busy runner is drained first — it stops claiming
new work and finishes its in-flight job — before it's destroyed, so no running job is dropped.

records.title: Getting Started
records.text: Getting Started. Quick start guide — sign up, connect a cloud provider, design a Project, and deploy.

records.title: Getting Started
records.heading: Getting Started
records.text: This guide walks through the complete flow from sign-up to a running Kubernetes cluster with ArgoCD.

records.title: Getting Started
records.heading: Prerequisites
records.text:
- An AWS, GCP, or Azure account with admin-level access
- A GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket account

records.title: Getting Started
records.heading: Sign Up
records.text:
Open the Console and sign in with a supported social provider (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or Google) or with a 6-digit email OTP. Your account is created automatically on first login.

After sign-in, you'll land on the dashboard — empty, with no projects or jobs.

records.title: Getting Started
records.heading: Connect a Cloud Provider
records.text:
Go to **Connectors** in the sidebar. Connect your cloud account:

 
 
 1. Click **Connect** on the AWS card
 2. Run the setup script in **AWS CloudShell** (or apply the OpenTofu module) — it creates an IAM OIDC provider trusting the Alethia issuer + a role (no access keys, no external id)
 3. Paste the resulting **Role ARN** back into Alethia
 4. Alethia verifies the new cloud identity by assuming the role via `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`
 
 
 1. Click **Connect** on the GCP card
 2. Run the provided setup script (or OpenTofu module) — it creates the **Workload Identity Pool** + OIDC provider + provisioner service account in your project
 3. Enter the two values it prints — **Project ID** and **Project Number** (Alethia assembles the WIF config; there is no JSON to copy)
 4. Alethia verifies the new cloud identity via Workload Identity Federation
 
 
 1. Click **Connect** on the Azure card
 2. Run the setup script in **Azure Cloud Shell** — it creates a **User-Assigned Managed Identity** in your own subscription with a federated credential trusting the Alethia issuer, and a least-privilege provisioning role (you register no app, store no secret)
 3. Enter the three values it prints

records.title: Getting Started
records.heading: Connect a Git Provider
records.text: On the same Connectors page, click **Connect** on GitHub (or GitLab/Bitbucket). This uses standard OAuth — authorize the app, and you're connected.

records.title: Getting Started
records.heading: Design a Project
records.text:
Start a new project — there's no persistent "Design a Project" sidebar item; use a **Create a project**
CTA (e.g. from the Jobs or Clusters empty state), which opens the design workbench at `~/new`. It's a
node-graph canvas where each infrastructure domain is a configurable node:

- **Project Basics** — name your project, select environment (production/staging/dev)
- **Network** — create a new VPC or select an existing one
- **Cluster** — choose Kubernetes version, instance types, node scaling
- **Database** — add Aurora/Cloud SQL/Azure Database instances
- **Cache** — add Redis/Valkey instances
- Additional nodes for NoSQL, messaging, DNS, secrets, container registries, and repositories

The **cost sidebar** shows estimated monthly costs as you configure. Click **Create project** when ready.

records.title: Getting Started
records.heading: Plan
records.text:
From the project detail page, click **Plan**. Select a Runner (or "Any available") to execute. The Runner runs `tofu plan` and streams the output in real-time.

Review the plan: how many resources will be created, what they'll cost.

records.title: Getting Started
records.heading: Apply
records.text: Click **Apply** to provision the infrastructure. The Runner runs the [verify gate](/console/jobs/plan-and-apply#verify-gate) then `tofu apply`, provisions all resources, installs ArgoCD, and reports back with cluster credentials.

records.title: Getting Started
records.heading: Access Your Cluster
records.text:
Go to **Clusters** in the sidebar. Your new cluster shows:
- Cluster endpoint
- ArgoCD URL, plus a command to retrieve the admin password
- kubeconfig command (generated for AWS clusters)

records.title: Getting Started
records.heading: Ask Elench
records.text:
Click **Ask AI** (top-right) to open [Elench](/console/assistant), the in-console assistant. Ask it
*"Build a dashboard of my infrastructure"* or *"Are my connectors healthy?"* — it answers from your real
state as stat cards and charts, and can propose changes for you to approve.

 

 
Full cluster provisioning takes ~20 minutes (EKS) due to AWS control plane creation time. The Alethia UI shows real-time progress via log streaming.

records.title: Getting Started
records.heading: What's Next?
records.text:
- **[Dashboard](/console/dashboard)** — manage projects
- **[Assistant (Elench)](/console/assistant)** — the in-console AI: workspaces, a knowledge base, dashboards, artifacts
- **[Design a Project](/console/design-project)** — deep dive into each form section
- **[Jobs](/console/jobs)** — understand job types and monitoring
- **[Concepts](/concepts)** — technical deep dives on security, job queues, real-time, etc.

records.title: Console
records.text: Console. Alethia's web control plane for multi-cloud infrastructure orchestration.

records.title: Console
records.heading: Console
records.text: The Console (`apps/console`) is Alethia's web control plane. It provides a visual interface for configuring infrastructure, managing [cloud identities](/console/connectors), monitoring [jobs](/console/jobs), and viewing provisioned clusters — all from the browser. Alethia is the platform; the Console is the web app you drive it from.

records.title: Console
records.heading: Tech Stack
records.text:
Layer Technology 
 ------- ----------- 
 Framework Next.js 16 (App Router, Server Actions) 
 Database PostgreSQL + Drizzle ORM with org-scoped Row Level Security 
 Auth Better Auth (social OAuth: GitHub, Google native; GitLab, Bitbucket genericOAuth; email 6-digit OTP) 
 Realtime Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY → SSE ([how it works](/concepts/realtime)) 
 Storage S3-compatible storage (default SeaweedFS) for OpenTofu state and plan artifacts 
 UI Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Zustand state management

records.title: Console
records.heading: Key Pages
records.text:
Project overview grid, plus project detail with services and infrastructure.
 
 
 The in-console AI — grounded in your real infrastructure, with per-project workspaces, a knowledge base, dashboards, and artifacts.
 
 
 Visual canvas for configuring multi-cloud infrastructure with real-time cost estimation.
 
 
 Connect AWS, GCP, Azure, Alibaba, and Hetzner cloud accounts (each a cloud identity) plus GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket Git providers.
 
 
 Monitor infrastructure operations with real-time log streaming.
 
 
 Register, monitor, and manage Runner execution agents.
 
 
 View provisioned Kubernetes clusters with ArgoCD access.
 
 
 Runner, CLI, and Auth API endpoints.

records.title: Console
records.heading: Architecture
records.text:
A[Next.js App Router]
 A --> SA[Server Actions Drizzle · org-scoped RLS]
 A --> API[API Routes Runner + CLI token auth]
 A --> SSE[LISTEN/NOTIFY → SSE]
 SSE --> ST[Live job-log & message streams]
`} />

All database access goes through Drizzle with org-scoped RLS policies enforcing per-org data isolation through a Policy Decision Point (PDP). Server Actions set the current org context (`app.current_org` via `set_config`) automatically.

records.title: Console
records.heading: State Management
records.text:
Server data lives in **TanStack Query** (React Query) — projects, jobs, runners, clusters, and cloud inventory are fetched, cached, and revalidated there. Zustand holds only **client-side UI and ephemeral state**: filter selections, and form/canvas working state. Key stores:

 Store Purpose 
 ------- --------- 
 `useWorkspaceStore` The active organization the session is scoped to (drives the PDP + RLS) 
 `useCloudProviderStore` Selected provider, cloud identity, and cached cloud-resource inventory 
 `usePricingStore` Region price data during project creation 
 `useProjectsStore` Starred (favorite) projects on the overview 
 `useJobsFilters` / `useRunnerFilters` Filter selections for the jobs and runners lists 
 `useCanvasStore` The Design-a-Project architecture graph (nodes and edges) 
 `useElenchStore` Elench assistant UI state 
 `useNotificationsStore` Read-notification ids 

Real-time job logs and support messages stream over SSE (Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY). See [Real-time Architecture](/concepts/realtime) for details.

records.title: Jobs Overview
records.text: Jobs Overview. Job list page with status and type filtering, search, and real-time updates.

records.title: Jobs Overview
records.heading: Jobs
records.text: Every infrastructure operation is modeled as a **job**. The Jobs page shows all jobs with filtering, search, and real-time status updates. For the technical deep dive on how jobs are queued and claimed, see [Job Queue Pattern](/concepts/job-queue).

records.title: Jobs Overview
records.heading: Job List Page
records.text: Located at `/{org}/~/jobs`, the page shows:

records.title: Jobs Overview
records.heading: Filters
records.text:
The page follows the console filter standard — one filter bar backed by server-side filtering and facet counts. Each control is a multi-select popover, the counts come from the unfiltered facet universe, and every selection syncs to the URL:

- **Search** — free-text match over project name and slug, environment name, Runner name, and the error message.
- **Date range** — a quick-range preset picker (default: last 12 months) plus a custom range.
- **Authors** — the org member who initiated each job.
- **Environments** — the job's target environment.
- **Projects** — the target project (hidden when the list is scoped to a single project).
- **Statuses** — QUEUED, CLAIMED, PROCESSING, SUCCESS, FAILED, CANCELLED.
- **Types** — PLAN, DEPLOY, DESTROY plus the Runner-lifecycle and scan/utility job types; each option shows its live count.

records.title: Jobs Overview
records.heading: Data Table
records.text:
Column Description 
 -------- ------------- 
 Type Job type with icon and description 
 Status Grayscale status badge with inline run duration 
 Project Target project name with its cloud provider icon (hidden in a project-scoped view) 
 Runner Name (or short ID) of the runner that claimed the job 
 Environment Target environment name and stage 
 Initiated Relative time plus the initiating member's avatar 

Click any row to navigate to the [job detail page](/console/jobs/job-detail).

records.title: Jobs Overview
records.heading: Live Updates
records.text: The list stays current through TanStack Query polling: it refetches every 5 seconds while any visible job is in-flight (QUEUED, CLAIMED, or PROCESSING) and every 30 seconds otherwise, so new rows and status changes appear without a page refresh. (Per-job log streaming on the detail page uses a Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY → SSE subscription — see [Real-time Architecture](/concepts/realtime).)

records.title: Jobs Overview
records.heading: Runner Select Popover
records.text:
When triggering Plan, Apply, or Destroy from a project, the **Runner Select Popover** appears:

- Lists all registered Runners with a grayscale status dot (state is shown by the dot, never color)
- "Any available" option for automatic assignment
- Only ONLINE Runners can be selected; DRAINING and OFFLINE Runners are disabled

The selected Runner's ID is stored as `assigned_runner_id` on the job.

records.title: Job Detail & Logs
records.text: Job Detail & Logs. Real-time log streaming, status polling, and job actions.

records.title: Job Detail & Logs
records.heading: Job Detail & Logs
records.text: The job detail page (`/{org}/~/jobs/{id}`) shows the full execution state of a job with real-time log streaming. For the underlying streaming architecture, see [Real-time Architecture](/concepts/realtime).

records.title: Job Detail & Logs
records.heading: Header
records.text:
- Job type icon and label
- Status badge
- Duration (elapsed or final run time)
- Job ID (first 8 chars)
- Runner ID (first 8 chars) — the runner that claimed the job (shown once a runner has claimed it)
- Created time (relative)
- Action buttons

records.title: Job Detail & Logs
records.heading: Log Viewer
records.text:
A full-height, monospace, auto-scrolling log area showing the runner's `tofu` (OpenTofu) output in real-time. Each log row carries a `stream_type` of `STDOUT`, `STDERR`, or `SYSTEM`:

- **STDERR** — rendered in the destructive (error) style
- **STDOUT** and **SYSTEM** — rendered in the normal foreground style

Logs are streamed via a Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY → SSE subscription (`/api/stream/jobs/{id}`) over the `job_logs` table, filtered by `job_id`. The server sends the backlog on connect, then pushes new rows in near-real-time as the Runner writes them.

Auto-scroll pins to the bottom as new logs arrive.

records.title: Job Detail & Logs
records.heading: Collapsible Details
records.text:
Three expandable sections below the logs:

- **Job Details** — full metadata (ID, type, runner, project, and the created/started/completed timestamps)
- **Config Snapshot** — the project configuration at time of job creation (JSON)
- **Execution Metadata** — OpenTofu outputs, cost data, cluster info, and the **`verify_result`** report (JSON)

For PLAN and DEPLOY jobs, `execution_metadata["verify_result"]` carries the [verify gate](/console/jobs/plan-and-apply#verify-gate) report — the fail-closed policy evaluation over the plan JSON. The Console renders it as the **Verify Report** in the project's Plan tab; see [engine internals](/elench/engine-internals).

records.title: Job Detail & Logs
records.heading: Actions
records.text:
Button When Visible Effect 
 -------- ------------- -------- 
 **Cancel** QUEUED, CLAIMED, or PROCESSING Sets status to CANCELLED, Runner terminates gracefully 
 **Apply** PLAN job with SUCCESS status Opens Runner Select Popover → creates DEPLOY job 
 **Re-run** Any terminal status (SUCCESS, FAILED, CANCELLED) Creates a new job with the same configuration

records.title: Job Detail & Logs
records.heading: Status Polling
records.text: The page polls `getJob(jobId)` every 3 seconds while the job is in-flight (QUEUED, CLAIMED, or PROCESSING), then idles once it reaches a terminal state. This query drives the header status and any error message — the full log streaming happens via the Realtime subscription.

records.title: Job Detail & Logs
records.heading: Status Banner
records.text:
When the job reaches a terminal state, a banner appears:

- **SUCCESS** — neutral banner with a checkmark ("Job completed successfully.")
- **FAILED** — destructive banner with the error message ("Job failed")
- **CANCELLED** — muted banner ("Job cancelled")

records.title: Job Types
records.text: Job Types. Reference for every provisioning job type Alethia runs, with its Console label and what it does.

records.title: Job Types
records.heading: Job Types
records.text:
Every infrastructure operation is modeled as a [job](/console/jobs). Each job has a **type** drawn from the `provision_job_type` enum. The Console renders each type with a label, an icon, and a short description from a single catalog (`lib/jobs/format.ts`), shared by the jobs data table and the overview's recent-jobs card.

The table below lists every job type.

 Type Label Description 
 ------ ------- ------------- 
 `PLAN` Plan Dry-run infrastructure plan 
 `DEPLOY` Deploy Provision infrastructure from config 
 `DESTROY` Destroy Tear down infrastructure 
 `DEPLOY_RUNNER` Deploy Runner Provision a runner into your cloud account 
 `UPDATE_RUNNER` Update Runner Update a runner to a newer version 
 `DESTROY_RUNNER` Destroy Runner Tear down a provisioned runner 
 `ANALYZE_REPO` Analyze Repo Scan a repository for infrastructure config 
 `DETECT_DRIFT` Detect Drift Refresh-only check for drift between state and live cloud 
 `AUDIT` Audit Audit bring-your-own IaC (terraform plan or k8s manifests) with elench 
 `CHART_SCAN` Chart Scan Scan a bring-your-own Helm chart for security issues (elench verify) 
 `IAC_SCAN` IaC Scan Validate a bring-your-own IaC module and pin the commit it deploy

records.title: Job Types
records.heading: Infrastructure jobs
records.text:
`PLAN`, `DEPLOY`, and `DESTROY` run OpenTofu against a project's configuration.

- `PLAN` is a dry run. It produces a plan and the fail-closed [verify gate](/console/jobs/plan-and-apply#verify-gate) report, which the runner forwards on `execution_metadata["verify_result"]`.
- `DEPLOY` provisions the infrastructure. An **Apply** action on a successful `PLAN` job creates a `DEPLOY` job; see [Job Detail & Logs](/console/jobs/job-detail#actions).
- `DESTROY` tears the infrastructure down.

An environment promotion does not add a new type — it reuses `PLAN`, then `DEPLOY`.

records.title: Job Types
records.heading: Runner jobs
records.text: `DEPLOY_RUNNER`, `UPDATE_RUNNER`, and `DESTROY_RUNNER` manage the lifecycle of a runner provisioned into your cloud account.

records.title: Job Types
records.heading: Scan jobs
records.text:
These jobs inspect code or configuration before it is deployed.

- `ANALYZE_REPO` scans a repository for infrastructure config.
- `CHART_SCAN` clones a bring-your-own Helm chart, runs `helm template`, and evaluates the rendered manifests with elench verify.
- `IAC_SCAN` scans a bring-your-own IaC module: it clones the repo, pins the commit, inventories providers and modules, and runs `tofu validate`. Its result gates the environment's `PLAN` and `DEPLOY` jobs (both require a fresh scan that pinned the commit to apply). `DESTROY` is not gated on the scan — it gates on the commit that created the deployed state, so a failed re-scan never traps live infrastructure.
- `AUDIT` audits bring-your-own IaC (an OpenTofu plan or Kubernetes manifests) with elench.

records.title: Job Types
records.heading: Reconciliation jobs
records.text:
- `DETECT_DRIFT` runs a refresh-only check for drift between the recorded state and the live cloud.
- `PROBE_CLUSTER` dials the cluster's Kubernetes API server and records reachability. An unreachable cluster is a **successful** probe with `reachable=false`; the job only fails when the probe itself could not run.

records.title: Job Types
records.heading: Build jobs
records.text: `BUILD` builds and pushes service images in-cluster. For each service whose source is a repository, it schedules an in-cluster kaniko Job that builds from the git context and Dockerfile and pushes to the provisioned registry, then reports a per-service image digest map in `execution_metadata.build_result`.

records.title: Job Types
records.heading: Break-glass jobs
records.text: `STATE_SURGERY` is an operator-initiated, two-person-approved, fully-audited repair of a corrupt or stranded OpenTofu state. It is queued as a normal job so it flows through the same claim and state-lock path as any other job. The runner-side executor ships **inert** and fail-closed: it refuses to run unless the runner explicitly opts in via `ALETHIA_BREAKGLASS_STATE_SURGERY_ENABLED`.

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.text: Plan & Apply. The Plan-Review-Apply workflow for infrastructure provisioning.

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: Plan & Apply
records.text: Infrastructure provisioning follows a strict **Plan-Review-Apply** workflow. Nothing is provisioned without explicit user confirmation.

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: Generate Plan
records.text:
From the [project detail page](/console/dashboard/project-detail), click **Plan**. Select a Runner to execute. A `PLAN` job is queued.

The Runner:
1. Mints short-lived cloud credentials via keyless OIDC ([how](/concepts/authentication))
2. Generates OpenTofu variable files (`tofu.OverrideTfvarsFromMap`) from the project's config snapshot
3. Runs `tofu init` — state goes through the Console **state proxy** (`backend "http"` → `/api/jobs/{id}/state`), so the runner holds no object-storage credentials
4. Runs `tofu plan -out=plan.tfplan`
5. Runs `tofu show -json` for structured output
6. Evaluates the [verify gate](#verify-gate) over the plan JSON and attaches the `verify_result` report
7. Optionally runs Infracost for cost breakdown ([cost estimation](/concepts/cost-estimation))
8. Uploads the plan artifact and reports resource change counts and costs

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: Review Plan
records.text:
The Plan tab in project detail shows:

**Plan Summary Bar:**
- Resources to **create** (green count)
- Resources to **update** (yellow count)
- Resources to **destroy** (red count)
- Estimated monthly cost

**Resource Groups:**
Collapsible sections grouped by resource type (e.g., "AWS EKS", "AWS VPC", "AWS RDS"). Each resource shows:
- Resource address (e.g., `module.eks.aws_eks_cluster.main`)
- Action: create / update / delete
- Per-resource monthly cost (from Infracost)

**Verify Report:**
The Plan tab renders the [verify gate](#verify-gate) result (`execution_metadata["verify_result"]`) — per-control pass / fail / `not_evaluable` outcomes over the plan JSON. See [engine internals](/elench/engine-internals).

**Cost Breakdown:**
Total estimated monthly cost with per-resource itemization.

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: Apply
records.text:
Click **Apply** to provision. Select a Runner. A `DEPLOY` job is queued. `DEPLOY` runs through `provisioner.RunDeployV2`.

The Runner:
1. Validates the config hash against the referenced PLAN job — if the project was modified after planning, the apply fails with a hash mismatch error
2. Runs `tofu plan -out` and `tofu show -json` from the config snapshot
3. **Verify gate** — evaluates `packages/core/verify` over the plan JSON; this is **fail-closed** (see [below](#verify-gate))
4. Runs `tofu apply` (only if the gate passes or an authorized override waives it)
5. Installs ArgoCD via Helm / scaffolds its manifests ([GitOps](/concepts/gitops-argocd))
6. Reports cluster metadata back to the Console

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: Finalization
records.text:
On DEPLOY success, Alethia's `finalizeDeployment()` server action:
- Updates `project_cluster` with cluster name, endpoint, ARN, ArgoCD URL and password
- Updates `project_databases` with writer/reader endpoints, credentials ARNs
- Updates `project_caches` with primary/reader endpoints
- Sets the environment's provisioning `status` (on `project_environments`) to `ACTIVE`

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: Verify gate
records.text:
Between `tofu plan` and `tofu apply`, the runner runs the [Elench](/elench) verification gate
(`packages/core/verify`, invoked from `provisioner.RunDeployV2`) over the OpenTofu **plan JSON**. It
evaluates the plan against a catalog of security controls (keyless auth, least-privilege, OIDC-subject
pinning) and produces a structured `verify.Report` — per-control `pass`, `fail`, or an honest
`not_evaluable` for anything the plan JSON can't prove.

The gate is **fail-closed**: a hard control failure **blocks before `tofu apply`** unless an authorized
`verify.Override` waives the specific failing controls (audited, expiry-bounded). PLAN jobs evaluate and
attach the report too, so you see the outcome before ever applying.

The report rides back on `execution_metadata["verify_result"]` and the Console renders it in the **Plan
tab**. For the control catalog, the `not_evaluable` honesty rule, and the signed evidence receipt, see
[Engine internals](/elench/engine-internals).

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: Config Hash Validation
records.text:
The DEPLOY job references a specific PLAN job. Before applying, the Runner compares:
- The project's current configuration hash
- The plan's configuration hash (captured at plan time)

If they differ (user modified the project after planning), the job fails with:

> "Configuration has changed since the plan was generated. Please re-plan."

This prevents applying a stale plan that doesn't match the current desired state.

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: Destroy Workflow
records.text:
Destroy follows a simpler flow — no plan step required:

1. Click **Destroy** from project detail
2. Select a Runner
3. A `DESTROY` job is queued
4. The Runner runs `tofu destroy -auto-approve`
5. Environment status → DESTROYING → DESTROYED

 
Destroy permanently removes all cloud resources (VPC, cluster, databases, etc.). OpenTofu state is preserved so accidental destroys can be recovered by re-applying, but data in databases will be lost.

records.title: Plan & Apply
records.heading: Free plan limits
records.text:
Community (free) organizations have two limits on provisioning jobs. Paid plans are unbounded on both.

- **Concurrency** — at most **2 jobs** run at once (enforced when a runner claims a job). Extra jobs wait in the queue rather than being rejected.
- **Daily volume** — at most **25 provisioning jobs you start** in any rolling 24-hour window. Reaching it blocks the next plan/apply/destroy/scan with an upgrade prompt; the limit clears as older jobs age out of the window.

Only jobs **you** start count toward the daily limit. Background jobs the platform runs on your behalf — drift detection, cluster probes, reconciliation, and ephemeral-environment cleanup — are never counted and never blocked, so day-2 automation keeps running regardless of the cap.

 
Upgrading to a paid plan removes both limits. See the [billing commands](/docs/cli/commands/billing) or the **Billing** page in the console.

records.title: Verify Override
records.text: Verify Override. Waive specific failing verify controls on a queued DEPLOY job so a fail-closed apply can proceed deliberately.

records.title: Verify Override
records.heading: Verify Override
records.text:
The [verify gate](/console/jobs/plan-and-apply#verify-gate) is **fail-closed**: a hard control
failure blocks before `tofu apply`. A verify override is the deliberate, accountable exception —
it waives **specific** failing control IDs on one DEPLOY job so the apply can proceed, without ever
disabling the gate wholesale.

An override is time-boxed and stamped with the actor who authorized it, so the waiver stays auditable
and the runner seals it into the apply's evidence receipt as a recorded exception.

records.title: Verify Override
records.heading: Before you start
records.text:
- The failing controls must come from the [verify report](/console/jobs/plan-and-apply#verify-gate).
 Read `execution_metadata["verify_result"]` on the PLAN job (the **Verify Report** in the Plan tab,
 or **Execution Metadata** on the [job detail page](/console/jobs/job-detail)) to get the exact
 control IDs that failed — for example `LEASTPRIV-001` or `AZURE-FED-001`. See the
 [control catalog](/elench/control-catalog) for what each ID checks.
- You need **edit** authority on the job.
- The DEPLOY job must be **QUEUED** — set the override after clicking **Apply** but before a runner
 claims and processes the job. An override cannot be set once the job leaves the QUEUED state.

 
An override waives a security control on a single apply. Only the control IDs you list are waived;
every other control still evaluates fail-closed.

records.title: Verify Override
records.heading: Record the override
records.text:
The override is recorded by the `recordVerifyOverride` server action:

recordVerifyOverride(jobId, controls, reason, ttlHours);

records.title: Verify Override
records.heading: Collect the failing control IDs
records.text: List the exact IDs from the verify report as `controls`. The array must contain at least one ID.

records.title: Verify Override
records.heading: Write a reason
records.text: Provide a non-empty `reason` explaining why the waiver is justified. It is stored with the override.

records.title: Verify Override
records.heading: Set an expiry (optional)
records.text:
Pass `ttlHours` to bound how long the waiver is valid. It defaults to **24** hours. The action
computes `expiry` as the current time plus `ttlHours`, stored as an RFC3339 timestamp.

records.title: Verify Override
records.heading: Submit
records.text:
The action verifies your edit authority, confirms the job is QUEUED, and writes the waiver to
`jobs.verify_override`.

records.title: Verify Override
records.heading: What gets stored
records.text:
The action writes a JSONB `verify_override` value on the job:

 Field Source 
 ------- -------- 
 `controls` The control IDs you passed 
 `reason` Your reason (trimmed) 
 `by` Stamped server-side to the authorizing actor — you cannot set it 
 `expiry` Now + `ttlHours` (default 24), as an RFC3339 timestamp

records.title: Verify Override
records.heading: What the runner does
records.text:
When a runner claims the DEPLOY job, it reads `jobs.verify_override` and passes it to the fail-closed
gate. The gate applies the waiver only to the listed controls, lets the apply proceed, and records the
waiver as an exception in the signed [evidence receipt](/elench/engine-internals) for the apply.

records.title: Verify Override
records.heading: Errors
records.text:
The action rejects an override that cannot be honored:

- **No control IDs** — the `controls` array is empty.
- **No reason** — `reason` is blank.
- **Job not found** — no job matches the ID in your scope.
- **Job is not QUEUED** — the job has already been claimed or has reached a terminal state.

records.title: Runners
records.text: Runners. Registering, monitoring, and managing Runner execution agents.

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Runners
records.text: Runners are the execution agents that run OpenTofu (the `tofu` binary) on behalf of users. The Runners page manages their lifecycle. Every runner sits on a two-axis taxonomy — **operator** (`managed` `self`) × **provisioning** (`deployed` `registered`, for `self` only). For how Runners work internally, see the [Runner Agent](/runner) documentation.

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Runners Page
records.text: A two-column layout: the left column stacks the warm **Pools** (managed-fleet, self-managed operators only) and the **Versions** changelog; the right column is a filterable, paginated grid of runner cards.

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Filter Bar
records.text:
Follows the console filter standard: a name search plus chip and facet filters.

- **Search** — filter by Runner name
- **Cloud** — supported providers (or "Any")
- **Status** chips — Online, Offline, Draining
- **Operator** chips — Managed, Self · Deployed, Self · Registered
- **Region** and **Version** facet popovers

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Runner Cards
records.text:
Each runner renders as a card (grayscale — status reads through a badge dot + mono label, never colour):

 Field Description 
 ------- ------------- 
 Name Runner name, with a star if it's the default runner 
 Status Badge: ONLINE, OFFLINE, DRAINING — plus in-flight lifecycle states PROVISIONING, UPDATING, DESTROYING while a job acts on the runner 
 Operator Badge: `Managed`, `Self · Deployed`, or `Self · Registered` 
 Cloud Supported provider icons (or "Any") 
 Region Deployment location — shown for **managed** runners 
 Version Runner release version (click to view release notes; an "update available" badge appears when outdated) 
 Provisioned / Last seen Managed runners show provisioned hours; self runners show time since last heartbeat 
 Active job The in-flight job (if any), linking to the job detail — QUEUED, CLAIMED, or PROCESSING 
 Actions Default-runner star toggle; **Destroy** (self · deployed with cloud resources) or **Remove** (registered runners)

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Versions Panel & Updates
records.text: The **Versions** panel (left column) shows the latest release, a changelog of recent releases, and — when runners are behind the latest version — an **"Update all"** button that queues `UPDATE_RUNNER` jobs for the runners it can roll in place (deployed runners with a stored token). Runners it can't roll are flagged as needing a re-deploy.

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Adding a Runner
records.text:
Click **Add runner** to open a sheet that chooses between two paths — **Deploy to a cloud** or **Register your own**:

 
 
 Provisions a Runner into your **AWS** account automatically (an existing runner runs OpenTofu to stand it up — ECS Fargate via `infra/templates/runner/aws`). This is a `self`-operated, `deployed` runner:

 1. Select an AWS cloud identity and region
 2. Click Deploy → queues a `DEPLOY_RUNNER` job
 3. The job provisions: ECS task definition, IAM roles, CloudWatch log group, security groups
 4. After ~2 minutes, the Runner appears as ONLINE

 **This path is AWS only.** The account picker lists verified AWS identities alone, because `infra/templates/runner/` holds one template. A deploy into GCP, Azure, Alibaba Cloud or Hetzner is refused when you queue it — in this form and in `alethia runner deploy`. Use **Register your own** for those clouds; a registered Runner provisions every cloud Alethia supports, wherever it runs.

 Deployed Runners support [scale-to-zero](/runner/scale-to-zero) — they shut down when no jobs are queued and restart automatically when needed.
 
 
 For bringing your own Runner — your own IaC (OpenTofu/Terraform), or just `alethia runner star

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Status Indicators
records.text:
Status is determined by heartbeat recency:

 Status Meaning Heartbeat 
 -------- --------- ----------- 
 **ONLINE** Ready to accept jobs Seen within the last 45 seconds (runners heartbeat ~every 10s) 
 **DRAINING** Finishing current job, not accepting new ones Sent with DRAINING flag 
 **OFFLINE** Missed heartbeat, jobs will be requeued No heartbeat for > 45 seconds (the sweep flips stale ONLINE or DRAINING runners to OFFLINE)

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Live Updates
records.text: The Runners page polls every 10 seconds while the tab is focused (TanStack Query pauses the interval in the background), so heartbeat-driven ONLINE/OFFLINE changes, new registrations, and job assignments surface on the next poll.

records.title: Runners
records.heading: Version Tracking
records.text:
Each Runner reports its version on heartbeat. The page shows:
- Current version per Runner
- Latest available version (from the `runner_releases` table)
- A **Release Notes** popover showing the changelog for each version

When a new Runner release is published via the CI pipeline, existing runners are rolled onto the new image via `UPDATE_RUNNER` jobs — ECS force-new-deployment for self·deployed AWS runners; VM replacement for the managed Hetzner fleet.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.text: Enterprise setup. The end-to-end runbook for turning on the licensed Enterprise edition — packages, migrations, OpenFGA, and the license.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: Enterprise setup
records.text:
The ordered checklist to take a deployment from Community to
 Enterprise . None of this is needed for the open-source edition — see
[Licensing](/editions/licensing) for the mechanism this turns on.

 
 Everything below is **additive and reversible.** If the license is removed, the deployment degrades back to
 Community behavior without data loss.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: Prerequisites
records.text:
- A commercial **license key** for Alethia Enterprise.
- The Enterprise package `@alethia/ee` (ships with the Enterprise distribution; absent from the open-source build).

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: Install the Enterprise dependencies
records.text:
`@alethia/ee` and its peers add the organization/SSO/OpenFGA machinery:

pnpm install

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: brings in @alethia/ee, @openfga/sdk, @better-auth/sso (+ samlify, jose)
records.text: The core never imports these — they're loaded only through the `lib/enterprise.ts` seam at runtime.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: Run the database migrations
records.text:
The org/team/SSO/authz tables ship as ordinary migrations (inert in Community — never written without the
plugins). Apply them:

pnpm -F console db:migrate # applies all pending migrations + programmables (RLS, triggers)

Then reconcile the Better Auth org/team/SSO tables against the plugin's expected shape:

npx @better-auth/cli generate

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: (Optional) Bring up OpenFGA
records.text:
Enterprise runs fine on the Postgres engine. To use the [OpenFGA fine-grained engine](/access-control/openfga),
start the `enterprise` compose profile (OpenFGA + its own datastore):

docker compose --profile enterprise up -d openfga

Create a store, then point the app at it:

OPENFGA_API_URL=http://openfga:8080
OPENFGA_STORE_ID= 

On boot the app writes the authorization model (generated from the registry) and backfills tuples from your
existing grants and hierarchy. Leaving `OPENFGA_*` unset keeps `PostgresRbacPDP` as the engine.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: Activate the license
records.text:
Install the signed license so the Enterprise entitlements resolve to `true`. The license is a compact
EdDSA (ed25519) JWT that Alethia Labs mints offline; the console verifies it **offline** against the
issuer public key you bake in — no phone-home:

ALETHIA_LICENSE_KEY= 
ALETHIA_LICENSE_PUBLIC_KEY= 

Restart the console. The org switcher, Members, Teams, Roles (custom), Access, SSO, and activity export now light
up.

 
 `ALETHIA_LICENSE_ACTIVE=true` is a **non-production dev bypass only** — it is ignored in production,
 where a signed `ALETHIA_LICENSE_KEY` is required. Verification is fail-closed: a missing, expired, or
 forged license leaves the instance unlicensed and degrades to per-org billing (Community), never a boot
 crash.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: (Optional) Register an SSO provider
records.text:
In **Settings → Single Sign-On**, register your IdP over [OIDC or SAML](/access-control/sso). Members signing
in with a matching email domain are routed to it and provisioned into the org.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: Verify
records.text:
- Create an organization, invite a second member, and confirm the [invite lifecycle](/access-control/members-and-invitations).
- In **Settings → Access**, grant a role to a member or team, then add a **deny** exception
 ([grants & scopes](/access-control/grants-and-scopes)) and confirm it takes effect.
- If OpenFGA is on, run the parity check — the two engines must agree across roles, scopes, and actions.

records.title: Enterprise setup
records.heading: What you get
records.text:
Once the license is active, the full Enterprise surface is available — see the
[feature matrix](/editions/feature-matrix) and the [Access Control](/access-control) reference.

records.title: Feature matrix
records.text: Feature matrix. The authoritative, capability-by-capability comparison of the open-source Community edition and the licensed Enterprise edition.

records.title: Feature matrix
records.heading: Feature matrix
records.text:
The single source of truth for what each edition includes. Community is free and
open-source (AGPL-3.0); Enterprise is licensed.

records.title: Feature matrix
records.heading: Authorization core
records.text:
Everything here is **open-source** — the authorization model is the same in both editions.

 Capability Community Enterprise 
 --- :--: :--: 
 Policy Decision Point (`can` / `enforce` / `bulkCheck` / `listAccessible`) ✅ ✅ 
 Built-in roles — owner · admin · operator · viewer ✅ ✅ 
 Per-resource grants + Org → Project inheritance ✅ ✅ 
 Explicit **deny** with hierarchy + exceptions ✅ ✅ 
 Single-permission grants (not just roles) ✅ ✅ 
 Row-Level Security tenant isolation (the blast wall) ✅ ✅ 
 Full **Activity log** (every action + denials) ✅ ✅ 
 Registry-as-code (resources × actions, exhaustively typed) ✅ ✅

records.title: Feature matrix
records.heading: Organizations & teams
records.text:
Capability Community Enterprise 
 --- :--: :--: 
 Personal organization (single owner — you) ✅ ✅ 
 **Multi-member organizations** — ✅ 
 **Member invitations** (email → accept → join) — ✅ 
 **Active-organization switcher** — ✅ 
 **Teams** (group-based grants) — ✅

records.title: Feature matrix
records.heading: Roles & access
records.text:
Capability Community Enterprise 
 --- :--: :--: 
 Built-in role catalog (read-only) ✅ ✅ 
 **Custom roles** — the permission-matrix editor — ✅ 
 **Access portal** — AWS-IAM-style grant assignment — ✅ 
 Grant to a **user or a team**, allow/deny, any scope — ✅

records.title: Feature matrix
records.heading: Authentication
records.text:
Capability Community Enterprise 
 --- :--: :--: 
 Email OTP + social sign-in (GitHub · Google · GitLab · Bitbucket) ✅ ✅ 
 **SSO — OIDC** (Okta · Entra ID · Google · AWS IAM Identity Center · …) — ✅ 
 **SSO — SAML** — ✅

records.title: Feature matrix
records.heading: Activity
records.text:
Capability Community Enterprise 
 --- :--: :--: 
 Browse the Activity log in the console ✅ ✅ 
 **Export** the Activity log (CSV) — ✅

records.title: Feature matrix
records.heading: Engine
records.text:
Capability Community Enterprise 
 --- :--: :--: 
 `PostgresRbacPDP` — the Postgres-backed engine ✅ ✅ 
 **OpenFGA fine-grained engine** (ReBAC at scale) — ✅ (optional) 
 Dual-write tuple sync (Postgres → OpenFGA) — ✅ 

 
 The OpenFGA engine is **optional even with a license** — Enterprise runs perfectly on `PostgresRbacPDP`.
 Turn OpenFGA on when you want a dedicated relationship-graph engine. See the
 [OpenFGA operator guide](/access-control/openfga).

records.title: Feature matrix
records.heading: How the line is drawn
records.text:
Community is a **complete single-tenant product**: roles, grants, hierarchy, deny, the PDP, RLS, and the Activity
log all ship open-source. Enterprise is about **organizations of people** — inviting and grouping members,
authenticating them with SSO, authoring fine-grained custom roles, assigning access through the portal, and
(optionally) deciding it with OpenFGA.

Next: [how licensing works](/editions/licensing).

records.title: Editions
records.text: Editions. Alethia is open-core — a free, open-source Community edition and a licensed Enterprise edition. What each includes, and why the split is where it is.

records.title: Editions
records.heading: Editions
records.text:
Alethia is **open-core**. There are two editions, built from the *same codebase*:

- Community — the free, **open-source** edition, licensed **AGPL-3.0**. The complete
 single-tenant product. You can run it for yourself or your team forever, at no cost, with no license key.
- Enterprise — the **licensed** edition (commercial). Everything in Community **plus**
 multi-member organizations, teams, SSO, custom roles, the fine-grained access portal, the OpenFGA policy
 engine, and activity export.

 
 You can **self-host either edition.** "Self-hosting" is about *where Alethia runs* (your own
 infrastructure); "edition" is about *which features are licensed*. Community needs nothing extra; Enterprise
 needs a license key and a couple of extra services (see [Licensing](/editions/licensing)).

records.title: Editions
records.heading: The dividing line
records.text:
The simplest way to think about it:

> **Everything you need to run Alethia for yourself, or for a team that shares one account, is free and
> open-source. The Enterprise edition is about *many people, many identities* — organizations with multiple
> members, the teams and roles to organize them, the SSO to let them in, and the engine to authorize them at
> scale.**

Concretely:

 
 
 The Policy Decision Point, built-in roles, per-resource grants with Org → Project inheritance,
 Row-Level Security tenant isolation, and the authorization Activity log — all open-source. Your account is a
 single-owner "personal organization".
 
 
 Multi-member organizations, teams, member invitations, SSO (OIDC + SAML), configurable custom roles, the
 AWS-IAM-style access portal (allow/deny, per-resource), the OpenFGA fine-grained engine, and activity export.

records.title: Editions
records.heading: Why open-core?
records.text:
The authorization *model* — how a decision is made — is the same in both editions, and it's open. What
Enterprise adds is the machinery for **organizations of people**: ways to invite and group them (members,
teams, invitations), authenticate them (SSO), describe what they can do (custom roles, allow/deny), and decide
it quickly at scale (OpenFGA). None of that is needed to run Alethia for a single tenant — so it isn't in the
free core.

The boundary is enforced in code: **the open-source core never depends on the Enterprise package, and runs
completely without it present.** See the [open-core architecture](/access-control/open-core) for how that's
guaranteed (a one-way dependency + CI guards), and [Licensing](/editions/licensing) for how a license turns
the Enterprise features on.

records.title: Editions
records.heading: Next
records.text:
- The complete [**feature matrix**](/editions/feature-matrix) — every capability, Community vs Enterprise.
- How [**licensing**](/editions/licensing) works (entitlements, activation, graceful degradation).
- The [**Enterprise setup runbook**](/editions/enterprise-setup) — turning Enterprise on, end to end.
- The [**Access Control**](/access-control) section — the full authorization reference.

records.title: Licensing
records.text: Licensing. How the Enterprise license works — entitlements, activation, and graceful degradation back to the open-source defaults.

records.title: Licensing
records.heading: Licensing
records.text:
The Enterprise features are gated by a license. This page explains the mechanism;
the [Enterprise setup runbook](/editions/enterprise-setup) walks through turning it all on.

records.title: Licensing
records.heading: Entitlements, not scattered checks
records.text:
Alethia never sprinkles `if (licensed)` through the code. Instead, the licensed layer answers a small set of
**entitlements**, and the product reads those:

 Entitlement Unlocks 
 --- --- 
 `organizations` Multi-member orgs, members, invitations, the active-org switcher 
 `teams` Team (access-group) management — create teams and scope grants to them 
 `sso` SSO sign-in (OIDC + SAML) 
 `customRoles` The custom-role editor + the access portal 
 `activityExport` CSV export of the Activity log (viewing is free) 
 `alerting` The alerting surface — policies, channels, and the delivery activity log 
 `advancedAlerting` Security/governance alert rules sourced from PDP Activity events 
 `byoRunners` Bring-your-own runners — deploy into your cloud or register your own 
 `managedPools` Managed warm-pool fleet operations (pools, versions, economics) 

A license also carries runner-scheduling `quotas` (max concurrent jobs, priority band, included
runner-minutes, activity retention).

Without a license, **every entitlement is `false`** and the console shows the open-source experience: a single
personal organization, the four built-in roles (read-only), and a browsable (non-exportable) Activity l

records.title: Licensing
records.heading: Where entitlements come from
records.text:
Entitlements are produced by the Enterprise package (`@alethia/ee`), which the core loads through **one
tolerant seam** (`lib/enterprise.ts`). The rule that makes this open-core:

> **The open-source core never imports the Enterprise package, and runs completely if it's absent.** The seam
> tries to load `@alethia/ee`; if it isn't installed, the core falls back to the Community defaults — nothing
> breaks.

So there are really two ways a deployment is "Community":

1. **The open-source build** — `@alethia/ee` isn't installed at all.
2. **An Enterprise build without an active license** — `@alethia/ee` is present, but the entitlements resolve
 to all-`false`.

Both behave identically: the Community product. See the
[open-core architecture](/access-control/open-core) for the boundary guarantees and CI guards.

records.title: Licensing
records.heading: Graceful degradation
records.text:
Because the seam is tolerant, an Enterprise deployment **never hard-fails** if the license is missing or
expires — it degrades to Community behavior. Members already in an organization keep their data; the org
simply stops accepting new enterprise-only operations until the license is restored.

records.title: Licensing
records.heading: Activating Enterprise
records.text:
At a high level, enabling Enterprise is: install `@alethia/ee`, provide a license, run the extra migrations,
and (optionally) bring up OpenFGA. The full, ordered checklist is in the
[**Enterprise setup runbook**](/editions/enterprise-setup).

 
 Self-hosting an Enterprise deployment requires a commercial license. Running the **open-source Community
 edition** never does. If you only need a single-tenant Alethia, you never touch any of this.

records.title: Agent harness
records.text: Agent harness. One tool registry exposed read-only to external agents, per-agent identities with isolated memory, a stateless executor, and a supervisor that delegates to a colony.

records.title: Agent harness
records.heading: Agent harness
records.text:
The harness exposes the platform's tools **once** and reuses them everywhere — the in-app agent, and the
customer's own agents (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini) — without ever forking the tool definitions. It then
layers scoped agent identities, isolated memory, and a supervisor on top.

records.title: Agent harness
records.heading: Tool registry — the single source of truth
records.text:
Every agent tool is an AI-SDK `tool()` definition in `apps/console/lib/ai/tools/`, classified by
**audience** in `registry.ts`:

 Audience Who sees it 
 --- --- 
 `in-app` Dashboard agent only — HITL proposals, canvas-context tools, and job-queuing writes. 
 `external` / `both` Read-only, PDP-gated, stateless — safe to expose to a customer's agent. 

`buildExternalAgentTools()` is the **read-only projection** (`externalToolsOnly`, audience
`external both`). An anti-drift test (`assertAudienceCoverage`) fails CI if a new tool ships without an
explicit audience, so the external surface can never silently widen.

 
 Authorization is **not** re-implemented in the registry. Each tool's `execute` still resolves the
 actor and enforces its PDP verb at call time; the audience map only decides *visibility*.

records.title: Agent harness
records.heading: The MCP surface — read-only at launch
records.text:
The remote MCP server (`app/api/mcp/route.ts`, OAuth 2.1 via Better Auth + actor binding) consumes
`buildExternalAgentTools()` — so HITL proposals, canvas tools, and job-queuing writes (`scan_repo`) never
reach an external agent. A single endpoint serves Claude Code, ChatGPT, Codex, and Gemini/Zed-via-ACP.

 
 Writes stay **out** of the external surface until an approval-over-MCP design exists: a multi-turn
 HITL approval (propose → human click → resume) does not project onto a single stateless MCP
 `tools/call`. The endpoint is a connector, not the moat — the moat is the governed, provable execution
 behind it.

records.title: Agent harness
records.heading: The proof surface over MCP
records.text:
The evidence half of elench is readable by an external agent, not just the dashboard:

 Tool Audience Returns 
 --- --- --- 
 `get_plan_result` `both` A job's status + the elench `verify_verdict` / `verify_result` (the signed gate report). 
 `get_drift_posture` `both` The latest day-2 [drift `Posture`](/elench/engine-internals) for a project environment. 
 `audit_infrastructure` `in-app` Queues an `AUDIT` job over a bring-your-own plan / manifests (a job-queuing write → stays in-app). 

So a customer's own agent can ask "is this cluster still in sync, and did the last deploy pass the gate?"
over the read-only MCP surface — the "keep proving it" evidence, not just the build.

records.title: Agent harness
records.heading: Agents are DATA, not processes
records.text:
A "colony of per-project agents" is realized as **durable per-tenant data on stateless compute**, not
standing daemons (a long-lived in-context process accrues context rot). An agent is a row
(`agent_identities`, migration `0045`): persona, mission, tool-scope, and a memory namespace. A stateless
executor reconstructs context per turn.

Memory lives in `agent_memory`, keyed by `(namespace, path)`. The namespace is the per-tenant prefix
(`org/{orgId}` for the organization, `org/{orgId}/project/{projectId}` for a project); the path is
validated by the tenant-isolation guard `lib/agent/memory-path.ts`, which **rejects every traversal
escape** (`..`, absolute paths outside the `/memories` mount, backslashes, null bytes) so one tenant can
never read another's memory.

Alongside memory, a scope carries **pinned context** — custom instructions and named knowledge documents
— in `agent_context`, one row per `(org_id, project_id)` (the org row keyed with a null project). Its
`(organization, project)` shape mirrors the memory namespace 1:1. On each turn the executor layers the
org context under the project's and appends live, auto-derived project facts, all into the cached system
prompt — so

records.title: Agent harness
records.heading: The stateless executor
records.text:
`lib/agent/executor.ts` is the deterministic core of running a turn *as* an agent:

- `buildAgentSystemPrompt(identity, memorySummary?)` composes the persona + mission (+ just-in-time
 memory) into a system prompt.
- `scopeToolsToAgent(tools, tool_scope)` narrows the tool set to the agent's allowlist (least privilege
 per agent — deployer / auditor / cost-optimizer roles).

The agent-scoped chat route (`/api/agent/[agentId]`) loads the identity, applies these, and runs the turn
via the AI SDK — mirroring the main agent route, tools still PDP-gated at execute time.

records.title: Agent harness
records.heading: The supervisor / colony
records.text:
`lib/agent/supervisor.ts` is a deterministic, replayable orchestrator. It delegates tasks to sub-agents
and drives them via a **Magentic-style Task / Progress ledger** (facts + plan + per-task status) with a
**stall counter that triggers a bounded re-plan** (`stall > 2 → re-plan`). The actual sub-agent execution
is **injected** (`SubAgentRunner`) — exactly the "AI executes, deterministic code decides" pattern, so the
control flow is testable without a model and always terminates.

 
 **Use it where it pays.** A standing colony costs roughly 15× the tokens of a single agent and loses on
 work over one convergent state (e.g. IaC plan/apply). The supervisor is for breadth-first **read**
 fan-out (drift / cost / security surveys across accounts) and tenant-isolated tasks; write/converge
 work stays on a single-threaded path.

records.title: Architecture
records.text: Architecture. The full system — repos to a verified GitOps Kubernetes cluster on your cloud. The "A" (infer-and-generate) and "B" (bring-your-own + audit) flows, stage by stage, and where the elench proof layer sits.

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: Architecture
records.text:
Alethia is **one product**: connect your repos and get a **verified GitOps Kubernetes cluster on your own
cloud**. Two operators — **managed** (Alethia's runner fleet assumes a role into your account) and
**self** (a runner you run) — and two entry flows that share the same design surface, provisioner, and
proof layer:

- **"A" — infer & generate.** Scan repos → infer the stack → propose a project → provision the cluster +
 backing services + ArgoCD → generate app manifests → GitOps deploy → **verify**.
- **"B" — bring your own + audit.** Point at existing OpenTofu/Terraform or Kubernetes manifests →
 **audit** them with the same engine → get a signed report.

 
 **Core vs Enterprise.** The generate/provision **"A" flow is core** (open-source, self-hostable). The
 **elench proof layer — verify · audit · drift · agent · MCP — is Enterprise.** This page is the map;
 the proof-layer pages carry the badge.

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: The "A" pipeline
records.text:
Each stage names its source-of-truth code so the docs stay honest to the implementation.

 connect 1:N] --> scan[scan Go scanner · per-svc]
 scan --> infer[infer + merge lib/scanner → to-project]
 infer --> propose[propose canvas design]
 propose --> provision[provision RunDeployV2 · tofu]
 provision --> generate[generate manifests .FromServices]
 generate --> gitops[GitOps ArgoCD apps · path .]
 gitops --> verify[VERIFY elench gate + receipt]
 verify --> drift[day-2 drift DETECT_DRIFT → Posture loop]
`} />

1. **Connect repos (1:N, monorepo-aware).** `project_source_repos` (migration `0050`) holds every scanned
 repo + its detected services.
2. **Scan.** `packages/core/scanner` clones + statically reads a repo (never executes it) into a
 `RepoDigest`, and detects per-directory **services** (Dockerfile / workspace manifests) — so a monorepo
 yields several deployable services, not one blob.
3. **Infer + merge.** `apps/console/lib/scanner/infer.ts` turns the digest into an `InferredStack` (LLM,
 structured output); `to-project.ts` `mergeScansToFormData` folds **N repos / services** into one
 guaranteed-valid `ProjectFormData` (union backing needs, de-duped names, one `source_repos`

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: The "B" pipeline — bring your own + audit
records.text:
The verification engine is **plan-agnostic**, so auditing infrastructure Alethia *didn't* generate needs
no new controls:

 B[AUDIT job]
 B --> C[verify same controls]
 C --> D[signed report]
 D --> E[VerifyBlock]
`} />

- **OpenTofu / Terraform plan:** `verify.ParseCustomerPlan(planJSON)` → `Evaluate` — the same AWS/GCP/Azure controls.
- **Kubernetes:** `verify.EvaluateManifests(yaml)` → the k8s [control set](/elench/control-catalog).
- The `AUDIT` job (migration `0052`) runs on the runner (`executeAudit`) and posts the report to
 `jobs.execution_metadata.verify_result`, surfaced by the existing `get_plan_result` tool + the
 `VerifyBlock`. Queue it from the assistant (`audit_infrastructure` tool) or `queueAudit`.

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: The data model
records.text:
Table / field What it holds 
 --- --- 
 `project_source_repos` (0050) Scanned source repos (1:N) + detected services (JSONB). 
 `environment_drift` (0051) Latest day-2 `Posture` per environment. 
 `jobs.job_type` `ANALYZE_REPO` · `PLAN` · `DEPLOY` · `DESTROY` · `DETECT_DRIFT` · `AUDIT` · `*_RUNNER`. 
 `jobs.execution_metadata` `repo_digest` · `verify_result` (the signed report) · `drift_posture`.

records.title: Architecture
records.heading: Where to go next
records.text:
How AWS / GCP / Azure all deploy apps: cloud-agnostic InfraFacts, per-cloud workload identity, and
 manifest generation.
 
 
 The Evaluate seam, the bring-your-own + manifest audit entry points, signed receipts, and the drift
 loop.
 
 
 The core form → snapshot → ProjectConfig → OpenTofu stages the "A" flow rides on.

records.title: Control catalog
records.text: Control catalog. The authored controls per cloud, what each detects, the engine's blind spots, framework mapping, and catalog versioning.

records.title: Control catalog
records.heading: Control catalog
records.text:
The current catalog is **`elench-controls-0.5.2`**. `Evaluate` detects the plan's cloud and runs that
provider's control set (a mixed or unknown plan runs all of them, so nothing is silently skipped). Every
control records its `provider`, so a uniform posture UI can never imply coverage a control does not have.

records.title: Control catalog
records.heading: AWS
records.text:
ID Title Hard-fail on 
 ---- ------- -------------- 
 `KEYLESS-001` No static IAM access keys creating an `aws_iam_access_key` (use OIDC federation instead) 
 `OIDC-001` Federated trust bound to a specific subject a federated role — trust `Action` covering `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`, literally or via a wildcard grant (`sts:*`, `*`) — whose trust **lacks a `:sub` condition**, or binds `sub` only with a **`StringLike` wildcard** (the "any repo can assume" footgun) 
 `LEASTPRIV-001` No over-broad IAM grants (named patterns) `Action:"*"` + `Resource:"*"`; `Allow` + `NotAction`; attaching `AdministratorAccess` / `PowerUserAccess` / `IAMFullAccess`. **Warns** on sensitive service wildcards (`iam:*`, `kms:*`, …) with `Resource:"*"`. **Not-evaluable** when the policy body is computed or referenced only by ARN. 
 `ACCESS-ANALYZER-001` No sensitive actions grantable (opt-in) a policy AWS IAM Access Analyzer proves *could* grant any action in a sensitive denylist.

records.title: Control catalog
records.heading: GCP
records.text:
ID Title Hard-fail on 
 ---- ------- -------------- 
 `GCP-KEYLESS-001` No static service-account keys creating a `google_service_account_key` (use Workload Identity) 
 `GCP-WIF-001` WIF providers are attribute-conditioned a `google_iam_workload_identity_pool_provider` with an empty `attribute_condition` 
 `GCP-LEASTPRIV-001` No project-wide primitive roles binding `roles/owner` (fail) — **warns** on `roles/editor` — via `google_project_iam_member`/`_binding`

records.title: Control catalog
records.heading: Azure
records.text:
ID Title Hard-fail on 
 ---- ------- -------------- 
 `AZURE-KEYLESS-001` No static app/SP secrets creating an `azuread_application_password` / `azuread_service_principal_password` (use a federated identity credential) 
 `AZURE-FED-001` Federated credentials bind a subject an `azuread_application_federated_identity_credential` with an empty or wildcard `subject` 
 `AZURE-LEASTPRIV-001` No Owner/Contributor assignments an `azurerm_role_assignment` of `Owner` (fail) — **warns** on `Contributor` — scope annotated

records.title: Control catalog
records.heading: Alibaba Cloud
records.text:
Alibaba has a real RAM/OIDC authority surface — **RRSA** (RAM Roles for Service Accounts) is its
workload-identity mechanism, the analogue of AWS IRSA / GCP WIF — so its control set mirrors the AWS
one. RAM trust and policy documents share AWS IAM's statement shape; the one Alibaba-specific
difference is the trust action (`sts:AssumeRole`, not `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`). On both
clouds a wildcard action grant (`sts:*`, `*`) covers the assume call and keeps the role in scope.

 ID Title Hard-fail on 
 ---- ------- -------------- 
 `ALI-KEYLESS-001` No static RAM access keys creating an `alicloud_ram_access_key` (use RRSA / AssumeRoleWithOIDC instead) 
 `ALI-OIDC-001` RRSA trust bound to a specific subject an `alicloud_ram_role` whose Federated (RRSA) trust **lacks an `oidc:sub` condition**, or binds it only with a **`StringLike` wildcard** (any pod from the issuer can assume). Service-principal roles are out of scope; a computed trust doc → **not_evaluable**. 
 `ALI-LEASTPRIV-001` No over-broad RAM grants (named patterns) an `alicloud_ram_policy` granting `Action:"*"` on `Resource:"*"` or using `Allow` + `NotAction`; or a **role/user/group** policy attachment of an admin-famil

records.title: Control catalog
records.heading: Hetzner
records.text:
Hetzner is **token-auth** — the API token is the ceiling, with no OIDC/federation/IAM surface to bind —
so its controls assert **network/firewall posture**, the attack surface a Hetzner plan can actually
misconfigure. They are tuned so the shipped Talos template evaluates to **warns only** (never a
hard block of the nightly apply).

 ID Title Hard-fail on 
 ---- ------- -------------- 
 `HCLOUD-FW-001` Every server is behind a firewall an `hcloud_server` with **no firewall anywhere** — no known `firewall_ids`, no configuration reference to an `hcloud_firewall`, and no `hcloud_firewall_attachment` covering it (a bare public node). **Not-evaluable** (never a false brick) for unresolvable expressions, `label_selectors` / `apply_to` selection, or a plan without a configuration section. 
 `HCLOUD-NET-001` No world-open SSH; management ports flagged a firewall rule opening **tcp/22** to the whole internet — including split-CIDR spellings that union to full coverage (Talos runs no SSH daemon; world-open 22 is always wrong). **Warns** on world-open Kubernetes API `6443` / Talos apid `50000`/`50001` (open by design today), any other world-open inbound rule, and very broad partial sources on

records.title: Control catalog
records.heading: Kubernetes
records.text:
A separate input path — `EvaluateManifests(yaml)` — decodes (multi-doc) manifests and runs the Kubernetes set
(`provider` = `k8s`). It backs the [bring-your-own audit](/elench/engine-internals) and grades the
manifests Alethia *generates* (which pass by construction).

 ID Title Hard-fail on 
 ---- ------- -------------- 
 `CONTAINERSECURITY-001` Containers run non-root, unprivileged, on pinned images a `privileged` container, `runAsUser: 0`, or a mutable `:latest` / untagged image. **Warns** when `runAsNonRoot` is unset (may run as root). 
 `RBAC-001` No wildcard RBAC or anonymous bindings a `ClusterRole`/`Role` rule granting `"*"` verbs on `"*"` resources in `"*"` apiGroups; a binding to `system:anonymous` / `system:unauthenticated` 
 `HOSTACCESS-001` Pods don't reach the host namespace or filesystem `hostNetwork` / `hostPID` / `hostIPC: true`, or a `hostPath` volume 
 `RESOURCES-001` Containers declare CPU + memory limits a container missing CPU and/or memory `limits` (**warn** — reliability, not a breach) 

Coverage is honest the same way the cloud controls are: a control with no in-scope resources is a vacuous
pass, and workload kinds without a decodable pod spec are simply no

records.title: Control catalog
records.heading: Blind spots
records.text:
The gate inspects what the plan JSON can actually show. It is honest about the rest rather than
 guessing:

 - **Computed bodies** (`after_unknown`) — interpolated IAM/trust/bucket policies → `not_evaluable`.
 - **Managed-policy bodies** — AWS-managed (non-admin) policies attached by ARN, and Alibaba's
 non-admin System policies, have no body in the plan → coverage gap, not a pass.
 - **Cross-state / cross-module** — resources created in another state or module, permission
 boundaries, and SCPs are out of view.
 - **AWS is deepest; Alibaba mirrors it.** GCP/Azure cover the static-credential, federation-binding,
 and primitive-role cases; Hetzner is network **posture** (token-auth has no authority surface to
 audit); the per-cloud `provider` on each control + the report makes coverage explicit.

records.title: Control catalog
records.heading: Framework mapping
records.text:
Each control carries a small, conservative set of framework references (CIS / SOC 2 criteria), surfaced
in the posture and the receipt. These map to controls, not certification — see
[security & compliance readiness](/standards/security-and-compliance) for how the evidence supports an
audit rather than replacing one.

 
 A wrong control-to-framework mapping (e.g. claiming a control satisfies "SOC 2 CC6.1" when it does
 not) is **worse than no mapping** — it manufactures false assurance. Mappings are kept deliberately
 small, owned, and reviewed, never auto-generated.

records.title: Control catalog
records.heading: Catalog versioning
records.text:
`CatalogVersion` is part of the evidence. **Bump it whenever a control's logic changes in a way that
could alter a verdict** — an old receipt is only meaningful against the catalog (and provider schema)
that produced it. The version is recorded on every report and sealed into the receipt.

records.title: Drift
records.text: Drift. How Alethia detects when the live cloud has diverged from the state it provisioned, and what the drift posture on the Evidence page means.

records.title: Drift
records.heading: Drift
records.text:
Provisioning proves an environment was correct **at apply time**. Drift detection is the other half —
it keeps proving the live cloud still matches the state Alethia provisioned, so a change made outside
Alethia (a console edit, a manual `kubectl`, a deleted resource) surfaces instead of hiding.

records.title: Drift
records.heading: How it works
records.text:
A scheduled `DETECT_DRIFT` job runs `tofu plan -refresh-only -json` against the environment's state and
feeds the plan to the `drift` analyzer. The analyzer walks the plan's `resource_drift` section, skips
data sources and no-ops, and classifies every managed resource that diverged:

- **modified** — the resource still exists but one or more attributes changed.
- **deleted** — the resource is gone from the cloud but still in state.
- **other** — a divergence that is neither of the above.

The result is a **posture** stored per environment: `in_sync` (nothing diverged), a `drifted` count, and
the per-resource details (address, type, kind) you see in the drawer's **Drift** tab.

records.title: Drift
records.heading: What the Evidence page shows
records.text:
Mark Meaning 
 --- --- 
 **In sync** The last refresh-only scan found no managed resource had drifted. 
 **N drifted** That many managed resources diverged from the provisioned state. 
 **Not scanned** No drift scan has run for this environment yet — an honest unknown, never a green pass.

records.title: Drift
records.heading: Running a scan
records.text:
Drift scans run on a schedule (tiered by environment criticality) and can also be triggered for a
project or environment from the project view. Verification and drift are complementary: verification
checks the **plan** before apply; drift checks the **live cloud** after.

records.title: Drift
records.heading: Known limit
records.text:
