AppProject — `tenant-boutique-boutique-dev` and `tenant-boutique-boutique-staging`. The AppProject is
what stops one tier's manifests from touching the other's namespace.

 
 Those four object names are the ones our acceptance test asserts by name
 (`test/e2e/t2_fabric_demo.go`). If this page and that test ever disagree, the test is right.

records.title: Deploy the enterprise demo
records.heading: Step 6 — The part worth noticing
records.text:
Look at the bill, and at `alethia cluster list`.

**One cluster.** Two environments, delivered independently, with different application versions and
namespace-level isolation between them — and one set of infrastructure underneath. The `staging` tier
additionally has its own Kubernetes API server, so a controller installed there sees only its own
resources, without a second control plane to pay for.

Adding a third tier is another `project env add` and another `component add`:

alethia project env add qa --project boutique --stage development \
 --placement-mode namespace --namespace boutique-qa

No new cluster.

records.title: Deploy the enterprise demo
records.heading: Step 7 — Tear it down
records.text:
Not optional. This is real infrastructure and it bills by the hour.

alethia project destroy --project-id boutique --wait

Then confirm nothing survived:

alethia cluster list

Your cloud console is the final authority — check it. A destroy that reports success while leaving a
network behind is rare but it is the failure that costs money, and the per-cloud page tells you where
to look.

records.title: Deploy the enterprise demo
records.heading: What this proved, and what it did not
records.text:
**Proved:** that one Fabric can carry environments at different isolation levels; that each
environment delivers its own application version through GitOps; that the apply is gated by a signed
verify receipt — one you can check yourself with
[`alethia verify receipt --job `](/cli/commands/verify), which exits non-zero if the signature
does not hold; and that the whole path is drivable from a terminal, so it is drivable from CI.

**Did not prove:** anything about scale, failure behaviour, or day-2 operations. You built a demo on
two nodes. Drift detection, promotion between environments, cost ceilings and the add-on marketplace
are all real and all untouched here — see [Day-2 operations](/console) when you want them.

records.title: Tutorials
records.text: Tutorials. Learn Alethia by building something real, start to finish, on a cloud you own.

records.title: Tutorials
records.heading: Tutorials
records.text:
A tutorial is a **lesson**, not a reference. It has one path, it says what to type, and it ends with
something running that you can look at. Where the [how-to guides](/console) answer "how do I do X"
and the [concepts](/concepts/fabrics-and-placement) explain why the product is shaped the way it is,
a tutorial is for the first time you use Alethia at all.

Each one is written to be followed exactly. If a step does not produce what the page says it
produces, that is a bug in the page — the commands here are the ones our own acceptance tests run.

records.title: Tutorials
records.heading: Available tutorials
records.text:
**[Deploy the enterprise demo](/tutorials/enterprise-demo)** — one cluster hosting two independently
delivered environments, a real application in each, and a signed receipt proving what was built.
About 40 minutes, most of it waiting for a cluster. Pick a cloud when you get there; Hetzner is the
cheapest by a wide margin.

records.title: Tutorials
records.heading: Before any of them
records.text:
- The [CLI installed](/cli/installation) and `alethia login` done.
- An account on one cloud, with permission to create clusters and networks in it.
- A [runner](/runner) — `alethia runner register` if you will run one yourself, which works on any
 cloud, or `alethia fleet set` for a managed one.

 
 These tutorials **provision real infrastructure and cost real money.** Every one ends with a
 teardown step, and none of them is finished until you have run it. The per-cloud pages give a
 cost-per-hour figure so you can decide before you start rather than after.
